"Perception" (*saṃjñā*) means mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Thus, the conviction regarding one's own and others' welfare is of the highest-middle degree.
Furthermore, from the words "Moreover" (*punaraparam*) until the end of the chapter is the eighteenth [section].
The excellence of practice (*caryātireka*) is as stated in the Sūtra.
Thus, the resolve for the welfare of oneself and others (*svaparārthādhimukti*) is the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātrādhimātrā*).
"Immeasurable," and so forth.
Here, "stūpa" refers to a *caitya*,
and "perfection" (*pāramitā*) refers to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Upholding is of two kinds: first, making it exist in the form of a book and placing it externally for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma; second, establishing it within oneself through means such as receiving, memorizing, and so forth.
That which possesses immeasurable qualities is called "the one possessing immeasurable qualities. That which is so described and is also a *pāramitā*—that and the *stūpa* form a *dvandva* compound.
The "veneration" (*satkāra*) of those two is worship with flowers and other offerings.
The chapter that designates this is the "Chapter on the Veneration of the Stūpa that Holds Immeasurable Qualities."
The third chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.

4. The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Qualities. Resolutions have been the subject; therein, nine [resolutions] for one's own benefit and nine indeed for the benefit of both oneself and others have been taught.
In this section, however, exactly nine points for the sake of others (parārtha) are to be stated.
Among them, the nineteenth ends with the words "in the relics of the Tathāgatas.
It is precisely the Perfection of Wisdom that is absolutely worthy of worship because it is the Dharma-body.

Likewise, regarding the meaning that the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is the body of truth (*satyakāya*), the faith and serene confidence (*śraddhā-prasāda*) therein, as well as the excellence of measure understood through its functional capacity, constitute here the excellence of practice (*caryātireka*).
The "relics" (*dhātu*) of the Tathāgatas' bodies [are so called];
the genitive case is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
It is filled by them. Is it merely by pervasion? No, he says:
"bound together like a topknot."
"It would be given" means it would be proposed;
"being invited by one of the two" means being entreated with the words, "Take one of these two."
"Treating it as a wonder" means an exceeding degree of reverence;
for the Blessed Lady is indeed more venerable than those [other relics],
since this is her very body.
That which is the perfection of wisdom is the true object and the reality;
because it is conjoined with that, it is "possessing the true object."
It is called *sat* because it perishes (*sīdati*);
it is impermanent. This body is a *satkāya*, meaning a perishable body, specifically the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of the perfection of the *dharmakāya*":
here, "dharma" refers to the noble path (*āryamārga*),
and that which has reached its ultimate excellence is none other than the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
It is not impermanent because it is eternal as a continuum.
Regarding the phrase "manifested by the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*): *bhūta* refers to realities; their *koṭi* is the pinnacle or summit.
Because there is no reality superior to that,
[the Buddha] is manifested and expressed within that very [reality] due to identity with it.
To the question "Which body is it?", he says:
"Namely," and so forth.
The meaning is that the *prajñāpāramitā*, which perceives that [reality], is the ultimate truth consisting of mere suchness (*tathatā*) and is not distinct from it.
Is this then a lack of respect for the *tathāgata*-elements? No; he says:
The passage beginning with "not indeed" and so forth is easy to understand.
Thus ends the weakest of the weak degrees of conviction regarding the welfare of others.
The twentieth [verse] begins with "But rather" (*api tu*) and extends up to "let it be" (*tiṣṭhatu khalu*).
The word *api tu* has the sense of a qualification;
its meaning is: "even though I have respect for them, nevertheless..."
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is used because it was already mentioned as a qualifier previously.
Although "produced" (*nirjātāni*) functions as a qualifier, its nature as a reason is understood; the meaning is "because they have been produced.

The phrase beginning with "just as" (*tadyathāpīti*) provides an illustration. Because it serves as the location for the assembly of the gods, the "assembly of the gods" (*devasabhā*) is a great hall in which Śakra teaches the Dharma to the thirty-three [gods].
For this very reason, it is called Sudharmā. And as for this divine city of Sudarśana, in its southwestern quarter is the Great Man, Īṣā (or Śo).
Its designation is *pratibhāsa*, meaning "inclination.
One who possesses great branches (*mahatī śākhā*) is called *maheśākhya*;
the meaning is "one of great mind."
And here, that which is the nature of gnosis is the Perfectly Awakened One; its causal nature and conditional nature constitute the causes and conditions for him. Therefore, he said:
"Of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
In this context, the knowledge of the omniscient one is like that of Śakra;
the elements (dhātu) of the Tathāgata do not serve as its causes or conditions.
(RSt 45) Like the throne of Śakra,
in the former case it was the form-body (*rūpakāya*) itself that was described as the support of the body;
here, however, it serves as the seat for the knowledge-body (*jñānakāya*) of one who possesses great majesty.
In this sense, that which consists of faith and serene confidence is the excellence of practice;
thus, the resolute conviction for the sake of others is weak-middling.
From the words "let it be" up to "in the bodies of the Tathāgatas," this is the twenty-first [verse].
In this context, the faith and serene confidence regarding the majesty of the Blessed Lady as described here constitute the excellence of practice.
Thus, this is the weak-strong degree of resolute belief for the sake of others.
Furthermore, from the beginning up to the end of the Tathāgata’s relics, this is the twenty-second [point]:
for the Tathāgata, because he has transcended all worlds, is more worthy of worship and most worthy of worship; and he is the wisdom of omniscience.

Therefore, if the relics are worthy of worship because they serve as the support [for the Buddha], then his mother is even more worthy of worship than they; what need is there to mention the relics? Such is the meaning in which faith and the like constitute an excellence of practice.
This is the middling-mild degree of conviction regarding the welfare of others.

The twenty-third [section], beginning with "But rather... and ending with "...became vessels," should be understood through the analogy of the jewel described here as the qualities of the perfection of wisdom and the knowledge of the omniscient one (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Just as that jewel-casket remains desirable even when the jewel has been removed, so too is this case.

Thus, even though the Blessed One has entered final nirvāṇa, the Buddha remains as that alone through his qualities, and the relics continue to be worthy of worship; in this sense, there is an excellence of practice consisting of faith and so forth.
This is the middling-middling resolve for the welfare of others.

The twenty-fourth [verse], beginning with "And just as the Blessed One" and ending with "in the bodies of the Tathāgatas," [shows that] because it is born from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Dharma of the teaching is worthy of worship even when being expounded by others.

And just as a king’s official, by virtue of the king’s majesty, is fearless and honored everywhere, so too, because they are born from the perfection of wisdom and by virtue of its majesty, the relics are worthy of worship. In this sense, there is an abundance of merit, and faith and the other [faculties] constitute an abundance of practice.
Thus is the medium-superior conviction regarding the welfare of others.

The twenty-fifth [verse], ending with "by means of 'api tu' and so forth... worship is performed," concerns the fact that by worshipping the Bhagavatī, the Tathāgatas of the three times become worshipped; in this sense, faith and the other [faculties] constitute an excellence of practice. Thus is the superior-mild resolve for the welfare of others.
Furthermore, from the words "Moreover" (*punaraparam*) up to "sees" (*paśyati*), the twenty-sixth [verse] is presented.

The meaning is that it is the Blessed Mother alone who, by way of the *dharmatā* (true nature) of the Tathāgatas of the three times, is the revealer; in this regard, faith and so forth constitute the excellence of practice.
The point is that *dharmatā* is the *dharmakāya*, and that is none other than the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Even before Śakra had finished speaking, the Blessed One said, "It is so," and so forth,
up to "I too have fully awakened.
The word *āgamya* means having reached or having taken as a cause.
By this much, it has been stated that the Blessed Lady is the cause of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), but not that she is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
To indicate this further, Śakra said:
"The Great Perfection" (*mahāpāramitā*), and so forth.
"He understands correctly" means that he knows by means of non-proliferated (niṣprapañca) gnosis.
"He sees clearly" means that he sees in all its aspects. To make this clear, the Blessed One said:
"Thus it is," and so forth;
this is the superior-middle conviction regarding the welfare of others.
Now, from the words "Then indeed Śakra" until the end of the chapter is the twenty-seventh [section].
The entirety of the Mahāyāna is subsumed by the perfections (*pāramitās*).

Among these, the Blessed Mother (the *Prajñāpāramitā*) is preeminent because she is the precursor and the subsumer; in this sense, there is an excellence of practice consisting of faith and the other [faculties].
"Embraced by skill in means" is the brief statement (*udddeśa*);
"dedicated toward the knowledge of all aspects through the perfection of wisdom" is the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*).
In that regard, the analogies for the perfections by nature are various trees, such as those with diverse flowers and so forth.
However, the single flavor of their shadow—being embraced by skillful means—is the illustration.
Thus, the conviction regarding the welfare of others is the highest of the high.
Because the Perfection of Wisdom is the subject at hand, this chapter is so named as it is a proclamation of its qualities.
This is the fourth chapter of the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
5. The fifth chapter, titled "The Section on Merit.
It has been stated that "activity and resolute belief" have been explained; now "praise, laudation, and eulogy" must be discussed. "Praised" (*stuta*) refers to the act of praising (*suti*).
"Stobhitam" means praise; it is derived from the root *sub* with the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
"Śaṃsaḥ" means the act of praising (*śaṃsanam*).
One who possesses that [quality] is a "śaṃsī"; the state of being such is "śaṃsitā," meaning one who praises.
Therefore, the scripture says:
[50] Praise, exaltation, and commendation regarding the perfection of wisdom are held to consist of three sets of nine degrees of resolute conviction.

The meaning is that the resolve regarding the *prajñāpāramitā* previously mentioned—divided into those for one's own benefit, for both, and for the benefit of others—consists of three sets of nine resolves.
The manifestation of its virtues is intended "by means of three sets of nine" [qualities] respectively;
the singular form in the phrase "praise (*stuti*), exaltation (*stobha*), and commendation (*praśaṃsā*)" is used because each of these terms is connected individually with the preceding.
In that regard, the distinctions of weak, middling, and intense in the manifestation of qualities are praise (*stuti*), eulogy (*stobha*), and laudation (*praśaṃsā*). Furthermore,
the meaning is that these also have ninefold subdivisions— three groups of three— ranging from the weakest of the weak up to the most intense of the intense.
Of these, there are two causes: the Bodhisattva’s power to accomplish the welfare of others and his preeminence in the welfare of others.
Among them, the first begins from the words "Furthermore" up until "In this regard.
In this [first stage], the Bodhisattva’s resolve (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the three objects is more firmly established, which constitutes his power to accomplish the welfare of others.

Regarding the instruction on what is to be done, Śakra first speaks—beginning with "He who... and ending with "...should have faith"—concerning the qualities of the Blessed Lady and his own duty toward her.
The grammatical connection is: "O Blessed One, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family should have faith."
To the question "What should one have faith in?", he says:
"This," and so forth, which includes everything.
One should listen to and take up this Perfection of Wisdom with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*).
"Until there is no deficiency in the guidance"—how so? He says:
"having generated the mind for the sake of awakening, for the sake of awakening."
Of what kind is his serene mind? It is toward this very [object]. How so? By means of resolute conviction (*adhimucya*), having ascertained it absolutely as being non-erroneous.
And to show that this is done "by means of faith," he says:
"having full confidence and being convinced of this very [truth]."
The suffix *śatṛ* is used here in the sense of the causal agent;
that is to say, by means of this very faith. It is called "intention" (*āśaya*) because wholesome qualities rest (*āśerate*) within it.
It is like a reservoir of water.
Furthermore, it consists of faith and aspiration. An *adhyāśaya* is a superior, excellent intention (*āśaya*).
Therefore, one should hear it both in its textual form and in its meaning;
one should grasp it, recite it,
and retain it— that is, establish it in one's heart.
"Should recite" means he should cause others to recite; "should master" means he should understand it in every respect. By this much, his own purpose has been stated.
"One should cause [it] to proceed" means one should transmit it to others;
this is the summary (uddesa), and the following is the detailed explanation (nirdeśa).
One should "expound" by means of the words;
one should "teach" by means of the meaning;
one should "point out," that is, provide instruction.
The benefit for others is of such magnitude;
therefore, one should study [the text] with even greater diligence,
practicing it repeatedly because it accomplishes one's own welfare.
"And he should reveal it to others" means he should constantly reveal it by way of the text; "in detail" means by revealing it to many;
"he should explain" likewise refers to "in detail."

"One should examine with the mind" means that having understood through the consciousness and joined [the object], one should see; this is because of the arising of calm abiding (*śamatha*). "Thorough investigation" means because of the arising of insight (*vipaśyanā*) through analytical inquiries.
By this much, the practice has been described.
To state an alternative in the absence of this,
he says "the book," and so forth.
For this very reason, there is the word "even" (*antaśaḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "contained in a book," it means that one should uphold this very [teaching].
One should make it imperishable;
"one should establish" means in one's own home or similar location.
[This is done] with three aspirations.
The Noble Ones are peaceful;
their path of Dharma is the True Dharma (saddharma). Its long endurance is [the purpose].
"For that cause" means for that purpose;
for this [teaching] is common [to all].
This first aspiration, "the true Dharma," is directed toward all noble ones (ārya).
The Buddhas are the teachers of the world, and we ought to be grateful to them. This is their guidance, this wisdom that brings about the attainment of enlightenment;
having produced it through exertion over three incalculable eons, they have established it within their own lineage for the sake of future generations.
(RSt 48) "As long as she has not come to us, let there be no severance of the Buddha's guidance"— thinking thus, one should establish her as well.
This is the second aspiration concerning the Buddhas.
Furthermore, one must provide assistance and support to the bodhisattvas;
and that shall be accomplished through this stability and the non-deficiency of the guidance.
"Thus one should establish this"—this third aspiration is directed toward the bodhisattvas.
The word "iti" (thus) is also connected with what precedes, [meaning] "lest [it be otherwise].
By this much, the twofold instruction on what is to be done has been stated.
"This instruction" refers to the teaching on what is to be done.
"Thus it is of great benefit," and so forth:
it is called "of great benefit" because its purpose and activity are great.
This is the summary; the following is the detailed explanation;
"great benefit" refers to the benefits as they have been described.
It has great fruit by way of being a stream-enterer,
a once-returner, and a non-returner.
By means of arhatship,
by means of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and by means of perfect enlightenment.
"Great fruition through all miraculous powers and manifestations;
endowed with many great qualities"—this is the concluding summary.
By this much, the qualities of the Blessed Lady have been described.
They are not to be abandoned because they have been acquired and should not be relinquished;
they must be protected against fire, mice, and the like,
and they must be guarded against thieves and the like.
Because it is extremely difficult to obtain;
by this much, what one must do oneself has been stated.
"Thus" means that one should have faith in these three points.
One should determine it to be exactly thus.
And if there were no engagement [in activity], resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) would not be firm.
Therefore, by this much, the capacity for accomplishing the welfare of others has been explained.
When that [faith] exists, he who does not perform even a small amount of benefit for others, or performs only a small amount, possesses little merit;
the other, compared to him, possesses much greater merit.
These are his praises, hymns, and eulogies.
Therefore, from the words "by himself indeed" (*svayameva*) up to "the second birth" (*dvitīyaprasavati*), there is the first praise.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "by oneself alone" (*svayam eva ca*) serves to draw back the word "who" (*yaḥ*);
it does not, however, [refer to] honors from others (*paraiḥ pūjām*).
The meaning of the particle *eva* is "causes [others] to do.
"Having honored" means having performed all forms of worship.
"Arthana" means "requesting."
"Desirous" (*arthikāya*) refers to one who has the wish for worship; "eager" (*chandikāya*) refers to one who possesses that [wish] to an exceptional degree;
"supplicating" (*yācamānāya*) refers to one who is entreating the Blessed Lady in order to perform worship.
"One should give" means one should agree; "one should offer" means one should bring together; "one should deliver" means one should cause to be received.
One should relinquish it without regret;
"even unto the end" means to that extent.

"Having even made it into a book" means having written it oneself, or having had it written by another, or having had it transcribed for its price or for one's own cost; "relinquishment" means giving it away, and "one whose intellect/intention is directed toward that" refers to one who has the desire to do so.
"One should reveal" means [reveal it] both by way of its qualities and its essential nature.
"One should give" means for the purpose of worship. "One should share" means by giving to those who are more extensive or to those who are spreading [the teaching].
"Vistāra" means extensiveness; that which proceeds by means of it is "vaistārikī. "Pratyātmam" means by oneself alone.
The remainder is easily understood.
Thus ends the "mild-mild" praise.
Furthermore, that which begins with "punaraparam" and precedes the next "punaraparam" constitutes the second [section].
The word "tat" refers to that which was praised first;
thus ends the praise of the mild-moderate degree.
Furthermore, from "another" up to the word "remain," the third case [is used].
"Should cause to undertake" means one should cause them to correctly grasp [the precepts];
"should establish" means by way of non-transgression.
"Having full faith" means having faith in the qualities of the Blessed Lady;
otherwise, one would not be a proper donor. "Having full faith" means...
Otherwise, he would not be a worthy recipient of gifts;
this should be understood in the same way for the subsequent cases as well.
*Kilāsitā* means one who is indolent (*kusīda*).
Vigor is tirelessness;
by means of it, one should accomplish the task as described.
Being diligent and devoted, one should cause this Bodhisattva to grasp the Blessed Lady.
One should demonstrate it through speech as being the means for accomplishing enlightenment;
likewise, one should show it by means of logical arguments;
and thereafter, one should encourage others to undertake it through activities such as recitation and worship.
One should encourage and inspire those who have already engaged [in practice] by explaining the virtues of vigor and the faults of laziness;
one should gladden those who have initiated vigor with words of praise.
If it is argued that this is not possible because the world is deluded, he says "speech," and so forth.
The world is of three kinds: the faithful, the averse, and the indifferent.
In that case, he will lead away the faithful merely by his speech;
for he departs from one who is highly esteemed solely through his words,
and he will cause him to perish while turning his face away.
By refuting the wrong views [of others] through reasoning, he will lead those who are indifferent toward [the teaching];
he will cause them to take delight by proclaiming the virtues of the Blessed One.
Thus, having been made into a worthy vessel, whoever shall reveal its meaning to him [will succeed].
When this meaning has been thus elucidated, he will purify the mind of this person by refuting those with wrong views;
furthermore, he will render one who still harbors doubt free from uncertainty through other lines of reasoning.
"Train yourself in the three trainings.
He explains this very point with the words "For here," and so forth;
[it means] training by means of reflection.
Exerting oneself through tranquility (*śamatha*), which is capable of [stabilizing] conduct, and through insight (*vipaśyanā*),
one [perceives] the realm of sentient beings, the mass of sentient beings.
Because it is ultimate, it is unsurpassed.
The "substrata" (upadhi) are the aggregates (skandhas), whether they are with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava).
Their complete exhaustion is the total destruction of them all.
For that reason,
you will attain mastery through the destruction of all obscurations;
the realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is the state in which only that remains.
"By means of the thought of renunciation" means by means of the thought of renunciation in all its aspects.
"From that" refers to the second [stage], because it is praised and because it establishes one in the ten wholesome paths of action.
This is the praise for the weak-intense [level].
From this point onward, the first part [of these five praises] consists of the section beginning with "tiṣṭhantu" and ending with "pratiṣṭhāpayet.
Thereafter, the second part begins with "tat kiṃ manyase" and extends up to, but not including, "punar aparaṃ.

In these passages spoken in the Sūtra, there is an abundance of merit, as well as an abundance of faith and so forth, an abundance of capacity understood through implication, and an abundance of conduct.
"By this method" means by way of abiding in the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the three objects.
Thus, in due order, there is praise that is middling-weak, middling-middling, middling-strong, strong-weak, and strong-middling.
From "punaraparam" up to before "punaraparam," there are five [sections] ending with the ninth;
this is because only a single ninth [section] is designated in sequence.
If it is argued that even so, there is a great difference between [this] and the eighth [section]:
This is not a fault;
it is like [the merit of] as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges within a single world-system.
Through the excellence of faith and so forth, there is an excellence of practice beyond the merit described in the sūtras.
Deficient passages are to be completed by means of what precedes and follows.

Regarding "in the four dhyānas," the Sūtra states here: "Detached from sensual desires, detached from unwholesome and evil states, he, possessing applied thought and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of detachment and characterized by rapture and pleasure."

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal clarity and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness.

With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, "He who has equanimity and is mindful dwells in happiness. Thus, he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna, which is devoid of rapture.

“With the abandoning of pleasure and with the previous abandoning of pain, and with the disappearance of elation and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.”
"Secluded from sensual desires" means:
because of the non-association with the desire for afflictions (*kleśa-kāma*),
and because of the non-apprehension of objects as sensual desires (*vastu-kāma*).
"Secluded from evil, unwholesome states" means secluded from the misconduct of body,
speech, and mind caused by afflictions and sensual desires.
"Accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought" [is as follows].
Because it is associated with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), which are the antidotes to sensual desire;
"born of seclusion" means born from seclusion from sensual desire.

"Accompanied by joy and bliss" means that, due to the accomplishment of desired aims and the pliancy of body and mind, it is accompanied by joy and bliss. "Having attained the first dhyāna" means having entered into meditative absorption.
"He dwells" means he experiences [it];
"he" refers to that very same practitioner.
Having seen the fault in applied and sustained thought—that they cause agitation of the mind—he turns the mind away from them and composes it.
"Through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought" means by the power of meditative concentration;
"through the one-pointedness of the mind" means through the non-occurrence of applied and sustained thought without interruption.
"Without applied thought and without sustained thought" means that those [two] have been abandoned in every respect.
"Through detachment from joy" means through detachment from that [joy] which is coarse.
"Equanimous" means because of the relinquishing of applied thought, sustained thought, and joy.
"Possessing mindfulness and clearly comprehending" [is added].
Because of the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā-bahulīkāra*) in order to provide manifold opportunities for joy,
there is "happiness" (*sukha*); that is, the happiness of feeling (*vedita-sukha*) and the happiness of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*).
"By the body" means by the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the mind-body (*manaḥkāya*). "The noble ones" (*āryāḥ*)— means:
The disciples and the Buddhas,
up to those who dwell in happiness—
this very person is that meditator; this is the remainder [of the statement].
In that regard, the abandoning of pleasure occurs through the fourth dhyāna,
and the abandoning of suffering through the first;
for this very reason, it was said:
"Even previously" means:
by the third [member] for mental pleasure (saumanasya),
and by the second for mental pain (daurmanasya).
Because of the continuation of the phrase "precisely as before," equanimity itself is the feeling (*vedanā*) here;
therefore, he says:
Regarding "neither-painful-nor-pleasant":
this is because those two have attained ultimate purification here.
In that regard, the first dhyāna has five factors:
applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the factors of the antidote;
joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) are the factors of benefit.
One-pointedness of mind is the factor that serves as the basis for both of those.
The second [dhyāna] has four factors:
internal serenity is the factor of the antidote;
the remaining factors are as before.
The third [dhyāna] has five factors:
equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension are the factors of the antidote; and bliss is the factor of benefit.
The limb of reliance is as previously described.
The fourth [dhyāna] has four factors:
purity of equanimity is the factor of the antidote;
neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the factor of benefit.
The limb of reliance is as before.
One should establish them in these four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*);
the rest is as before. This is the highest-of-the-high praise.
Furthermore, the first *stobha* begins with "another" (*punarapara*) and ends with "manifestation" (*prabhavanatā*).
The filling of the deficiency is as before.

One should establish [beings] in the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*), up to all the meditative concentrations, immeasurables, formless attainments, and superknowledges together.
The meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) have been explained.
The four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and have sentient beings as their object.
The four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) have immeasurable sentient beings as their object.

These are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Through these modes— namely, "O, may all sentient beings be endowed with happiness," "may they be separated from suffering," "may they not be separated from happiness," and "may they be liberated from afflictions"— there arise the intention for union with happiness, the intention for separation from suffering, the intention for non-separation from happiness, and the intention for the absence of affliction.
On the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), all four [types of compassion] have sentient beings as their object;

on the seven stages beginning with the Joyful (*pramuditā*), they have suchness (*tathatā*) as their object; and on the Immovable (*acalā*) and subsequent stages, they are without an object (*anālambana*).

Regarding the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the Sūtra states: "With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*)— vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, free from ill-will, unobstructed, unhindered, all-pervading, well-cultivated— he dwells having suffused and attained one direction, the entire world, as far as the limit of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the end of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*)."
He dwells having pervaded and attained [this state] as far as the ten directions;
likewise with that which is accompanied by compassion,
and likewise with that which is accompanied by sympathetic joy.
"In this way, with that which is accompanied by equanimity."
In that context, "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness" is a description of the possessor of qualities;
the remainder [of the passage] refers to the qualities themselves.
"Vast" indicates greatness in terms of intention.
"By the great" means by way of increase;
"by the immeasurable" means by way of the object;
"by the non-dual" means by way of having a single nature due to being free from conceptual construction.
"By being without enmity" means through the abandonment of opposing factors (*vipakṣa*).
In this regard, the opposing factors of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others are, respectively:
malice (*vyāpāda*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), and dissatisfaction (*arati*).
And there are attraction and aversion.
"By being perfected" means through the subsiding of sloth and torpor;
"by being unobstructed" means through the subsiding of restlessness and remorse.
"By non-affliction" means that the mind is free from turbidity by means of these very three qualities.
"Pervading everywhere" means that it functions toward all three—friends, neutrals, and enemies. "Well-cultivated" means that it functions with equanimity toward all three.
"Having pervaded" means having suffused in the manner described.
"The world" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
"Entirely" means endowed with all its various divisions, such as gods, *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, and so forth.
"One direction" means extending toward a single direction.
To the question "Where?", he says:
"In the world," that is, in the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*), "as far as the limit of the dharma-realm."
"Endless as the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)" means that its limit is like that of the realm of space (ākāśadhātu); thus it is so described.
"Having attained, he dwells" means that having concentrated his mind, he dwells in the noble dwelling (āryavihāra).
"In the ten directions" means those situated in the ten directions;
the rest is easily understood.

The formless attainments are the four formless [realms]. Regarding them, the Sūtra states: "By completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] 'space is infinite,' one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space."
“By completely transcending the perception of the sphere of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
By completely transcending the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing at all,’ he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness.
By completely transcending the perception of the sphere of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
The perceptions of form are the perceptions of blue, yellow, and so forth.
For one who is detached from them, because of the cultivation of the perception of space everywhere,
there is the transcendence of those [perceptions] due to their non-appearance.
"Of perceptions of resistance" refers to perceptions of obstructions such as walls and enclosures.
"Of perceptions of diversity" refers to perceptions of palaces, gardens, mountains, rivers, the moon, the sun, and so forth.
It is described thus because its objective support (*ālambana*) is the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), characterized by the thought, "Space is infinite."
How is there the transcendence of the sphere of infinite space?

By means of that very knowledge through which he was resolved upon the sphere of infinite space, he resolves upon that same [knowledge] as infinite; thus, by turning away the perception of space everywhere, there is the transcendence of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Having emerged from that, he perceives no object whatsoever—neither an external referent nor consciousness.
Taking non-possession (*akiñcanatā*) itself as his object, he enters meditative absorption;
this is because he has transcended the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).
Having become detached even from the perception of nothingness (*ākiñcanyasaṃjñā*), he turns that away as well;
the perception of something (*kiñcanasaṃjñā*) had already ceased previously.
Therefore, there is neither perception (*naiva saṃjñā*).
However, subtle perception (*saṃjñā*) does indeed arise from that; therefore, it is not "without perception" (*asaṃjñā*).
That meditative absorption (*samādhāna*) in which there is neither perception nor non-perception is described as such.
[There are also] the five supernormal knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
Knowledge of the methods of supernormal power,
the divine ear,
and knowledge of the minds of others.
The knowledge of recollecting past lives and the divine eye.
Regarding this, the Sūtra says: "He experiences various kinds of supernormal powers."
He causes even the earth to tremble;
having been one, he becomes many;
and having been many, he becomes one.
He experiences both manifestation and disappearance;
he passes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and even through mountains;
he also traverses the sky.
"He performs the acts of emerging and submerging even in the earth;
he walks upon water as if on earth; he even smokes and he even blazes," and so forth in detail.
With the divine ear-element, which transcends that of humans, he hears sounds—both divine and human.
He also knows, as it truly is, the minds of other beings and other persons with his own mind;

that is to say, he knows as it truly is a mind with passion as being with passion, a mind free from passion as being free from passion, a mind with hatred as being with hatred, a mind free from hatred as being free from hatred, and a mind with delusion as being with delusion, or a mind free from delusion as being free from delusion.
He understands, as it truly is, up to the unsurpassed mind; he recollects one birth, two, three... [births].
He recollects even hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of births;

he recollects one day, two, three, up to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. He remembers: "In that place, I had such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such a long duration of life, and such a limit to my lifespan."

Having passed away from there, he remembers his various former abodes in their many aspects—where he was reborn, and having passed away from there, how he came to be reborn here—along with their modes, locations, and specific characteristics.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings—those passing away and those being reborn; he discerns beings who are beautiful and ugly, lowly and exalted, in happy destinies and miserable destinies, according to their karma.
"These worthy beings were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; they did not revile the noble ones and possessed right view."

By reason of that wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, upon the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods. But these beings, friends, being possessed of misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind,

revilers of the noble ones and holders of wrong views, by reason of undertaking actions based on wrong views, after the dissolution of the body, following death, [fall] into a state of deprivation, a bad destination, and ruin.
“They are reborn in the hells.

For with the divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, he knows, as it truly is, the passing away and rebirth of beings belonging to the six destinies throughout the worlds in the ten directions—in all world-systems that reach the limit of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and extend to the end of the realm of space (ākāśadhātu). Thus [it is said].

The connection is that one should establish [beings] in these meditative concentrations (dhyāna), immeasurables (apramāṇa), formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), and supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), both individually and collectively.
The remainder is easily understood; thus ends the first encomium (stobha).

From this point onward, the [stobhas] beginning with *tiṣṭha* and ending with *pratiṣṭhāpaya*, each joined respectively with the section beginning with "What do you think of that? (*tat kiṃ manyase*) and ending with "manifestation" (*prabhāvanatā*), constitute the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth stobhas.
Thus, there are the soft-moderate, the soft-intense, the moderate-soft, the moderate-moderate, and the moderate-intense stobhas.
The seventh [chapter], from "Furthermore" (*punaraparam*) up to "Furthermore" (*punaraparam*).
Giving to others after the two Blessed Ladies (*bhagavatī*) also exists in the preceding [chapters].
However, here, both reciting oneself and giving to others after having written it down constitute an excellence of practice; thus, this is the "very great, mild" stage of rejoicing (*stobha*).

From "Furthermore" up to "before the eighth," it was previously stated that one should explain the meaning of this [verse]; that was intended with reference to the coarse form of the perfections and so forth which inspires faith in those who are resistant.
Here, however, he speaks with reference to the ultimate truth, beginning with the non-apprehension of the three limits.
"From one skilled in the meaning," and so forth.
In that context, "recitation by one skilled in the meaning" means reciting while keeping that very meaning in mind.
"Together with the meaning" means accompanied by that very meaning.
"With the phrasing" (*savyañjanam*) means that the phrasing (*vyañjana*) is that which expresses the very meaning [of the teaching].
One should "teach" (*upadiśet*) by means of the *sūtra* because it flows together with that meaning;
one should "elucidate" (*paridīpayet*) it by means of logical arguments (*yuktibhiḥ*).
This is the eighth excellence of conduct.
"This" refers to one abiding in the eighth [stage].
"From that" refers to having proceeded from the seventh.
The question—"Should this also be taught?"—is posed through the use of intonation (*kāku*) or by means of the head and body.
The intended meaning is: "It should certainly not be taught, because [the recipient] is not clear [in his understanding].
The term "of one who does not understand" refers to one of dull intellect (*jaḍadhī*).
Because it has been correctly grasped through both reasoning and scripture, no one can shake it by means of another's words;
for who indeed could move this?
To explain this, he asks: "For what reason?"
To this, the following reply is given: "It will arise," and so forth.
That description of its meaning in a contrary manner by the Teacher himself, the Blessed One, is its counterfeit.
For by that very [word], there is the deception of the dull-witted and the faithful;
because of the rule stating "the suffix *ṇvuc* occurs in the senses of production, exchange, debt, and arising" (*utpattau ṇvuc paryāyārhaṛṇotpattiṣu ṇvuḥ*),
the word "therein" (*tatra*) means "that being so."

"May he not perish" means that he should not be lost or fallen away from the path to perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*). The root *ṇas* (or *śas*) in the sense of "disappearance" belongs to both the *radhādi* and *puṣādi* groups.

Therefore, although this is the formal application [of the rule], nevertheless, the augment *aṭ* and the *vṛddhi* substitution do not occur, because those two are prescribed for the *parasmaipada* endings.
And because a rule preceded by a specific designation is not universally applicable (*anityatva*),
both how this [perception] becomes a counterfeit and how it does not have been explained at length in the two great scriptures of the Blessed One:

"Whoever [perceives] form, feeling, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), through the application of signs (*nimittayoga*) by way of the aspects (*ākāra*) of impermanence, suffering, non-self, emptiness, and impurity..."
He who cultivates the perfection of wisdom by means of apprehension is cultivating it [falsely];
he will not attain the first bodhisattva stage, nor even the tenth, nor even unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Whoever teaches in this way teaches a counterfeit [teaching].
How will he not teach?
Form is empty of intrinsic nature;
and that which is the intrinsic nature of form is non-existence.
"That which is non-existence is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In it, even form does not exist; how then could there be permanence or impermanence? and so forth.
"He who teaches in this way will not be teaching a counterfeit [teaching]."
Therefore, here too, Śakra’s question beginning with “How, Blessed One,” and so forth, is for the sake of fully understanding the counterfeit [teachings];
the Blessed One’s reply begins with “They will exist, Kauśika,” and so forth.
The five material sense-faculties are called “bodies” (*kāya*) because they are comprised within the body, or because they are an accumulation of atoms.
Because they have not cultivated and have not practiced restraint, they are described as such; because their sense faculties are unrestrained, their ethical discipline (*śīla*) is uncultivated;
consequently, their minds are uncultivated and their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has not been practiced.
Therefore, those who have not cultivated wisdom possess only the knowledge of things as they truly are when their minds are concentrated;
consequently, those with poor wisdom hold perverted views.
Consequently, they are like the deaf-mute because they do not hear well-spoken words;
they are devoid of wisdom because their right view has been destroyed. "The impermanence of form" is an illustration;
suffering and the other [characteristics] are also to be understood in this way.
In the Mahāyāna, impermanence is the state of not being eternal;
the term "destruction" is employed for the purpose of excluding that [eternal state].
The meaning is that impermanence has the characteristic of destruction.
For there is no destruction of existing things, nor of those that have not yet arisen;
therefore, one who perceives destruction would find those dharmas as entities,
as well as their existence, arising, and destruction.

Thus, it is stated that the teaching of right view— which is comprised within the Lesser Vehicle— as being the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by way of being an antidote to the four perversions such as [the notion of] permanence, is merely a counterfeit of it. Now, as to whether or not a bodhisattva should cultivate the meditation on the impermanence, suffering, and so forth of these [phenomena] such as form, he says:
"Furthermore, not indeed," and so forth.
"Should be seen" means it should be cultivated.
To address the question, "If one were to cultivate it, what fault would there be?", he says:
"Sa cet" and so forth.
"In the counterfeit" (prativarṇikāyām) means in the Hīnayāna.
Thus, having briefly shown the counterfeit in this Bhagavatī, its practice is prohibited.
However, it was indicated from the very beginning that [this teaching] is not a mere counterfeit, by such statements as "one skilled in the meaning should recite it.

Furthermore, as an antidote to the misconceptions held by those who consider themselves Mahāyānists regarding terms such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), the activity of non-misconception (*aviparyāsa-kāritra*) was taught in the two great *Bhagavatīs* within the section on the activity of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

In this *Bhagavatī* as well, non-misconception has been clearly explained in the middle [of the text] in relation to the attainment of nirvāṇa, the departure toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the eightfold profundity.
Therefore, it must be determined from that very source.
Thus ends the intermediate-strong trembling.

Furthermore, from "another" up to "before another," five [stages] remain; the ninth is the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*). Thus it is manifested, and it is accomplished among sentient beings.
This is the intense shaking (*adhimātra-stobha*).
Furthermore, from "another further [point]" up to "prior to another further [point]," there are five standing in the first [position]:
the fruit of a once-returner.
Thus is the praise of the soft-soft [level].
From "Furthermore" up to "prior to the next," there are five instances of the second case-ending;
[this refers to] the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Thus ends the praise of the weak and middling [levels].
Furthermore, from "punaraparam" up to before "punaraparam," there are five [sections] which constitute the third [chapter]. Arhatship (*arhattva*) is the state of an Arhat.
Thus ends the praise of the weak-intense [level].

Furthermore, there is another [etymological derivation]: for those who abide [in their respective states], the fourth case ending is used first. A *buddha* is one who has awakened by himself; a *pratyekabuddha* is one who has awakened for himself alone.
Thus ends the middling praise.
"Let it be," and so forth with the five [terms], constitutes the fifth [degree].
Thus is the praise of the medium-medium degree.
Furthermore, before the subsequent [rules], the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies to two things that stand [in apposition].
"Someone" (*kaścid eva*) is the first;
"whoever" (*yaś ca*) is the second.
The third [alternative] is "or who knows. "Should offer" means he should give. To what [recipient], one asks, does he offer? It says:
"Right here," and so forth; "gone to increase" means having attained it; "this one" refers to the third.
"Therefore" refers to both the first and the second [stages].
This concludes the praise of the middling-superior level.
"Let it be; [let it be] with the fifth beginning with 'ādi'—this is the seventh [case]. Thus ends the praise of superior supernatural power (*adhimātra-ṛddhi*).
Furthermore, there is another [point]:
"O Blessed One, even the number [of such merits]," and so forth.
In that context, "number" refers to how the subsequent merit is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and so on, compared to the preceding merit.
Calculation (*gaṇanā*) refers to being multiplied tenfold, hundredfold, and so forth. Simile (*upamā*) refers to being multiplied by the number of sands in the Ganges River, and so forth.
Analogy (*aupamya*) refers to being multiplied by the number of sands in ten Ganges Rivers, and so forth.

"An *upaniṣad* is [a number] ten times a hundred Ganges-river-sands, and so forth. Since such a magnitude is absolutely impossible, the *upaniṣad* in that sense is 'sitting near' (to that number); even that is not easy to accomplish."
Thus ends the praise of the highest-middle degree.
The ninth [verse] begins with "Let it be" (*tiṣṭhatu*) and so forth.
With the words "Just as" (*yathā-yathā*) and so forth, Kauśika explains the arising of an abundance of merit.
With the words "Excellent, excellent! (*sādhu sādhu*) and so forth, Subhūti encourages him with supporting arguments.
Thus ends the highest-of-the-high praise.
The synonyms and divisions of merit; that which illuminates them is a "turning" (parivarta), and thus it is called a *puṇyaparyāyaparivarta*.
The fifth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
6. The sixth chapter, titled "The Immeasurable Nature of Rejoicing.
Praise, hymn, and eulogy have been explained;
now the mental application of dedication must be discussed.
Concerning this, the treatise states:
[51] "But its supreme activity is the transformation into distinction."
And this has the form of non-apprehension, characterized by the absence of error.
[52] It is solitary, the sphere of mindfulness whose nature is the flood of a Buddha’s merit;
it possesses skillful means, is signless, and is commended by the Buddhas. // 2-22 //
[53] Furthermore, there is another threefold dedication that does not enter into the triple world;
it consists of the mild, the medium, and the intense, and its nature is the arising of great merit. // 2-23 //

It is called a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) because by means of it, the flood of merit consisting of generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation belonging to all sentient beings is excelled and surpassed.
Furthermore, this consists in its being the cause of perfect awakening for the sake of preeminence among all sentient beings.

This is because of the reading in the two great [scriptures]: "Having made it common to all sentient beings, one dedicates it toward unsurpassed perfect awakening, and that by way of non-apprehension."
By that distinction, there is "transformation."
He said this to him, beginning with "Then indeed, Maitreya," and so forth. "Of a bodhisattva" means of one who has generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
He is a "Great Being" (mahāsattva) because he is distinguished by the aforementioned specific qualities; he is a "Great Being" because his resolve is directed toward dedication (pariṇāmanā).
"Accompanied by rejoicing" refers to the wholesome merit associated with rejoicing (anumodanā).
And that [dedication] will be explained in detail at the beginning of the dedication of non-apprehension;
it is the dedication of that [merit],
and it is accompanied by that [non-apprehension].

The phrase "this very [thing]" is connected with the subsequent term *puṇyakriyāvastu* (basis of meritorious action). From that— that is, from the merit consisting of giving and so forth belonging to all sentient beings— it is declared to be the foremost, up to being declared the unequaled-of-the-equal (*asamasama*).
Therefore, it is "foremost" (*agra*) and so forth;
because it is the cause for the foremost fruit and so forth.
Why is that?
This is because they are, respectively, the causes for the accomplishment of one's own and others' welfare as comprised within the eleven stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā).
Although all [the Buddhas] are synonymous, by virtue of their capacity for appropriation,
those Buddhas who have no equal possess a common excellence that is "equal to the unequaled" (asamasama).
On the stage of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā*);
how is it equal on the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*)? Because of its equality with the peerless.

“Because of the statement: ‘A bodhisattva who is a lord of the ten stages (daśabhūmīśvara) should be regarded as a Buddha indeed, but not as a perfectly enlightened one (samyaksaṃbuddha),’ thus, by means of the preceding text beginning with the words ‘supreme’ (agra) and so forth, the distinguished dedication (viśeṣapariṇāma) has been explained. Through those words beginning with ‘supreme,’ its ‘supreme activity’—the distinguished dedication together with its activity—is [described].”
With the words "When it was said thus," etc., he explains the transformation of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-pariṇāma*).
"In these ten directions" means in the world of the ten directions, that is,
in the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) which has the dimensions of space.
"From all sides" means in all those directions.
"By way of omnipresence" means by way of pervasiveness, that is to say, by way of density.
In the case of "immeasurable" and so forth, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is for the purpose of connecting [the qualities] individually with each of the directions.
"In infinite and boundless" means in those that are endless and limitless.
Thus, this is a repetition in meaning, not in words.
In that regard, they are immeasurable because the directions and locations cannot be delimited.
They are "innumerable" because they cannot be delimited by number;
they are "immeasurable" because they cannot be delimited by the vastness of space;
and they are "inconceivable" because they are impossible to contemplate individually.
They are "infinite" because they extend to the very end of those very thoughts.

Thus, in their entirety, in each of the infinite three-thousandfold world systems in every direction—referring to that single three-thousandfold system in each direction—the connection is: "of immeasurable and immeasurable Tathāgatas," up to "infinite and boundless."
Here too, the repetition [of "trisāhasra"] is for the purpose of connecting each individual [trichiliocosm];
if it is asked, "Is there not only one Tathāgata in a single trisāhasra, and not immeasurable ones and so forth? he says: "In the past time."
A Tathāgata exists at one time, but not at all times.

Furthermore, the past time is immeasurable because it is beginningless; therefore, even within a single world-system, there have been immeasurable Tathāgatas throughout the past time, as it cannot be delimited by the length of time. And they are "innumerable" (asaṃkhyeya) because they cannot be delimited by number.
They are immeasurable because they cannot be delimited by their vastness when established transversely by the mind;
they are inconceivable because they cannot be conceived one by one;
they are infinite because there is no reaching an end even when considering them one by one.
"Of such Tathāgatas who have entered parinirvāṇa," but not while they are still remaining [in the world].
"Arhats" because they have slain their enemies, which are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Perfectly Awakened Ones" (*samyaksambuddha*) because of their knowledge of all phenomena (*dharma*) without error.
By these two phrases, the perfection of abandonment and knowledge is expressed.
Because it is the path of existence (*bhavapatha*), there is the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) regarding this Dharma;
the suffix *ni* is used in the sense of "obstructing" (*vṛti*).
It is like a reservoir that holds water;
furthermore,
the augment *muṭ* is applied because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the path to existence (*bhava*).

As it has been said: "The conceit 'I am' (asmimāna) is called the father, and craving (tṛṣṇā) is called the mother. Because these two have been uprooted, they are those for whom the path is severed and those whose paths are cut off.
Proliferation (prapañca) is the conceptualization of duality.
"Bhava" means cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Their two guides or leaders are, respectively, the view of phenomena (*dharma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of persons (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*).
Through the complete exhaustion of these two, they have severed the guide to cyclic existence characterized by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and have dried their tears.
When there is no further becoming, there is no further bondage, no sorrow, and no tears; therefore, for those whose tears are completely exhausted,
"thorns" refers to wrong views, because they share the same nature as thorns.
Because they have crushed them, their thorns are trampled;
the remainder has already been explained in the *Nidāna*.
The first production of the thought [of awakening] is like the earth.
"Taking that as the basis" means starting from that point; "in this interval" means within such a span of time;
"the aggregate of morality and so forth" refers to the mass of morality and the other perfections.
Bodhisattvas also possess powers and so forth,
but they have not reached the further shore;
therefore, the term "perfection" (pāramitā) is employed to exclude them.
The untainted path is thorough knowledge;
the wisdom of omniscience is perfect enlightenment.
Previously, these were associated with the qualities of a Buddha and so forth.
With the words "And those who... and so forth, he also speaks of the qualities of the Buddha and others.
Perfectly complete enlightenment itself is bliss because it is the bliss of tranquility. Sovereignty over all phenomena is mastery (*vaśitā*).
The manifestation of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is an activity;
it is unobstructed because of its purity,
and it is unattached because of its independence.
It is unimpeded because it functions with respect to all objects of knowledge in all their aspects;
it is incomparable because there exists no illustrative example for its specific characteristics that could serve as a basis for inference;
and its "measure" (*parimāṇa*) consists in its complete delimitation.
Direct perception grasps form without any intervening obstacles whatsoever;
because others do not exist within it, it is immeasurable.
Such is the Tathāgatas’ knowledge of things as they truly are, their correct cognition.
That very power is so called because it overcomes all;
that which is called the "power of Buddha-knowledge" is the strength and capacity of Buddha-knowledge for performing the welfare of the world in every way and without limit.
The connection is as follows: it is the Buddhas' vision through knowledge (*jñānadarśana*) regarding the powers (*balāni*), which is the attainment and realization;
it is the realization of one's own qualities (*svadharmāṇām*) that is perfectly fulfilled by the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and it is the realization of the Dharma.
How is that [realization]? It is through the production—that is, the accomplishment—of the correct knowledge of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena (*sarvadharmāṇām*).
The Dharma is supramundane gnosis characterized by three turnings and twelve aspects. That itself is the wheel because it moves among gods and humans;
its setting in motion occurs throughout the ten directions.
This is the summary;
its detailed explanation consists of nine members.
The speech that illuminates that very Dharma is called "the teaching of the Dharma."
Its grasping is the mental stabilization [of that speech].
That very speech is the drum of the Dharma; its striking is the proclamation of victory to those to be trained.
Or rather, that very [emptiness] is the Dharma-conch;
its filling is the knowledge possessed by those to be trained;
and its sounding is the proclamation of that Dharma-conch.
Taking that very [object] as the focal point and attending to it with the mental aspect of its meaning, there is the perfection of reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

That supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*) which arises through the power of cultivation is itself the "sword of Dharma" (*dharma-khaṅga*). Striking with it is the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The activity of that very [Buddha] among many people is the rain of Dharma;
its pouring down is the sacrifice itself, because it is free from obstruction.
Its sacrifice is the warming,
the welcoming, and the serving of all sentient beings through the gift of that Dharma;
they are disciplined by means of the foundations of mindfulness.
They have been introduced to the truths; they are trained in the right efforts and the bases of psychic power;
and they are resolved through the faculties and powers because of their absolute certainty.
"Fixed because they do not turn back" refers to the assembly of Buddhas; this is a genitive of different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
The term *parinirvāpayatām* [is used] because the root *okh-* means "to dry up.
Regarding the phrase *buddhānām asya*: having made these [beings] the field of the Buddhas, there is mental cultivation (*mānasa-bhāvanā*) and delight (*rañjana*).
Those which are beneficial for that [cultivation] are "to be cultivated by the mind" (*manobhāvanīya*), meaning they are those which produce serene confidence (*prasāda*).
The connection is that one should rejoice "without remainder" and "without exception.
"In a single mass" means as a single heap. "Having condensed" is explained by the terms "having gathered together" and "having weighed together."
"With a concentrated mind" means having examined with the mental faculty;
"should rejoice" means one should take joy as the object;
"by means of rejoicing" means by means of generating joy.
"By 'foremost' (agrayā) is meant by means of excellence.
How, then, are there eleven terms?
Because of its excellence even with respect to the elevenfold objects of focus."
Why is that? Because it has as its object the roots of merit belonging to those Tathāgatas who reside in the ten directions in the interim, together with their retinues.
To explain how one dedicates [the merit], it says:
"May it become a bringer and an attractor of enlightenment."
Thus, with the words "Having spoken thus," and so forth, the Elder Subhūti has explained in detail how he rejoices and how a bodhisattva dedicates [merit].
However, in order to demonstrate how the yoga of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) should be practiced therein, he asks the Noble Maitreya with the words "Therein... and so forth.
By the phrase "by which things," he refers to the Tathāgatas and others in the ten directions.
"By those objects" means by those roots of virtue belonging to him;
"by those aspects" means by the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and so forth;
"that mind" refers to the mind of sympathetic joy.
"But rather" (*api tu*) means "however.
"They would be perceived" (*upalabhyeran*) is an optative used in the sense of possibility;
the question is whether they are capable of being perceived.
"To take as a sign" means to conceptualize;
otherwise, rejoicing and dedication would be impossible.
The noble Maitreya said: "They are not those," and so forth. The Elder said:
"In that case, they would be misconceptions."

Because of the grasping, the apprehension, and the determination of a sign (nimitta) that is actually non-existent, there occurs, respectively, the perversion (viparyāsa) of perception, mind, and view.
Passion (rāga) is the example for the purpose of establishing these; furthermore, the phrase "even so" anticipates the opinion of another, the sense being: "as is the yakṣa, so is the offering."
"Mind" refers to the mind of dedication;
"all phenomena" is the brief statement,
and "all realms" is the detailed explanation.
With the words "And if," etc., he states the fault:
"By which things and so forth? [The answer is:
by those connected with the mind of rejoicing.
“Mind” refers to the mind of dedication;
since that too is devoid of intrinsic nature, [the question] “where? means “in what?”
The intended meaning is that there would be no dedication (pariṇāmanā) whatsoever.
For this very reason, the noble Maitreya said:
"This is not so," and so forth;
for even that which might be, or could be...
Where? In [acts] such as rejoicing (*anumodanā*) and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
The inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding actual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).
Faith (*śraddhā*) is confident conviction (*saṃpratyaya*).
Affection (*prema*) is love (*prīti*);
clarity (*prasāda*) is the mind’s freedom from turbidity;
reverence (*gaurava*) is devotion (*bhakti*).
"Supported" means made firm. "Inclination" (*avalaya*) is the sinking of the mind; "sinking" (*saṃlaya*) is its subsiding.
Despair (*viṣāda*) is weariness (*kheda*). A lapse into despair (*viṣādāpatti*) is a continuous flow of weariness. Alarm and exertion (*uttrāsa*) is terror (*trāsa*).
Complete terror is *saṃtrāsa*;
the continuity of that is the occurrence of terror (*saṃtrāsāpatti*).
"In this way" means as follows.
"In the absence of women and so forth" means:
"by which," etc.;
"which" refers to the mind that approves [the action].
"Exhausted" is the general designation;
"ceased" because it has perished;
"departed" because it does not persist.
"That which has undergone transformation is nothing at all because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
"Conjunction" means simultaneity.
If it is argued that while the mind has ceased, the nature of the mind (*cittadharmatā*) is eternal, [the response follows].
"And not," etc.:
because that [emptiness], being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), cannot undergo transformation;
and because a well-grasped word cannot be transformed into something poorly grasped.
"Having begun" means having introduced the topic.
To the question "How?", he says:
"having made the basis the subject of the inquiry."
How is that so? Because of the statement "here, Maitreya," which means he addressed him;
starting from "here, Maitreya" up until the point where it is explained how there is no perversion of perception and so forth.
Thus the noble Maitreya spoke further, beginning with "If... and so forth.
"By which mind one dedicates" means that very mind by which one performs the dedication.
"In that" means in both [of them].
"Thus" means because it has been well-grasped. "Transformed" means well-transformed.
He speaks [the words] beginning with "Just as" in order to clarify;
the conclusion is given by the words beginning with "In this way."
To the question, "When, then, would there be error?
he says, "Now," and so forth.
Having thus resolved the objection regarding the consequence of error, he speaks in order to demonstrate the non-perception of the subject under discussion.
"Sa cet... and so forth:
"perceives thus" is the brief statement (uddesa);
"attends thus" is the detailed explanation (nirdeśa).
The meaning is that one attends to it without error.
Regarding the phrase "that," and so forth:
the connection is that "that very mind is being thus attended to."
One contemplates with such synonyms as "exhausted" and so forth,
thinking: "That is not possible,
because it does not exist, like the horn of a rabbit."
The "true nature of all phenomena" (*dharmatā*) is precisely their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
"In phenomena" refers to the qualities of a Buddha. The passage beginning with "If that... serves as the conclusion.
"Thus" means by way of non-apprehension;
that is to say, by a mental attention characterized by the single flavor of emptiness in all things.
This is what the noble Maitreya spoke concerning the Buddhas of the past.
Regarding the future, he says "furthermore" and so forth;
regarding the present, he says "furthermore" and so forth.
This is the second transformation through non-apprehension.
"Furthermore," and so forth.
Here, there is a brief rejoicing in the merit of the Buddhas and others of the three times;
their being "supreme" and so on is as previously described.
In order to demonstrate the absence of error here, he says:
"How is that for him? and so forth.
"Thus he attends" (*samanvāharati*) means *samanvāhāra*, which is correct mental attention (*samyag-manasikāra*).
Those phenomena are those which are to be dedicated;
and that phenomenon is inexhaustible,
namely, unexcelled perfect enlightenment, characterized by the perfectly pure nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
The meaning is that it is "thus dedicated" because of the absence of error.
No phenomenon (dharma) dedicates another phenomenon, because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva).
This is also the case.
This is also as before.
For this very reason, he said:
"So it is, Venerable Sir," and so forth.
With the words "If he... and so forth, he states another method;
with the words "This one... and so forth, there is the conclusion.
Thus ends the third transformation, which is free from error.
"Sa cet" and so forth:
the "formative activity of merit" (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*) is meritorious action;
"perception" (*saṃjñāna*) is attachment (*abhiniveśa*).
How, then, does he perform the dedication?
He says: "If [he thinks]... and so forth.
It is "secluded" and "peaceful" because it is empty, respectively, of self and others, and of the characteristics of self and others.
Furthermore, by the words "If, moreover," and so forth, he says this:
even if there is knowledge of solitude and tranquility, if there should be an adherence to the existence of those [states], then one does not correctly dedicate [the merit].
The conclusion is made with the words "In this way," and so forth.
The statement "perfection of wisdom" refers to that very [wisdom] because of its correct dedication; thus, the fourth is the secluded dedication.
The phrase "even that which... and so forth refers to recollection;
the phrase "of exactly such a kind... and so forth refers to discernment.

Because there is a constant connection [between the two], it is understood that just as that transformation is of exactly such a kind—namely, unexcelled perfect enlightenment whose intrinsic nature is the *dharmadhātu*—so too is that [recollection] of exactly such a kind.
The meaning is that it has the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
That root of merit (*kuśalamūla*) is exactly like that which is accompanied by rejoicing (*anumodanā*).
"By which" refers to the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
"Tadapi" means "that also," referring to both of them.
"Tajjātikam" means that which has that very genus (*jāti*) as its universal (*sāmānya*). "Tallakṣaṇam" means that which has that very universal as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Belonging to that group" means belonging to that collection;
"having that as its intrinsic nature" means having that as its fundamental character.
"If he perceives it thus" means...
If one becomes attached even to suchness and so forth as being a reality, then one does not perform the correct dedication.
Furthermore, with the words "that which is past," and so forth, he states another conceptualization of reality:
that which has not yet been reached is unarisen.
There is no persistence because, by its very nature, it is subject to destruction.
Therefore, even these three are not perceived; consequently, they are non-existent.
Thus, there is no sign at all, because there is no cause.
An object is not without a cause;
"if that," and so forth.
"In this way" means by way of its true nature, such as being subject to exhaustion and so on.
When one forms a sign, one perceives;
at that time, one does not attend to it, nor does one apply correct mental attention;
at that time, one does not perform the dedication correctly.
If it is argued that when one does not take [the object] as a sign due to lack of comprehension or lack of recollection, then there would be a correct transformation (*samyak-pariṇāma*), he says:
"Now," and so forth;
"even in this way."
Thus, even when one does not take [the object] as a sign (*animittīkaraṇa*), one does not perform the dedication;
the meaning is that there is an absence of even the mere act of dedication.
If so, when then does it become correctly dedicated? To this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth:
the word *atha* has the sense of *yadi* (if).
The word *tat* refers to suchness (*tādṛśatva*) and the like.
The signless and its having an object:
"sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the objective support (*ālambana*) of right knowledge;
"to attend" (*samanvāharati*) means to direct the mind correctly (*samyag-manasikaroti*).
"And he does not take it as a sign" means that he does not perceive it nor does he adhere to it. The conclusion is expressed by the words "Thus herein," and so forth.
Thus, the recollection [of the Buddha] is by way of that which is the intrinsic nature and the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the flood of merit belonging to a Buddha.
"Of rejoicing and so forth" refers to the fifth [perfection], which is the transformation through the recollection of the nature of the flood of merit of the Buddhas.
"This is that," and so forth. "This" refers to that which is the mental attention toward both [truths], yet not the formation of signs (*nimittīkaraṇa*).
The word "that" (*tat*) indicates what is well-known.
This well-known skill in means is what is referred to by the words "he who," etc., whereby the author states its benefits. Now, as to what the means is within this skill in means, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "atra ca" and so forth: "this very [nature]" means precisely that which consists of the sūtra.
"By one who has not heard [the Dharma]"—the ellipsis is "in this [perfection of wisdom]. That which is the dedication within the perfection of wisdom is itself the meritorious action;
the connection is that this very thing cannot be entered or fathomed.
"In that case" means "if it were so.
He should be told: "Do not speak thus. To the question "Who is he? he says:
"Ya ityādi" and so forth.
Thus ends the sixth [chapter], the Transformation with Means.
"Of what [is that]? and so forth;
the meaning is: from where does that which was stated as "this is that" arise?
"Bodies" (ātmabhāvāḥ) refers to physical forms (kāyāḥ).
Formations are the roots of wholesome merit;
therefore, they are peaceful, secluded, and devoid of intrinsic nature—this is the meaning.
And for this reason, being devoid [of such nature], they are not perceived through apprehension—this is the meaning.

"Nevertheless" (*api tu*): although they are not perceived, nevertheless, by taking as signs (*nimittīkṛtya*) such states as cessation and so forth exactly as they are and without error— that is, by way of grasping—
and by conceptualizing (*vikalpya*) them— that is, by way of dogmatic adherence.

One who perceives as "ceased" and so forth that which is a conceptual appearance not corresponding to reality should dedicate their own apprehension toward non-apprehension in the context of perfect enlightenment.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Of him," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "even parinirvāṇa," the word "even" (api) has the sense of an intensifier.
Because it is absolutely impossible for that [unmanifested state] to be made an object of perception,
it is "poisonous" and "thorny" due to its similarity to those states; thus ends the seventh transformation, that which is without an objective cause.
"Namely, for example" (*tadyathāpīti*) and so forth.
"Exquisite" (*praṇīta*) means due to the excellence of its color and other qualities.
"Even though" (*kiṃ cāpi*) has the sense of "although" (*yadyapi*).
"But rather" (*api tu*) means "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

"Indeed" (*khalu punaḥ*) is a rhetorical embellishment. "One might think" (*manyeta*) refers to [thinking] due to the acquisition of color and so forth. "Savoring" (*svādana*) is the act of tasting (*svāda*), that is, enjoyment (*paribhoga*).
"At the conclusion" means at the end;
"the fruit of maturation" (vipākaphala);
"by what is wrongly grasped" means by what is falsely heard.
"By that which is poorly characterized" means by that which is poorly reflected upon;
"by that which is poorly recited" means by that which is poorly practiced;
[this refers to] well-spoken words.
The word "iti" signifies the completion of the process.
"Thus he" refers to the one who has been described.
"Because it possesses poison" means because it is accompanied by an object.
"Poison" here refers to the capacity to cause harm;
"therefore" is the conclusion;
and "how," etc., introduces the questions.
The response beginning with "In this [case]" and so forth is a refutation;
it is a censure because it is made known through the speaking of what is untrue.
In the phrases beginning with "to be embraced" (*parigrahītavya*), "embracing" (*parigraha*) indicates "rejoicing" (*anumodanā*),
because it is invariably concomitant [with it].
By means of the Buddha’s gnosis (*buddhajñāna*), [it is] known (*jāta*).
The connection is that they will later see [it] with the Buddha-eye;
"and thus for him" is the conclusion.
To the question "From where does all this, such as its being free from poison, arise?", he says: "By means of the resolute intention," and so forth.
Thus ends the eighth [chapter], on dedication authorized by the Buddhas.
Furthermore,
"and so forth" means that the Tathāgata is the aggregate of morality and the other perfections;
