"unincluded" means not being contained within them.
"Because they are not included within the three times and the three realms"— this means because they are not contained within the three periods of time or the three worlds.
The underlying sense is that those [virtues], such as ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the rest, are nothing other than the *dharmadhātu* itself.
"Transformation as well" means dedication as well.
"In that Dharma" refers to perfect enlightenment.
"Undestroyed" means uncorrupted.

It is unconditioned. In order to demonstrate the equality between the dedication authorized by the Buddhas and the dedication to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) by virtue of its being the realm of phenomena itself, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatra" and so forth:
here, by the word "second" (*dvitīya*) and those following it, the meaning of "alternately" (*vā*) is understood.
This refers to the transformation that occurs through the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) of the *dharmadhātu*.
The connection is that "this is the correct dedication.
To the question "Which one? he says:
"by this," referring to that which was just mentioned.
The meaning is: "by means of a dedication that is not included [within the three realms].
The meaning of "just as the Buddha Bhagavāns [have dedicated]" and so forth is: "precisely by means of a dedication authorized by the Buddhas.
"And thus" is the conclusion.
Thus ends the ninth [type of] dedication, called "not included" (*aparyāpanna*).
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha khalu":
"yo hyayam" means that which is called "not included."
From the words "in this very [state]" up to "he dedicates," there is an exposition of dedication authorized by the Buddhas.
"In this" refers to these two modes of dedicating to the *dharmadhātu*.
Their status as "supreme" and so forth is due to their being the cause for the excellence attained on the eleven stages beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*).
The remainder is easily understood, up to the point that they may become attainers of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).

Regarding the arising of great merit mentioned here, that which consists of faith and so forth is the specific cause compared to the previous one; thus, the tenth is the mild transformation of the arising of great merit.
"Let it be so," and so forth, is easy to understand up to the point where they may become pratyekabuddhas.

Regarding the surplus of merit mentioned here, faith and the other [virtues] are the specific causes for the previous [merit]; thus, the eleventh is the middling transformation that gives rise to great merit.
"Let it be," and so forth.
From "Subhūti, those who... up to "...should give" constitutes the brief statement (*uddeśa*).
From "By this method... up to "...should give" constitutes the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*).
"By this" refers to what will be stated hereafter.
"Glāna" means illness; "pratyaya" means causes; thus, "glānapratyaya-bhaiṣajya" refers to medicines having that [illness] as their cause.
Requisites refer to items such as water-filters and the like;
"pleasures" refers to the causes of happiness; "by means of their offerings" refers to the presentation of these things.
"Easy contact" means a pleasant experience.
By means of that, whatever dwellings there are, such as walking meditation and so forth—
one should imagine each of these for every single sentient being.
Having established them separately as objects of service,
[the phrase] "all those bodhisattvas" is understood to apply to each one individually.
Having established each one separately as an attendant,
the connection is that "each single bodhisattva attends."
What would it attend upon?
Since they are the subject under discussion, it would be those very same *sarvasattvas*.
The genitive case in "ekaikasteṣāṃ sarvabodhisattvānām" is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
Suppose that among them, each individual were to give a gift;
[giving] to all those very sentient beings,
for as long as it has been accumulated over a vast period of time.
It was accumulated over such a long period of time; likewise, it was brought about through such great elaboration—
it was produced with such vast detail.
"Let it be, moreover," and so forth.

Previously, all the bodhisattvas who were attendants possessed the vigor of world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges for each of the beings possessing the vigor of world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

Herein, however, the distinction is that there are as many bodhisattva attendants as there are beings to be attended, each possessing the vigor of world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges for each of those beings.
"Those all sentient beings" refers to each one of them as previously conceptualized, as well as all bodhisattvas, as before.
The remainder is easy to understand.
Thus ends the twelfth [section], the superior dedication for the arising of great merit.
And the mental attention of dedication is completed.
The mental attention of rejoicing (anumodanā-manaskāra) should now be explained. With reference to this, the treatise states:
[54] Rejoicing in the roots of virtue through both skillful means and non-apprehension.
In this context, the cultivation of mental attention consisting of rejoicing is prescribed. // 2-24 //
This is what he says with the passage beginning "Then indeed, the Venerable... and so forth.
"Without remainder" means having made it free from remainder.
The fourteen qualities, beginning with preeminence (*agratva*), have been stated.
"How much is required for preeminence? is the question. "By this much it comes to be" is the answer.
What is the intended meaning here?
Because it takes as its object that which is foremost, the ten directions, and the three times, it becomes fourteenfold.
In that case, where there are thirteen items, they likewise become thirteenfold due to the distinctions of the ten directions and the three times.
How, then, is the central world-system included therein?

Because one takes that [central point] as a subtle limit and thereby grasps the directions, even a single portion of a world-system is designated as a "world-system. For example, it is said: "She gave birth after the passing of eight or nine months."
For when thirty nights constitute a month, there are eight [fortnights];
when even a portion of a month constitutes a month, there are nine.
It does not grasp [them] as objects of apprehension because they do not appear [as such].
One does not conceive [it] because it does not appear as a real entity;
one does not perceive [it] because it does not appear in its own form;
one does not conceptualize [it] by way of a general characteristic.
One does not conceptualize by means of specific characteristics;
one does not see by way of a view because of non-attachment;
one does not perceive continuously because of non-attachment.
Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is the imagination of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
Thus they are established and manifested;
they are unborn because they lack a seed (*nirbījatva*).
They are unarisen because they have not been produced;
they have no coming from the future time or from the previous world;
and they have no going to the past time or to the next world.
Thus, up to "nor does it cease," the reason is "because it lacks intrinsic nature" or "because it is a purely imagined reality. "Thus" refers to [the lack of] imagined intrinsic nature.
"These phenomena being thus" refers to the wholesome phenomena that have a dependent nature (*paratantra-rūpa*).
"Dharmatā" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) with respect to those intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) which are the domain of the intellects of the foolish.
Furthermore, even in the section on rejoicing (*anumodanā*), the statement "having rejoiced in such a way, one dedicates in just that same way" is made because dedication is necessarily required.
The remainder has already been explained up to the point where it says "is not appropriate.
Thus ends the first [type of] rejoicing through non-apprehension.
Furthermore, "and so forth" means the following:
liberation is nirvāṇa;

and that, from the perspective of ultimate truth, is the purification of all obscurations within the dharmadhātu. In this very same way, all [perfections] such as generosity and the rest are likewise [liberation]. This is the meaning.
Attachment is craving; because of its absence,
those who are unattached— being unbound due to the absence of birth caused by craving— are free from bondage.
Then, regarding those who are not liberated:
because even that [liberation] is unapprehendable when there is no application of transformation, he asks, "How so? and says:
"By way of non-transmigration and non-destruction.
For thus, transformation (*pariṇāma*) consists in the transmigration to another state, or the destruction of the preceding and the arising of the subsequent;
yet the *dharmadhātu* possesses no such states.
And it is neither a transition nor a destruction;
"having undertaken" means having taken up [the precepts] for a limited duration while practicing the course of conduct.
He was reviled, cursed, struck, beaten, and insulted with accusations—
both real and unreal— concerning various faults.
"Samāna" means "existent.
The connection is: "overcome by that [namely] *styāna* and *middha*.
In this context, *styāna* is the mind's lack of serviceability (*akarmaṇyatā*), its state of rigidity (*staimitya*).
That lack of serviceability of the mind characterized by rigidity, which prevents it from perceiving its own object, is indeed *styāna* (sloth).

*Middha* (torpor) is the involuntary functioning of the mind, a contraction of the consciousness. This contraction of the consciousness is the non-functioning of the faculties through the doors of the eye and so forth.
If the activity of the mind is not under one's own control, that is torpor (*styāna*). The remainder is easy to understand until the end of the chapter.
Skillful means is that which resembles liberation.
Therefore, because this rejoicing in the dharmadhātu is through non-apprehension, it is the second [type of] rejoicing, which consists in skillful means.
Rejoicing and dedication belong to it;
the chapter that expresses those two is the "Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication."
The sixth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
7. The seventh chapter, titled "Hell," concerns the mundane path of cultivation and the three types of mental attention;
this has been explained.
However, the supramundane path of cultivation was previously indicated as "non-accomplishment" and "ultimate purity.
Regarding that, with reference to accomplishment (*nirhāra*), the treatise states:
[55] Its intrinsic nature is excellence; it is the non-conditioning of all things.
The non-apprehension of phenomena and their dedication constitute its great purpose. // 2-25 //

There are five factors of accomplishment. "Of that" refers to the nature of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is a specific form of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Its "essence" extends from the fulfillment of the knowledge of omniscience up to the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Its "excellence" pertains to the six perfections.
The accomplishment of all phenomena is "non-conditioning" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
It is "dedication" (*arpaṇā*) because one dedicates all phenomena through non-apprehension.
It is "great purposefulness" (*mahārthatā*) because awakening is attained precisely through the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
Therefore, he says:
"Then indeed," and so forth.
For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: It is the perfection of the knowledge of the Omniscient One; for that reason, it is so called.
"Omniscience" refers to the knowledge that has abandoned all obscurations, habitual tendencies, and their continuities;
it means the perfection of knowledge accompanied by the perfection of abandonment.
That, too, is indeed omniscience itself.
In this context, "producing illumination" means that illumination is the abandonment of the darkness of all obscurations;
thus, "producing it" refers to the perfection of abandonment.
Alternatively, it is the illumination that is the manifestation of the ultimate reality of all phenomena;
its possession is the perfection of knowledge. Therefore, I now pay homage to this.
"Should be honored" means at all times in the future.
By a single word, two perfections are expressed.
Now, with two phrases, he speaks of abandonment:
"unsullied" because of the exhaustion of the stains of all obscurations;
"unsullied by the entire world" because of the exhaustion of the stains of the three realms.
Now, he explains gnosis with three words:
*āloka* (light) is the manifestation of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena;
[the next word] means "producing that."
Here he states two reasons with two phrases:
"timira" means ignorance;
its opposite, "vitimira," means knowledge—this is the meaning.
The entire totality of the triple world is the ultimate reality of the triple world;
therein it is free from darkness—
that is its function.
Thus is the pervasion of the object.
The afflictions and the views are themselves the darknesses;
"the remover of all those" means the destruction of all opposing factors.
By all of this, the fulfillment of one’s own welfare has been explained.
With reference to the fulfillment of the welfare of others, he says:
"To be relied upon," and so forth.
It is to be relied upon by those seeking all the stages—
the highest stages, beginning from stream-entry and once-returning up to pratyekabuddhahood—
as it brings them about.
The means for these are the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
They bring about their endurance by removing obstacles.
As long as supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*) has not been attained, they remain blind.

Because it produces those [qualities], it is "light-making. Since all fears and calamities have been abandoned, the supramundane path of cultivation itself is "light"; it is that which performs this function.
Thus far, the purpose of those belonging to the Hīnayāna has been explained.
With reference to the purpose of the Bodhisattvas, he says:
"The five eyes," and so forth.
For they are primarily devoted to the welfare of others.
For him, that very [wisdom] is the collection of means, accompanied by the five eyes according to the distinction of their objects;
without such distinction, it is simply the "eye," because of its vision of the ultimate reality of all phenomena.
There are three obstructions to all-pervading vision:
delusion, darkness, and cataracts.
Among these, delusion is ignorance.
It dispels the darkness of ignorance,
the cataracts, and the diseases of the eyes;
it is that which transforms and destroys them.
In brief, it is called "the dispeller of darkness" because it is common to all forms of darkness.
To the question "What does it produce?", he says:
"It is the non-production of all dharmas."
All phenomena consist of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
they have three natures:
the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected.
In that regard, the imagined nature does not act because it lacks existence according to its own characteristics;
the dependent nature is unreal imagination;
therein it acts because it is the antidote to that [imagined nature].
The perfected nature is the dharma-sphere;
it does not even produce that, because it is without beginning or end.
If it is argued that it produces correct cognition, we say no.
Since right knowledge is established precisely through the cessation of the delusion of the beginningless and endless continuum of consciousness, one asks:
"What, then, does it do? To this, he says:
"On the wrong path," and so forth.
The conceptualization of phenomena is a wrong path for those who have set out by means of it;
one must be introduced to the path, which is the knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena.
Of what [is this] the path?

Regarding the statement that "the perfection of the knowledge of the omniscient one is achieved to this extent," it has been shown that this applies even to the welfare of others. Furthermore, regarding what was called "omniscience," he states that it also pertains to the welfare of others.
By the words "omniscience itself," etc., the meaning is this:
when there is the abandonment of the continuity of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), that [state] is omniscience. Therefore, that perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the producer.
It has arisen as that which ceases and it has ceased;
he says "no," [explaining] "it is non-arising," and so forth.
"Non-arising of all phenomena" refers to those phenomena pertaining to purification; "non-ceasing of all phenomena" refers to those phenomena pertaining to affliction;
and "unborn and unceasing" refers to [the nature] itself.
The meaning is that [they exist] according to appearance from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
For the ultimate reality of these [phenomena] is the *dharmadhātu*.
Because of this, since they are without beginning or end, [they are] absolutely [devoid of existence] by way of the form appearing to the ignorant.
Because they are equal, there is neither arising nor cessation for them.
For this very reason, it says:
"by taking up the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics. Furthermore, it speaks by taking up their third nature, which is dependently originated.
"Mother," and so forth.
"Mother" means the progenitor.
Why? Because she is the giver of all the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*), which are themselves jewels.
For those very factors, when complete and in the state of being causes, constitute the body of the Bodhisattvas; therefore, because they give these [factors], she is their mother.
By the mention of "Buddhas," it is understood by implication that she is the mother of Buddhas.
However, one does not thereby understand any superiority on the part of the Buddhas.
Therefore, he spoke again of him by means of his distinguished qualities, beginning with "the one possessing the ten powers" (*daśabala*) and so forth.
There are ten powers of a Tathāgata; he is the one who possesses them.
What are the ten?
"The power of knowing what is possible and impossible;
the power of knowing the ripening of karma;..."
The power of knowing the various elements;
the power of knowing the various inclinations;
the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties.
The power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere;
the power of knowledge regarding the defilement, purification, and emergence from the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti);
and the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of former abodes (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti).
"The power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth,
and the power of knowledge regarding the destruction of the outflows.
Their characteristics are as described in the two great Bhagavatis.

In this context, possibility and impossibility refer to what is possible and what is impossible. For example, that evil conduct has an undesirable ripening is a possibility; that it has a desirable ripening is an impossibility.
Karma and its maturation;
the various elements, which are the resolute intentions that generate merit, demerit, and so forth;
and the various inclinations, such as the preference for hatred or passion among those who abide in passion, hatred, and the like.
The faculties are faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Their state of being superior or inferior constitutes their diversity;
that is, "this one has dull faculties," "this one has medium faculties," and so forth.
The path leading everywhere;
this path is the antidote to attachment,
this one to aversion, and so forth.

The defilement and so forth of the four dhyānas, the eight liberations, the three concentrations beginning with that with vitarka and vicāra, the four formless attainments, and the nine successive meditative attainments; therein,
"defilement" refers to [the mind] being tainted by relishing and so forth.
Purification is by means of non-apprehension and so forth;
emergence is by means of the lion’s yawn or by leaping over;
former abode refers to a previous birth.
In this context, *anusmṛti* means recollection.
The passing away and rebirth of sentient beings refers to their death and birth.

The outflows (*āsrava*) are the afflictions; their destruction, as well as the path by which that destruction occurs—both of these together constitute the "destruction of the outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*).

The correct knowledge of these matters— such as what is possible and what is impossible— for sentient beings, in every way and at all times, is here termed the "knowledge of what is possible and impossible.
That itself is a power, because it cannot be overcome by others.
Or, because she overcomes them, she is "unassailable," meaning she cannot be overcome. Why is this so? He says:
"Because it produces the four forms of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
Like a lion, one who is utterly fearless and speaks with reason is *viśārada*.
The state of being such is *vaiśāradya*.
The four grounds of self-confidence:
the ground of self-confidence regarding perfect enlightenment;
the ground of self-confidence regarding the destruction of the outflows.
The fearlessness regarding obstructive phenomena and the fearlessness regarding phenomena leading to liberation;
and the perfect awakening of the Tathāgata is the perfection of his knowledge.
The destruction of the outflows (*āśravakṣaya*) is the perfection of abandonment.
Both of these constitute one's own welfare (*svārtha*).
Obstructive factors (*āntarāyika-dharma*) are hindrances to *nirvāṇa*, while factors conducive to liberation (*nairyāṇika-dharma*) are those that lead to the attainment of *nirvāṇa*.
Both of these constitute the welfare of others,
because they communicate that [welfare] to others;
therein lies one's fearlessness.
The meaning is: "in establishing those vows.
They act for them; that is, for these helpless beings who have been wandering in the ocean of suffering since beginningless time, as there has been no protector even until today.
The Blessed Buddha is their lord and protector; by performing those [deeds],
it is established that this is the perfection of the knowledge of the Omniscient One.
In order to establish that this very [state] is omniscience,
he says "saṃsāra," and so forth.
Saṃsāra refers to the contaminated aggregates (skandhas).
Its antidote is the destroyer.
If it is argued that the dharmadhātu itself is its destroyer, he says:
"on account of its non-static nature."
For the *dharmadhātu* is immutable because it is of a single nature, being without beginning or end.
If it were the antidote, then *saṃsāra* would not have existed from the very beginning.
The *prajñāpāramitā*, however, has a beginning.
And that very [wisdom] which proceeds ever higher is its antidote.
By this, the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇasampad*) is stated.
He speaks of the perfection of knowledge (*jñānasampad*) with the words beginning "all," and so forth.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is the ultimate truth;
it is the "clear vision" because it is the manifestation thereof.
With reference to his own benefit and the benefit of others, he says:
"Complete," and so forth:
it is complete because it lacks not even a single [factor];
and it is the Wheel of Dharma consisting of three revolutions and twelve aspects.
Dharma is the teaching;
that itself is the wheel because it moves through the mental continuums of those to be trained.
Its "setter in motion" is the one who causes it to proceed.
Because it is set in motion by him in the same manner as by the Buddhas;
therein, the Wheel of Dharma consists of the Four Noble Truths,
and it has three turnings.
This is suffering;
this is the origin of suffering;
this is the cessation of suffering.
"This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—
this is the first chapter, which defines the intrinsic nature of the Four Noble Truths.
The second chapter defines them respectively as that which is to be fully known, that which is to be abandoned, that which is to be realized, and that which is to be cultivated.
The third [turning] is the discernment of that very [truth] through its own nature as being fully understood, abandoned, realized, and cultivated;
therefore, it is "threefold-turning."

The truth of suffering has three aspects: its nature as suffering, the state of being fully known, and the state of having been fully known. The truth of origination has three aspects: its nature as origination, the state of being abandoned, and the state of having been abandoned. The truth of cessation has three aspects: its nature as cessation, the state of being realized, and the state of having been realized.

Regarding the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), there are three aspects: its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the state of being cultivated (*bhāvayitavyatva*), and the state of having been cultivated (*bhāvitattva*).
Therefore, it possesses twelve aspects.
Now, one might object: even though this [cessation] has a dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) intrinsic nature, it is not itself a cessation or a peace.
Because the causes for the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are ineffective,
nor is there a producer of the factors of purification (*vaiyavadānika*), since right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) arises from mind alone once false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) has ceased.
This is not so.
Because the very production of a moment [of consciousness] that is barren constitutes the cessation of the continuum,
just as cold is ceased by fire;
for it is through the perfection of wisdom alone that false knowledge is ceased.
Because perfect knowledge, which did not previously exist for the Blessed One, has that [cessation] as its cause;
because it is impossible for a non-entity such as cessation to function as a cause;
and because perfect knowledge is simply the mind itself when its opposing factors have been ceased.
For otherwise, even at the time when all delusions have ceased, pervasive correct knowledge would not exist; such is the nature of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
From the words "How? up to "for the attainment of omniscience," [the text describes] its excellence.
"One should abide" means one should conduct oneself;
one should attend to it with offerings and by recollecting its qualities.
She is to be saluted with body, speech, and mind;
the introduction is the occasion for the inquiry,
while the cause is the excellence of the Blessed Lady.

The reason why the merit associated with the sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) of a Bodhisattva who is embraced by skill in means (*kauśalya*) regarding the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) surpasses the merit consisting of the five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*) of those who grasp at signs (*upalambhika*), is that this [perfection of wisdom] is their guide; therefore, it is "supreme.
"Without a guide" (*apariṇāyaka*) means devoid of a guide.
"Unfit" means unsuitable;
"become like one blind from birth" means resembling one who is blind from birth.
The remainder is easily understood.
Thus is its preeminence.
Now, indeed, by the passage beginning with "the venerable one," the actualization (*abhinirhāra*) [of the perfection of wisdom] occurs prior to that which was thus spoken in the second [chapter].
"Perfection of wisdom" refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
That which is the non-formation and non-apprehension of the five aggregates up to all phenomena—that is its actualization, its full accomplishment.
The meaning of the individual members is easy to understand;
such is the accomplishment.
When it is said, "Thus spoken," and so forth, up to "it reaches a number," what is that dharma? It is the untainted (anāśrava). [The phrase] "not any dharma" means...
And because there is no apprehension of the dedication of phenomena, there is dedication.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then Śakra," and so forth: prior to Śāriputra’s speech, Śakra thought, "If he does not bestow even a single dharma, then he does not bestow omniscience either," and thus he said, "What is this? and so forth.
It is indeed presented by some means;
however, as to how it is not presented, the Blessed One said "not as" and so forth.
Perception occurs through the apprehension of fools by way of form.
"Name" (nāma) is conceptualization (saṃjñā);
"formative activity" (saṃskāra) is mental construction (kalpanā).
He asks it according to how it causes one to suffer.

The question "How then? and so forth is posed, and the answer is given with the words "Just as... and so forth: because one does not bestow [anything], due to the non-conceptualization of the bestowing of phenomena.
"So be it.
By way of non-conceptualization:
"not anything," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is no conceptualization of phenomena such as their arising and so forth.

"For the sake of non-arising and non-cessation" means "not for the sake of arising and not for the sake of cessation," because it is an *asamartha-samāsa* (a compound of words whose members do not have the same referent).
And for this reason, it is "not present" because it is ineffective;
likewise, even as that which bestows omniscience,
it will "be kept at a distance" because it does not manifest before one.
"It will empty" means that the present cognition lacks that characteristic;
"it will make void" means that it lacks its fruit;
"it will not do" means that it will not arise.
"This is indeed a valid formulation," as you have stated.
"For what reason? means: why is there that [need for] distancing and so forth?
"In that which has been elucidated" means: in that which has been pointed out.
The meaning is that there is no phenomenon whatsoever, from form up to Buddhahood;
therefore, by seeing any phenomenon, one will distance oneself [from enlightenment],
and thus one should not do so.
"In what manner?"—the meaning is: "Is it by way of its great purpose?"
Subhūti said, "No," and so forth.
The meaning is that because there is an absence of duality among all phenomena which lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*),
it is neither contracted nor distracted.
Because it is non-dual.
"Even so" means even by virtue of its great purpose;
what, then, is the meaning of the word "even more"?
Having said "Thus," he explains that very point with the words beginning "In this way, I... and so forth.
"Outflow" (*niḥṣyanda*) refers to the subsequent determination;
the connection is that it is the apprehension of a sentient being (*sattva*).
A "sentient being" is a substantial person (*pudgala-dravya*); like that, its characteristic is a nature that is not born from intrinsic nature and lacks intrinsic nature.
"Birth" (jāti) means arising (utpatti).
It is devoid of those two.
This very point is explained by the passage beginning with "by the absence of intrinsic nature in sentient beings" (sattvāsvabhāvatayā), and so forth.
By way of elimination, it is understood that "unbornness" consists in the fact of being unborn as a sentient being;
"seclusion" is emptiness;
and "inconceivability" is the state of being non-objective for the mind.
Full awakening (*abhisaṃbodhana*) is direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Due to the absence of that, there is non-awakening (*anabhisaṃbodhanatā*),
which is "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*).
The object is truly existent;
the non-awakening to it, its non-apprehension, is *sattva*.
The perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is like that.

Just as the attainment of strength and the perfection of strength by a sentient being is not anything [inherently existent], so it is with the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom; such is its great significance.
Five factors of accomplishment have been stated;
the sixth and seventh are also present:
the cause of resolute conviction and the cause of the antidote.
With reference to them, the treatise states:
[56] Service to the Buddha, skillfulness regarding the means such as giving, and the causes of the ruin of the Dharma—these are the causes for the lack of resolute belief in this context. (2.26)
[57] Lack of conviction in the profound nature of phenomena due to the influence of Māra, attachment to the aggregates and so forth, and being under the sway of evil friends. // 2-27 //
Here, the three causes for lack of conviction (adhimukti) are stated by means of the first three quarters [of the verse].
The ruin of the Dharma (dharmavyasana) is its rejection;
its four causes are indicated by the remaining five quarters.
"Non-conviction" (*anadhimuktatā*) means the absence of conviction (*anadhimukti*).
In this context, "conviction" (*adhimokṣa*) refers to the conviction regarding this very path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); he speaks of that [non-conviction].
Now, from the words "Then indeed" up to "will not be slow," [the meaning is as follows]:

"He will resolve" (*adhimokṣayiṣyati*) means that he will perform a resolution (*adhimokṣa*), which is the ascertainment of a determined object, thinking "it is exactly thus and not otherwise. This is the meaning.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied because the root is listed in the *curādi* group as "to do that" (*tat karoti*).
He states the definition of that resolve (*adhimokṣa*) by means of three phrases in order to exclude other possible meanings;
therein, "doubt" (*kāṃkṣā*) is an obstacle (*bādhā*).
Since the desire for that which is neither to be sublated nor sublatory is merely a state of longing,
while "vicikitsā" is simply doubt,
and "dhandhāyana" is non-comprehension— these three are distinct modes of movement.
"Dhandha" means slow in comprehension;
"he will be slow" is expressed as *dhandhāyiṣyati*.
Because the root *lohita* belongs to the class of roots designated by their form (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the suffix *kyaṣ* is applied.
Such is resolute conviction.
There are three causes for resolute conviction;
therein, he asks two questions:
from where has he passed away to be born here, and how long has he been practicing?
"He" refers to the one who possesses resolute belief;
he is characterized by the activity of resolute belief (*adhimukti-kāritra*).
Therefore, he says this.
By the words "ya" and so forth:
"by way of meaning" refers to the eight realizations (*abhisamaya*);
"by way of the method of meaning" refers to those very [realizations] through their respective entities.

They will follow the *dharmatā* by means of these very names, phrases, and syllables; they will follow the "method of the Dharma" (*dharmanaya*) through concise and detailed explanations and so forth, because of their continuous pursuit of it.
He will realize it through such knowledge;
he will cause others to realize it in the same way.
For what reason? From what sign?
By the words "whosoever," etc., he states the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
"Seen by me" (*me dṛṣṭaḥ*) means "seen by me" (*mayā dṛṣṭaḥ*); the genitive case is used here because of the intended expression of a relationship (*sambandha*).
That is to say, he trains in what is well-spoken; as it is said,
"fire is never satiated with wood," he applies himself and practices with mindfulness.
"With respect" means out of devotion or preference;
"does not interrupt" means because he does not cause a break;
the conclusion is made with the words "for a long time," and so forth.
One who has the habit of protecting the perfections practiced over a long time is called "one who has practiced for a long time" (*ciracaritāvī*).
One by whom many Buddhas have been attended upon is described as such.
This refers to the conduct of serving the Buddhas, practicing generosity, and so forth.
The third cause for resolute conviction is skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Regarding this, he says from the words "Then indeed... up to "the Elder Subhūti."
"Is it possible, however," is a question expressing doubt;
[possible] to hear in terms of the words,
and to discern in terms of the meaning.
To attend means to remember at another time;
to produce means to bring to mind at the time of reflection; and to sustain means to stabilize it in the mind at the time of cultivation.
"This" refers to that which appears [as such];
"here or there" refers to the stream appearing [in those locations];
"by this" refers to that which appears [as the agent].
"By its form" means by its characteristic,
such as a cow being [identified] by its possession of a dewlap and so forth; "by its mark" means by an artificial sign.
For example, a cow by means of a bell or the like; "by a sign" means by a natural characteristic,
such as a cow's whiteness and so forth.
To explain it to others,
or to hear it from others—
the Blessed One said:
"‘Not so, for us’ and so forth;
‘by way of the aggregates and so on’ means by means of the aggregates and so forth.
The meaning is: ‘as the aggregate of form,’ up to ‘as the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).’"
Why is this so? He says: because this [emptiness] is isolated from all those very phenomena.
Why is that also so?
Because they lack intrinsic nature;
the meaning is that they lack an imagined nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).
And "not elsewhere" means...
And there is no other [entity], because that is the ultimate reality (paramārtha); such is the intended meaning.
For this very reason, the question is posed with the words "That" and so forth, and the answer is given with the words "The aggregates" and so forth.
Representational form consists precisely of the aggregates and so forth;
it is empty of the imagined nature of the aggregates and so forth.
That emptiness of the former by means of the latter is representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), which is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Therefore, this is non-duality, which is free from the conceptualization of duality.
[An objection: "Is this not the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and not of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)? To this, he says:
"Because of its emptiness," and so forth.
The aggregates and so forth are not apprehended according to their [intrinsic] characteristics;
that which is the non-apprehension of all phenomena is characterized by the apprehension of mere luminosity as being empty of them,
and not merely the cessation of apprehension.

Because of the statement: "The non-existence of anything is neither a realization nor a cause for realization," that which is non-apprehension is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) due to its being supreme knowledge and having gone to the further shore;
nevertheless, it is not that [perfection of wisdom] itself.
It might be so if, having experienced the emptiness of the aggregates and so forth, one were to determine them as aggregates and so forth,
just as one perceives mother-of-pearl when determining it to be silver.
To demonstrate this, he says:
"When," and so forth.
But when it produces a certainty regarding experience such that [one realizes] "there is no aggregate, no element, and no sense-field," then it is indeed the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Because the certainty regarding the non-existence of the aggregates and so forth is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that [certainty],
it is authoritative, just as the perception of mother-of-pearl follows from the certainty that it is mother-of-pearl.

Thus, the correct awakening to all that exists, that does not exist, and how the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) may or may not exist—that is skill in means (upāyakauśala), the third cause for resolute conviction (adhimokṣa).
Now, the ruin of the Dharma must be discussed;
and that is the destruction of the true Dharma (saddharma).
Why? Because it is a cause for the ruin of the Dharma.
The ruin of the Dharma is its destruction;
through dwelling in the long-lasting miserable realms, there is an absence of hearing [the Dharma] and so forth.
Because it is the cause for a long residence in miserable states of existence, it is the cause for the ruin of the Dharma;
therefore, it is the ruin of the Dharma. That itself is the karma conducive to the ruin of the Dharma.
Thinking that "this [result] evolves from that," he introduces that very point with the words "the Elder," and so forth;
[it refers to] the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
This indeed is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
In that [path], "attainment of yoga" (*yogāpatti*) is the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhāna*).
"Having analyzed" (*vibhajya*)—[refers to this].
How is it divided?
For some it exists because they have practiced for a long time, while for others it does not.
Why is that? Because of the diversity—that is, the difference—in the degrees of the faculties, such as faith and the rest.
He states this with the words beginning "it might be," etc.;
the connection is that there was a lack of respect for them [the Buddhas] in this regard.
"From the presence of the Buddhas": the ablative case is used here according to the rule *antike dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ*, meaning "in the vicinity of. The sense is "in their immediate proximity."
Lack of respect,
lack of service, and lack of faith;
as well as failure to attend upon the Blessed One and failure to inquire of the Buddhas.
"Thence" means due to the loss of faith. "Karma conducive to the ruin of the Dharma" refers to the rejection of the true Dharma (*saddharma*).
It is "committed" because of performing it even once.
It is "accumulated" (*sañcita*) because of being performed again and again;
it is "heaped up" (*ācita*) because it is complete; it is "built up" (*upacita*) because it has acquired the capacity to yield maturation (*vipāka*).
With the body, there is the coming together to listen;
with the mind, there is freedom from distraction;
and with speech, there is the avoidance of irrelevant talk.
Thus, by not providing the necessary conditions, they do not hear correctly;
they do not know [the teaching] from the perspective of the text,
nor do they see it from the perspective of its meaning.
They do not realize [the truth] by means of the distinction between the three natures;
consequently, due to their perverted understanding, they do not experience [liberation].
It has already been stated that "they lack faith," and so forth.
Its summary is given by the words "thus they," and so forth.
Rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) is abandonment by means of the mind;
repudiation (*pratikṣepa*) is [abandonment] by means of speech.
"Reproaching" means censuring.
"Having struck down" means having defiled. "Burnt" refers to the burning away of the roots of virtue.
Zeal is mastery;
conversely, lack of zeal is laxity.
Therefore, "they will cause them to lose their zeal" means they will cause them to become lax.
"They will analyze" means by mentally relinquishing; "they will turn back" means by not grasping again. By this much, the rejection has been explained.
He expresses rejection with the words beginning "not here" (*nātra*);
he expresses censure with the words beginning "this is not" (*na etat*).
"Those who have departed," "those who are liberated," and "those who are excluded" have one and the same meaning.
"In every way" means in all its constituent parts;
"in every manner" means in every possible form.
"Karmic formation" (karmābhisaṃskāra) refers to the performance of action (karma-kriyā).
"By that which has been brought near" means by that which has been performed;
"by that which has been aroused" means by that which has been accumulated;
"saṃvartanī" means dissolution.
From the Avīci hell up to the Brahma-world, that [world-system] which is consumed by fire is called the "destruction by fire" (tejaḥsaṃvartanī).
They will be cast forth with the body of the intermediate state (antarābhava);
they will be reborn with the body of the state of rebirth (upapattibhava).
Being equal,
there is indeed much suffering and that which is to be experienced as such, for which it was said [in the sūtra].
The three terms beginning with "counterfeit" (*prativarṇika*) have the same meaning.
Why is it that gain and honor should be directed toward them alone—
the very ones for whose sake they would be seen [and] corrupted?
For what reason is this?
The meaning is: from what cause does their non-perception and so forth arise?
"Kasambaka" means filled with putrefaction;
when not discarded, it destroys other leaves as well.
*Jāti* means "born.
Because they are born like *kasambaka* (weed), they are called *kasambakajāta*. *Kṛṣṇā* is a particular kind of grass.
In the vernacular language it is called *kaṇḍā*;
even that, if not removed from the field, ruins the field.
*Nirjāti* means completion.
Because their origin (nirjāti) is from a black [snake], they are called "black-originated" (kṛṣṇānirjātika).
For the black snake is poisonous; when it bites those who have come into contact with it, it makes them poisonous as well.
"By an improper way" means by a path other than those [virtues] such as faith and hearing heard from them.
"Calamity" refers to the suffering of hell and so forth.
"Severe affliction" refers to great pain.
"Should encounter" (nigacchet) means "should touch" (spṛśet), which is to say, "should attain. "Light" (āloka) refers to the knowledge of the ripening of the action under discussion.
"The white portion" (śuklāṃśa) refers to the wholesome part.
Through association with that, it is "partaking of the white" (*śuklāṃśika*). Association (*yoga*) means coming together (*samavadhāna*).
The rest is easily understood.
Thus ends the ruin of the Dharma.
Regarding the passage beginning with "When this was said," etc.:
here, by the phrase "possessed by Māra" and so forth, possession by Māra is explained;
lack of conviction regarding profound dharmas is explained as the absence of faith and serene confidence in them.
Furthermore, with the words "Moreover," and so forth, he states four causes.
One group consists of those who exalt themselves, disparage others, and look for faults in others;
for this very reason, he says:
"By these four as well," and so forth.
Thus, six causes for the ruin of the Dharma have been stated here;
however, in the treatise, they are summarized as four.
Because the remaining [faults],
such as self-exaltation and so forth, are included within the attachment to the aggregates and so on;
this chapter on "Accomplishment" (nirhāra) is so called because it illuminates the accomplishment of the seven limbs.
Nevertheless, because the section on the hells is extensive, it is called the "Hell Chapter."
The seventh chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
Chapter Eight: On Purification.
The accomplishment of the supramundane path of cultivation was explained in the seventh chapter;
purification must now be discussed at the beginning of the eighth.
He speaks first of the difficulty of resolving that purity with the words "Then indeed," and so forth. "By one who is without desire" means by one who has weak aspiration.
"Stupefied and struck dumb" refers to Subhūti’s question regarding spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), arising from a nature that is disinclined to listen and uninquiring:
"To what extent is it profound," and so forth.
To what extent is it profound? It means that it is difficult to resolve with faith.
The Blessed One’s reply begins with "Subhūti, form... and so forth.

The meaning is that form and the other aggregates, as well as the prior, posterior, and middle limits of form and the others, are neither bound nor liberated, because they lack intrinsic nature by virtue of their own-being and the three times.
The meaning is that it is "extremely difficult to resolve" because of its supreme profundity.
For it is well known that bondage is prior activity and prior impurity, while liberation is characterized by the subsequent cessation of that [bondage] and is purity;
however, in this [teaching], purity is the absolute non-existence of both bondage and liberation—thus, the characteristic of purification in the scripture is supremely profound.
[58] The purity of the fruit is indeed the purity of form and so forth; because these two are non-different and uninterrupted, purity is thus proclaimed. [2.26]

The "purity of the fruit" is that which is to be accomplished; and that is precisely the "purity of form and so forth," because it is declared that "the purity of those two consists in their being non-different and indivisible."
The characteristic of purity has been stated in the Sūtra.
Of what purity?
Of that purity for which it was stated that there is difficulty in being convinced (duradhimocatva).
"For what reason? and so forth; the meaning is:
"From where does this difficulty of conviction [regarding it] arise? The answer begins with "Because," and so on.
The sense is that this is its defining characteristic;
it is non-dual because of identity,
and undifferentiated because of non-deviation.
This is the explanation of these two [terms]: "undivided" (*abhinnam*) and "uninterrupted" (*acchinnam*).
The word *yā* is a restatement (*anuvāda*), while *sā* is the injunction (*vidhi*). It is thus made known that the property being restated is necessarily restricted to that which is being enjoined.
Therefore, because they share a common substratum, both are non-different;
because of their mutual restriction, there is no mutual deviation. Consequently, both are inseparable.
Thus, the very purification of the aggregates taken individually is itself the purification of the fruit;
and the very purification of the fruit is itself the other.
This is because they are mutually inseparable.
Mutual indication;
and that non-deviation [of the reason] is due to identity (tādātmya).
Therefore, he says:
The section beginning with "by the purity of the fruit" and ending before "furthermore" constitutes the characteristic of purity.
Four types of purity have been taught in the two great treatises of the Blessed One for the purpose of total inclusion;
however, they are not mentioned here because this work is concerned specifically with the path of the bodhisattva.
The purification of the path is said to be ninefold on each stage (*bhūmi*), distinguished by the categories of "weak-weak" and so forth, as well as "intense-intense" and so forth;
it serves as the antidote to each of the nine types of defects.
The stages of purification are nine:
the desire realm, the eight [levels] of the form and formless realms. Therefore, the treatise states:
[59] The path beginning with the soft-soft [grade] is purification in the nine stages, by way of being the antidote to the extremely intense and other grades of defilement.
Therefore, he explains the ninefold path with the words beginning with "Furthermore" and ending before "absolute impossibility.
"Omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) refers here to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Its purification is twofold:

that which is the purification of the aggregates individually and that of the perfections is the purification of the knowledge of all aspects; and that which is the purification of the latter is [the purification] of those [former ones]. Thus, there is a single purification of the knowledge of all aspects.

The second purification of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā-viśuddhi*) is the realization that the purification of each individual factor— from the internal emptinesses (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and the aggregates (*skandha*), up to the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*)— as well as the purification of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and the knowledge of all aspects itself, is all this indivisible and uninterrupted.
That [distinction] is not recited here; however, it should be understood as being implied because it serves as an illustration.
Thus ends the weak-weak path and the weak-medium path.
Now, "Then indeed," and so forth.
From this point onward, "perfection of wisdom" (prajñāpāramitā) means the purity of the perfection of wisdom.
It is profound and difficult to fathom because all phenomena are pure and absolutely empty; this refers to the path of weak-faculties.
"It brings illumination and dispels darkness because all phenomena are pure"—this is the medium-mild path.
"That light is vision because of its purity"—this is the middle-of-the-middle path.
Because it is pure, it is without reconnection and without transition into another existence; this is the medium-superior path.
That is non-affliction because of its purity, due to the fact that all phenomena are by nature unafflicted; this is the path of superior-mild intensity.
That non-attainment and non-realization—due to the purity of all phenomena and because of the non-attainment and non-realization [of them]—is the medium of the superior path.
That non-arising is due to the purity resulting from the non-arising of all phenomena; this is the path of the highest-of-the-high degree.
He said: from "an absolute impossibility" and so forth, up until the completion of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).
Therefore, the treatise states:
[61] "The state of being an antidote to the three realms is the equality of the means of cognition and the object of cognition."
And that path is intended as the refutation of that objection. (2.31)
Regarding its "being the antidote to the three realms," it is said:
"The perfection of wisdom is absolutely non-arising,
because it is pure within the desire realm and the others."

Because its non-existence is untenable within the desire realm and the others, it serves as the antidote to the three realms; and herein lies the "equality of the means of cognition and the object of cognition," as it has been said:
"Āha," etc.:
"does not know" means he does not grasp;
"does not perceive" means he does not conceptualize.
The question beginning with "What then... is intended to clarify; the answer beginning with "Form...
follows. The phrase "because of purity" means because of absolute equality.

Thus, just as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) does not become something to be grasped (*grāhya*), so too this [cognition] does not become its grasper; this is the equality of the mind with respect to the object of knowledge.
That which was called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) characterized by purity is not tenable, because there are eight faults in it; therefore, he says:
"That path is intended as the refutation of that objection.
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis and its position is displaced [from its logical place].
The term *codyasya* is used in the singular to denote the class [of objections].
The meaning is that this [objection] is intended to belong specifically to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because its challenges will be refuted from this point onward.

And here, by means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), the indication of the objection is shown as being dependent on a reason, namely: "From what [source] does this follow?"—this being the established tenet (*siddhānta*) itself.
The established conclusions (*siddhānta*) are the reasons for the refutations. In this regard, there are two objections raised by Śāriputra and six by Subhūti.
The established conclusion is that [the Bodhisattva] neither performs harm nor confers benefit.
Why is that? For if it were ineffective, how could it be the path? This is the objection. "Because of its purity" is the response.
For omniscience is the purity of the *dharmadhātu*, and that purity is pure by nature (*prakṛtiśuddha*).
Therefore, that [nature] is incapable of acting upon it;
it merely functions toward the destruction of adventitious obscurations.
The established tenet is that it neither grasps nor relinquishes.

Why is that? For if it were to grasp [an object], it would be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); if, on the other hand, it does not grasp [an object], then it would not even be wisdom (*prajñā*). This is the objection.
The rebuttal is based on its purity (*viśuddhatva*) and so forth.
For just as it is precisely because he does not see phenomena by means of the characteristics of phenomena that he sees them by means of their true nature (*dharmatā*);
for this very reason he is pure.
Because he is pure, he neither grasps nor abandons.
It is taught that through the purity of the aggregates (*skandha*), there is the purity of the fruit and the purity of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Furthermore, that purity of theirs [the aggregates] is due to the purity of the self (*ātman*). For the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is this: just as the purity of the self is absolute non-existence, so too is it for those [aggregates].
Why is that? For if the aggregates, the fruits, and omniscience were absolutely non-existent, then the objection would be that these [do not exist at all].
"Because of their absolute purity" is the response.
Phenomena are absolutely non-existent by way of their own specific characteristics;
for this very reason, they exist by way of the true nature (*dharmatā*) which has emptiness as its characteristic.
The established tenet is that, due to the purity of the self, there is neither attainment nor clear realization.

The objection is as before; the resolution is that it is because of their absolute purity. Precisely because phenomena (*dharma*) are absolutely non-existent by way of their phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), for that very reason they exist by way of their true nature (*dharmatā*).
And since that [nature] is pure by its very essence, and that purity itself is omniscience, the meaning is that there is neither its attainment nor its realization.
It is an established tenet that because the self is limitless, form, sensation, and so forth are also limitless. Why is that?
The objection is raised: "Since a limit of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is indeed perceived, how can they be said to be limitless?
The resolution is: "Because of their absolute purity.
For just as the self (*ātman*) has an absolute non-existence, so too do form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates lack existence by way of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Then, what is the limit of those things which are non-existent? If it is argued that they exist by way of their true nature (*dharmatā*), [there is] no limit; for form and so forth possess the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
No, because differentiation is not ultimately real.
Therefore, the meaning is that the very purity of form and so forth is itself the purity of the fruit, the purity of omniscience, and the purity of the perfection of wisdom.
The established tenet is that the realization of all phenomena as being thus absolutely non-existent is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Why is this so? [Objection: If it is a realization, then it is not an absolute purity.
[Response: Because it is an absolute purity. This is the rebuttal.
Thus, the eight sections concerning the knowledge of the paths within the path of cultivation for those who have reached the ultimate end are completed.
By the first chapter, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) has been taught;
by the next six and a half chapters, the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*); and by the two and a half chapters of the eighth and ninth, the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) is to be explained.
It has eight subjects, as stated previously:
"Through wisdom there is no abiding in existence; through compassion there is no dwelling in quiescence."
Through lack of skillful means there is distance; through skillful means there is no distance. (1-10)
The path of seeing of the Śrāvakas and others is held to be omniscience when it consists of the discordant factors and their remedies, the application, and its equality. (1.11)
Thus it is said. Regarding this, the treatise states:
[63] "Neither on the near shore, nor on the far shore, nor situated in between the two;
because of its union with the equality of the paths, the Perfection of Wisdom is so regarded. (3-1)
"Perfection of Wisdom" means omniscience;
"not on the near shore" means in saṃsāra;
"not on the far shore" means in nirvāṇa.
Nor does it abide in the interval between those two; the meaning is that the triad is not perceived. Why? He says:
"Because of the conjunction with the equality of the time-periods," means that the time-periods are equal by way of their true nature (*dharmatā*),
and because phenomena (*dharma*) are non-apprehendable according to their respective characteristics.
This is stated by means of the words "the Venerable One," and so forth;
the word "it" (seti) refers to the resolution previously mentioned.
Because it must be described by means of the specific attribute called "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*),
he says:
"as something distinct."
Because it is specifically the subject under discussion, or because it is present;
or else, why has it not remained?
Because it has been disturbed—that is, sublated—by the non-perception of the three.
The Blessed One stated the reason:
"Because of its absolute purity.
This means that because phenomena which are non-existent by their own characteristics are eternally pure by virtue of the characteristic of *dharmatā*.

The śrāvakas, however, seeking only the exhaustion of their own suffering, conceptualize cyclic existence and become utterly terrified by it; they conceptualize nirvāṇa and, longing for it intensely, attain parinirvāṇa very quickly.
Bodhisattvas do not act in this way.
"Desiring unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings" means not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
The Treatise states: [64] "By means of what is not the method, that [attainment] is far off, because of apprehension accompanied by signs;
apprehension accompanied by signs is 'not the method.'"
Because of that, she moves away;
thus he says,
"Venerable one," and so forth.
"Even thus" means both by way of name and by way of sign;
"he will abandon" means he will relinquish by way of name,
and he will distance himself from it by way of sign.
Thus is the state of being distant;
however, through skill in means, its correct proximity is declared. (3-2)
Non-attachment is the activity of perfect skill in means;
by that, one becomes near [to enlightenment].
Thus it is said:
With the words "Thus it was said," and so forth:
attachment (*saṅga*) is clinging (*sakti*), which is unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
That [attachment] exists both by way of name and by way of sign (*nimitta*).
Because those two also do not exist in the case of an already accomplished object;
the teacher has well-expounded [this] by means of the sixteen characteristics of the path of vision and the twelve applications.
It is perfectly established because it does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa;
it is perfectly pure because it avoids the extremes of attachment.
The word "hi" is used here as a rhetorical ornament.
The word "namely" (*nāma*) expresses wonder.
"These attachments as well" means that even the attachments about to be described are included;
therefore, the avoidance of attachment is skillful means (*upāyakauśala*), which constitutes being close [to awakening].
Furthermore, these attachments have been stated in general;
they must now be explained in detail.
Therefore, the treatise says:
[65] Regarding the emptiness of the aggregates such as form, regarding phenomena belonging to the three times,
and regarding the factors conducive to awakening such as generosity— perceiving these as "practice" constitutes an adverse state.
The "skandha" of all phenomena, such as form and so forth, is a heap or collection.

The "absence of perception"—whether by way of name or sign—regarding its emptiness, regarding phenomena belonging to the three times, regarding the perfections, the factors conducive to enlightenment, and the sphere of practice, is "the state of being without opposition.
The suffix *tal* is used here in its own sense, as in the case of the word "deity" (*devatā*).
That is the adverse side; that is attachment—this is the meaning.
He says this with the words "Then indeed," and so forth.
In this Bhagavatī, the term "notion of practice" (caryā-saṃjñā) is not recited.
Because it is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) of those [perfections] already recited, it is not explicitly stated.

To perceive that "I am practicing" from the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, and from the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the noble eightfold path—this is called attachment (*saṅga*). Regarding this, he speaks of excessive attachment.
By the words "to such an extent" and so forth,
those attachments have been stated; however,
how those attachments [arise] has not been stated.
Then follows Śakra’s question, beginning with "Now then," and so forth.
"By way of" means by way of a method.
"This, however, is the first thought of awakening."
"This is the first conceptualization, which is an attachment:
'I shall dedicate [this merit] toward awakening.
Having conceptualized in this way, dedication is the second."
How can these two attachments exist?
Because that mind, being past, does not exist,
and because awakening, being future, does not exist.
If it is argued that the nature of the mind (cittaprakṛti) exists eternally,
he says "and not," and so forth.
"It is not possible" because transformation is incompatible with that which is eternal.

Therefore, both [of these] are conceptual constructions because they involve the imagination of the unreal. As for the remaining [categories], they have already been explained previously according to their attachments.
Attachment to these has been described as something to be avoided previously.
Therefore, the treatise states:
[66] Absence of egoism regarding giving and so forth, and the enjoining of others to those same acts.
This "negation of millions of attachments" refers, by implication, to the absence of egoism regarding giving and so forth;
this was stated previously.
"Enjoining others to that" is stated by the passage beginning with "Therefore, then," and so forth.
"Therefore" means for the reason that he himself has abandoned attachment;
"then" refers to the time when he is demonstrating it to others and so on.
"Causing to see" means causing one who has not previously heard it to find it agreeable;
"causing to undertake" means causing one to correctly grasp it for the sake of practice.
"Causing them to rejoice" means encouraging those who are sluggish;
"causing them to exult" means [encouraging] those who have initiated vigor with words of praise.
The following of beings results from the abandonment of attachment.
Having thus undertaken [the practice], he says the following in order to demonstrate how one does not offend them:
"Thus," and so forth.
"He does not destroy" means he does not commit an offense against the Buddhas.
This states the benefit in following those who are self-arisen.
By the words "these" (*imāśca*) and so forth,
it is shown that thus, that which is "the absence of egoism regarding giving and the like," and "not enjoining others to those [virtues]," is this twofold negation of gross forms of attachment.
The scripture states:
"Attachment to Jinas and others is subtle. (3.4)
Attachment toward the Buddha and so forth is subtle;
this is what [the author] expresses with the passage beginning, "Then indeed, the Blessed One... and so on.
It cannot be transformed because it would entail the consequence of [being restricted to] the three times.
"It cannot be made into a sign, nor can it be made into an object of focus," because it is not a cause due to its being unprecedented,
and because it is difficult to comprehend.

Because it is not seen, heard, thought, or cognized by the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind, respectively, due to its being unperceived; the Perfection of Wisdom is profound because it is secluded,
and it is profoundly deep by nature because it is secluded by nature.
Therefore, they are worthy of homage;
for all phenomena are also by nature secluded,
and that which is their seclusion by nature is the perfection of wisdom.
Because they were not created by the Blessed One but were fully awakened to as such; because they are by their very nature nothing at all;
and because that which is their nature is non-existence (abhāva).
And that which is non-existence is their fundamental nature (*prakṛti*),
because they possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
In this way, all infinite points of attachment are completely avoided.
It is inconceivable because it transcends thought;
for it is not form, nor sensation, and so on, up to the Buddha-qualities.
The rest is easily understood.
Nor is it seen, heard, thought, or cognized, as has been stated by the passage beginning with those words.
Regarding this, the treatise says:
"Its profundity arises from the very nature of the discernment of the path of phenomena."
Knowledge of the single nature of all phenomena is the relinquishing of attachment. // 3-5 //
[68] By the negation of seeing and so forth, its difficulty of comprehension is declared;
because it is not cognized by means of form and so on, its inconceivability is maintained. // 3-6 //
"From discernment" (*vivekāt*) means because of its distinctness.
"The path of dharma" (*dharmapaddhatiḥ*) refers to the mass of dharma;
the connection is that it is the knowledge of dharmas.
Their nature is one, which is known as "renown" (*khyāti*); that has been explained accordingly.
Now, the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*) must be stated.
Why are attachment (*saṅga*) and non-attachment (*asaṅga*) mentioned?
Therefore, the treatise states:
[69] "In this way, according to what has been explained, this entire classification of the discordant factors and their antidotes should be understood within the system of omniscience. (3.7)
"Having done thus" means having made the designation of attachment and non-attachment. "As it has been stated" refers to the division as it was stated in the *Sarvajñatānaya*.
All of this should be understood as pertaining to the "adversaries and their antidotes.
For instance, attachment is apprehension, which is conceptual construction.
Non-attachment and non-apprehension are the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, attachment is the adverse factor (*vipakṣa*) and non-attachment is the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*); thus, these are the adverse factor and the counteragent.
The application and its equality must be explained;
therefore, the treatise states:
[70] Regarding form and so forth, their impermanence and so forth, and their non-filling and filling.
And the application of the practice [of non-attachment] consists in the negation of that [attachment]. (3.8)
[71] It is unchanging and not an agent; its application is threefold and difficult to perform.
It is considered fruitful because it yields results according to one's potential, and thus it is not barren.

[72] "That which is not dependent on another and which makes known the sevenfold [analysis]" refers to "in that which is impermanent and so forth," meaning in the impermanence or permanence of form and the other aggregates.
By the rule *iṭ radhādibhyaḥ*, the suffix *iñ* is applied;
thus, from *pariprapūriḥ* [is derived] *pariprapūraḥ*, meaning non-attachment (*asaṅga*).
By virtue of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), the word "attachment" (*saṅga*) is understood through that term.
This is a collective dvandva compound;
the meaning is "of attachment and non-attachment. A single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) compound, however, does not occur here because it is not so expressed.
"In form and so forth" means: regarding the impermanence or permanence of form and so forth;
regarding the incompleteness or completeness of form and so forth;
and regarding the attachment or non-attachment to form and so forth.
That which is "conduct" (ācaryā) is practice; by way of its negation, practice in the *Prajñāpāramitā* is "application" (*prayoga*) toward form and so forth.
These are the four, and the eight that follow.
"Unchanging and non-agent" [is the brief statement].

The twelvefold application consists of: that which is difficult to perform, that which is difficult to perform in its activity, that which is not barren, that which does not depend on another, and that which makes known the sevenfold teaching.
Therefore, he asks about it.
He said:
"By that [means], etc."—how should one practice?
How should the application be performed?

In this context, "all phenomena" refers to form and so forth; "aggregates," however, serves as an illustration. "He does not course in form up to consciousness" means that he does not perceive form and the other aggregates.
"Then one practices the perfection of wisdom"—this is the application regarding form and the other aggregates.

If he does not course in the thought that form is impermanent, up to and including that consciousness is impermanent; and likewise, if he does not course in the thought that it is permanent, or pleasant, or empty, or non-empty, or self, or non-self, or beautiful, or ugly, then he courses in the perfection of wisdom. This is the application regarding the impermanence and so forth of form and the other aggregates. Furthermore, if he [does not course] in the thought that form, up to and including consciousness, is incomplete or complete...

When one does not course in the thought that "the very same incompleteness and completeness of form and so forth is itself form and so forth," then one courses in this [perfection]; this is the practice of the non-completion and completion [of form and so forth].
With the words "When this was said," and so forth, he introduces the fourth [chapter].
The Blessed One said to him:
"Form is with attachment," and so on, up to the end of the section beginning with "should be practiced."
In this very context, he states the benefits with the words "practicing thus" and so forth,
beginning with "unattached" and so on.
She is unattached because of the absence of all clinging.
Therefore, they are not bound by the afflictions within the three realms;
therefore, they are not liberated from the afflictions;
nor have they transcended the three realms.
The conclusion is stated with the words "Thus indeed," and so forth.
This concludes the application regarding attachment and non-attachment to form and the other [sense objects].
The fifth [point], beginning with "Subhūti said" and ending with "there would be falling away," concerns the state of being changeless due to the absence of decrease and increase,
like space.
"Color is a quality.
This is an application [of the rule] without modification.

With the words "tadyathāpīti" and so forth, prior to the word "sthavira," there is the sixth [case]; the meaning of the word *saṃkliśyate* is "is obstructed," while for the second [verb], it is "is led toward."
Because there is no causing of decrease or increase through teaching, it is the application of non-agency.

The seventh [section], beginning with "O Elder" and ending with "desiring full enlightenment," is intended to explain the three kinds of difficulty. In this context, the Blessed One speaks of the difficulty of cultivation as a secondary point,
because for those established in that very [cultivation], the undertaking and so forth are difficult to perform.
"Practicing" means by means of calm abiding (*śamatha*);
he does not sink into laxity,
nor does he leap up with agitation.
The cultivation of space does not regress or turn back,
because it appears as having a single characteristic.
"This is the armor" refers to that which is for the sake of all sentient beings toward perfect enlightenment;
"by means of space" means by way of a yoga resembling space, because of not abandoning them.
Then, there is the difficulty for sentient beings due to their non-apprehension and due to its being infinite;
and because awakening is aimed at the welfare of the entire world,
that aim constitutes the "armoring," which is the application of the difficulty of the aim.
The eighth [chapter] extends from the words beginning with "ākāśam" up to "sannahyate. It concerns high flight, the felling of obstacles, and liberation.
Raising the eyes upward is the exertion;
such is the application for the sake of sentient beings,
and it is difficult to perform.

Because the mass of sentient beings is infinite like space, and because it is formless and not a substantial entity—this is the application [of the argument] regarding the difficulty of its realization.
Now, the ninth [chapter], beginning with "atha khalu" and ending before "atha khalu," concerns the fruit of application, which is activity (*kāritra*):
namely, the abandonment of defiled phenomena (*sāṃkleśika-dharma*) and the production of purifying phenomena (*vaiyavadānika-dharma*).
Both of these are difficult for the Blessed Lady because she does not perform them; thus is the application of the difficulty of her activity.
Now, the tenth [chapter] begins with "atha khalu" and extends up to "atha khalu.
"He who would thus attain yoga" refers to the causal state (*hetv-avasthā*);
"where he is" refers to the resultant state (*phala-avasthā*).
"Space" (*ākāśa*) refers to the sky, the path of the stars; however, here it refers to unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarā bodhiḥ*) by virtue of its similarity to that space.
"Open space" (*abhyavakāśa*) is a place above the earth that is uncovered and formless.
But here, by virtue of its similarity to that, there is inferior enlightenment;
both of those constitute the fruit.
Its non-futile application consists in the attainment of that fruit according to one's capacity.
Now, from the words "Then indeed" (*atha khalu*) up to "an entry" (*avatāram*), is the eleventh [section].
Śakra, desiring to provide protection, defense, and guardianship for that bodhisattva, spoke thus;
"guardianship" (*gupti*) is so called because it is accompanied by protection (*rakṣā*) and defense (*āvaraṇa*).
Subhūti said to him,
"Will you attain this?
He replied, "No."
To the question "What follows from that?", he says "In this way," and so forth.
"In this way" means by the non-apprehension of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanupalambhena*).
The remainder is easy to understand.

Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is shown that his protection depends solely on the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and not on anything else; this is the application of non-dependence on others (*aparapratyaya-prayoga*).
The twelfth [section] extends from the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) up to "fully understands" (*parijānāti*).
In the two great *Bhagavatīs*, the manifestation [of all phenomena] is taught in seven ways:
"All phenomena are like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, an echo, an optical illusion, a reflection, and a city of the Gandharvas."
And whatever sevenfold manifestation there is, all that is a subsequent manifestation.
For all phenomena—which abide as being empty of duality and possess the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva)—there is a manifestation as duality.
This can be demonstrated by even a single example.
For just as an echo does not manifest when there is no sound,
so too, when the intrinsic nature is devoid of duality, phenomena appear in the form of a non-existent duality.
Therefore, in this Bhagavatī, it is taught that [all things] are merely like an echo.
Therefore, the reading of the treatise regarding this [point] should be modified as follows:
"The other who is the knower of manifestation.
