Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is of two kinds: supramundane and pure, and mundane.

As it is said in the *Drumavikalpapraveśā-dhāraṇī*: “A bodhisattva established in the non-conceptual realm perceives all phenomena as equal to space through a gnosis that is indistinguishable from the object of knowledge;
subsequently, he perceives all phenomena as being like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a reflection, an echo, a mirror-image, the moon in water, and a magical creation.
Therefore, with reference to the supramundane, it is said:
"Of space," and so forth.
This is said with reference to pure mundane [knowledge].
"Why is that? and so forth.
"He fully understands" means:
what, then, is there for him to protect? The sense is that appearances are unreal.
This is the formulation of the proponent of anyathākhyāti (the theory of misapprehension).
The applications have been explained;
the equality of the application must now be stated. With reference to that, the treatise says:
The fourfold non-conceptualization regarding form and the other [sense objects] is considered to be equanimity. (3-10)
The meaning is that the fourfold non-conceptualization based on form and so forth is the equality of application (*prayogasamatā*).
As it is said in the *Mahatyau*:
"One does not conceive of form."
He does not conceive of form;
he does not conceive "form is mine";
nor does he conceive in form.
"The same applies to feeling and the others.
However, regarding this Blessed Lady [the Prajñāpāramitā], the reading of the treatise should be formulated otherwise:
"The eightfold mental cultivation regarding form and so forth is considered their equality."
The meaning is that the non-conceptualization of the subject in four ways and the object in four ways constitutes the equality of application (*prayogasamatā*).
He states this with the words beginning "Therefore" (*ataśca*) and ending before "Then indeed" (*atha khalu*).
"Therefore" (*ataśca*) means because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are like an echo.

And for this reason, he does not conceive of "those" all dharmas through adherence to their existence; he does not perceive them by means of a [wrong] view, nor does he know them by means of grasping.
"One does not perceive through conceptualization"—
thus is the fourfold conceptualization of the grasper.
In the same way, he explains the conceptualization of the grasped with the words "and those," and so forth.
"They are not felt" means they are not conceived as existing;
"they are not seen" means they do not appear;
"they are not found" means they are not grasped.
"Are not apprehended" means they are not conceptualized. Thus, by dwelling without conceptualizing the eightfold grasped and grasper, one courses in all dharmas.
To the question "What would happen from that?", he says "If [he]... and so forth, which is easy to understand.
Thus is the equality of practice.
Following upon the equality of practice, in order to inspire firm conviction in this teaching regarding the equality of instruction, he says,
"Then indeed," and so forth, until the end of the chapter.
"In the world-system" ...
[The eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Purity," ends here.
9. The ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Praise."

[73] The aspects, along with their applications; the qualities and faults together with their characteristics; the stages conducive to liberation and penetration; the learner; and the group of those who are non-retrogressive. // 1-12 //
Equanimity toward both existence and peace, supreme purification of the field,
and the complete awakening in all its aspects— this is [the path] together with skill in means. (1.13)
The aspects, the applications, the qualities, and the faults.
The characteristics, the factors conducive to liberation, and the factors conducive to penetration.
the irreversible Saṅgha, the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa,
and the purification of the Buddha-field.
Skill in means—these eleven topics constitute the complete awakening in all its aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*).
Since the explanation follows the order of the headings, the aspects (*ākāra*) are explained first.
Their definition is: "aspects are the modes of the knowledge of the objects. [75]
Because there are three types of omniscience, they are considered to be exactly threefold. (4-1)
The "entity" (*vastu*) is the objective support (*ālambana*), such as the Four Noble Truths; its "cognition" (*jñāna*); and its "aspects" (*prakāra*).
The term "aspects" (*ākāra*) refers to those modes by which that [omniscience] is encompassed, because they constitute its defining characteristics.
The plural form in "of the omnisciences" (*sarvajñatānām*) is used in the sense of a genus;
the meaning is "of omniscience" (*sarvajñatāyāḥ*).
How is that [knowledge] threefold?
It is the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Among these, first, there are twenty-seven aspects of the knowledge of all things. The treatise states:
[76] Beginning with the aspect of non-existence and ending with the form of immovability, there are four for each truth; these are recorded as fifteen on the path.
"Non-existent perfection" refers to the aspect of non-existence, up to "unshakeable perfection," which refers to the aspects of being unshakeable.
Among these, four aspects each are distributed among the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation;
fifteen are in the truth of the path.
The perfection of non-existent aspects;
the perfection of the non-existent;
and likewise all the subsequent ones as well.
In that regard, concerning suffering, there are four [aspects]: non-existence, equality, solitude, and the uncrushable;
[and] "equality with space" means the non-existence of form and so forth, like space.

For just as the absence of material substance is the defining characteristic of space, so too is the absence of intrinsic characteristics the [defining characteristic] of form and the other [sensory objects].
Regarding "the equality of the non-apprehension of all phenomena":
the very non-apprehension of all phenomena is the equality of pleasure and pain.

"Absolute emptiness" means emptiness with respect to both the person (*pudgala*) and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Suffering is the "afflicter" because it afflicts; the self (*ātman*) is that which is to be afflicted, being subject to crushing.
The self is uncrushable because it has that as its aspect;
thus, it is the "uncrushable perfection" (anavamṛdya-pāramitā),
based on the non-apprehensibility and the absence of objective support for all phenomena, including those that are oppressors and the oppressed.
Regarding origination (*samudaya*), there are four [aspects]. For instance: the "footprint" (*pada*) is the cause, namely the preceding aggregates (*skandha*);
the "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is the state of the self (*ātman*).
Bodily action, speech as vocal action, name as mental action, and the afflictions.

The absence of these, in their respective order, is their lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*). Because it takes that as its form, it is that perfection (*pāramitā*). [This refers to] "namelessness and bodilessness."
Name refers to the formless aggregates (skandhas),
while the body is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
The non-existence of these two constitutes "namelessness and bodilessness" (anāma-śarīratā).
Going and coming constitute bodily action;
the absence of these is non-coming and non-going.
Conceptualization is the cause of speech.
The absence of that is non-conceptuality. Regarding cessation, there are four possibilities:
for it would have to be either a going, or an object of apprehension, or a destruction, or an arising.
The absence of these, respectively, is non-going,
being unassailable, and being inexhaustible.
It is non-origination.
Because it has that as its form, it is that perfection.
It is the non-going of all phenomena, the absence of going.
All phenomena are ungraspable; for indeed, one phenomenon does not grasp another. Phenomena are simply exhaustion itself.
Through that, there is yoga;
because of the absence of that [duality], there is the state of being endowed with inexhaustible qualities.
*Abhinirvṛtti* means arising.

Due to the absence of that, there is non-arising. On the path, there are fifteen aspects: being without an agent, without a knower, without a seer; non-transmigration, non-discipline; like a dream, an echo, an optical illusion, a mirage, and a magical creation; non-affliction, non-purification, non-staining, and non-proliferation;
and non-conceptualization and immovability.
It is a perfection because its nature consists of the aspect of being without an agent and so forth.
The path is without an agent because an agent is not apprehended therein;
it is without a knower or a seer because a knower or a seer is not apprehended therein.

The path is non-transmigration, because one perceives the absence of connection between death and rebirth. The path is non-discipline, because there is no disciplining of the nature of phenomena (*dharmaprakṛti*), which is equal throughout the three times.
The path is like a dream, because it is like a dream and so forth, being blind even without a seer due to the darkness [of ignorance].
The path is like an echo,
because sound is perceived even when no sound exists;
it is like a reflection or a mirage— that is the path.
Because one perceives an object where no object exists, like a mirage appearing as a path; for there is the manifestation of a non-existent world-system, like a mass of water.
The path of illusion is so called because signs do not appear;
it is the state of making non-arising known.
For by all these five [factors], the path of non-arising is illuminated.
Because it appears in such and such ways even in the absence of a cause for appearance;
the path is non-affliction because passion and the like are not perceived therein;
the path is non-purification because afflicted sentient beings are not perceived therein.
The path is unstained,
because by means of it one perceives the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as being without stain, like space.
The path is non-proliferated (aprapañca), because it is the antidote to proliferation (prapañca).
The path is free from conceit,
because all conceits have been utterly eradicated;
the path is immovable.
Because it is eternal by virtue of having the *dharmadhātu* as its body;
thus end the aspects of omniscience.
Now, there are thirty-six aspects of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*).
Regarding the cause, the path, suffering, and cessation, they are proclaimed respectively as eight, seven, five, and sixteen. (4-3)
The cause is the origin;

therefore, the origin and the path are mentioned first because they are the means to the fruit. Suffering and cessation are mentioned afterwards because they are the fruits. Their aspects follow this same sequence.

"Eight, seven, five, and sixteen are proclaimed" in that Sūtra regarding the Truth of Origination. Therein, "eight" refers to: detachment (*virāga*), non-origination (*asamutthāna*), peace (*śānta*), faultlessness (*nirdoṣa*), freedom from afflictions (*niṣkleśa*), and absence of a sentient being (*niḥsattva*).
How are these eight?
Because within "faultlessness" there are three: non-attachment (*arāga*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), and non-delusion (*amoha*).
For the five aggregates of the past are the origin (*samudaya*). It is called "attachment" (*rāga*) because beings become attached to it;
it is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of phenomena.
"Passion has departed from this," thus it is "dispassion" (*virāga*), which is the origin [of suffering].
"[The suchness] of all phenomena"—
that is, the emptiness [of them] of an unreal, imagined intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The cause of the arising of afflictions is conceptual construction;
because that [construction] is absent in this [state], there is no arising of the origin [of suffering].
This refers to the non-conceptuality of all phenomena.
Because it is non-apprehending,
the origin is peaceful;
this means cessation.
Why is that? Because all signs of phenomena (*dharmanimitta*) and appearances of phenomena (*dharmapratibhāsa*) are not perceived within the appearance of ultimate reality (*paramārthapratibhāsa*).
For this very reason, it is the perfection of non-attachment (*arāgapāramitā*), the perfection of non-hatred (*adoṣapāramitā*), and the perfection of non-delusion (*amohapāramitā*).
"Perfection of qualities" refers to the perfection consisting in the exhaustion of passion, hatred, and delusion.
Because of the absence of all afflictions, the origin [of suffering] is free from affliction. "The non-existence of conceptual construction" refers to the non-existence of the grasper.
Moreover, [if it were otherwise], everything would be afflicted and suffering;
because that is absent, origination is devoid of a sentient being.
"The limit of reality" refers to the emptiness of phenomena and persons.
Regarding "seven on the path": the immeasurable, non-conformity with the two extremes, the undifferentiated, the unadulterated, the non-conceptual, the immeasurable, and the unattached.
The path is immeasurable, based upon the worldlessness of the non-arising of the arising of all phenomena.
The path is the non-approach to the two extremes;
it is the state of non-adherence to all phenomena. This means that one does not approach a thing either according to its appearance or through its emptiness.
The path is undifferentiated;
"undifferentiatedness" refers to the non-apprehension of differentiation. The path is unadulterated because of the lack of longing for the Lesser Vehicle.
The path is non-conceptual;
"the sameness of conceptualization" refers to the non-apprehension of conceptualizations.
The path is immeasurable.
"Based on the immeasurable nature of phenomena" means that because it has the immeasurable nature of phenomena as its object,
the path is unattached.
"Non-attachment toward all phenomena" means the state of being without objective apprehension (*nirupalambhatā*).
Regarding suffering, there are the five characteristics: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The five contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-pañcaskandha*) are suffering.
Therefore, in this regard, it is indeed impermanent;
that is, the unconditioned nature of all phenomena, which is their non-arising according to how they appear.
Suffering is suffering because it is characterized by the absence of pleasure, like space.
Suffering is empty because all phenomena are unapprehendable.
Suffering is non-self because it is impossible to have attachment to all phenomena as they appear.
There are three characteristics of the conditioned.
Birth, aging, and impermanence [constitute the characteristics];
because these are absent, suffering is without characteristics. "Non-arising" refers to the unconditioned state both as it appears and as it is in ultimate reality.
There are sixteen [aspects] regarding cessation;
for cessation is indeed emptiness itself, purified.
And emptiness is not differentiated, because no differentiators are perceived.
Therefore, cessation is infinite and boundless like space. Because it is not delimited by either sequential order or spatial extension, the sixteen emptinesses are, accordingly, of a single flavor.
Hence he says:
"This is the perfection of all emptinesses by way of its being infinite and boundless.
This refers to the perfection of internal emptiness, the perfection of external emptiness, up to the perfection of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and so forth.
And for this reason, there are sixteen aspects within the truth of cessation.
Thus are the aspects of the knowledge of the paths.
The aspects of the knowledge of all modes number one hundred and ten;
for it says in the treatise:
[78] Beginning with the foundations of mindfulness and ending with the aspects of Buddhahood, these are taught respectively for disciples, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. // 4-4 //
[79] These are considered to be thirty-seven, thirty-four, thirty, and nine, according to the distinction of the three types of omniscience, in accordance with the Truth of the Path. // 4-5 //
With reference to them, from the passage beginning "the foundations of mindfulness and so forth" until the end of the chapter, it is said:
"This is the perfection of the factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness.
The foundations of mindfulness and the others are divided into seven groups; thus, there are thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyadharma*).
Because each of these is not perceived, the perfections have those as their aspects... [The ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Praise"].
10. The tenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Proclamation of the Qualities of Retention":
...Enlightenment, ending with the turning of the wheel of Dharma, does not exist without a cause; thus, this is the application of the giver of the jewel of the fruit.
"Pure heap," and so forth, because of its excellence;
it is the "pure application" because those very fruits are seen to be as pure as space.
"An extraordinary thing," and so forth;
from "Then indeed, the Venerable... up until before that point:
"it would be written" means it is possible to write.
"It must be written"— the meaning is that it should be written in exactly that amount of time because there will be no obstacles for one who has made a firm resolve.
"For what reason?"— from where did this [thought] arise?
The meaning is "it is established.
The response begins with "For thus," and so forth;
the intention is that this is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"Kiñcāpi" means "even though.
"Na prasahiṣyate" means "he will not be able [to fulfill it].
"Acchidrasamādānasya" means "of one whose undertaking is without flaw," that is, of one whose undertaking is unbroken; this refers to the limit [of the vow].
Through transgression, the application becomes limited by a time-boundary.
The applications have been explained; the qualities must now be discussed. With reference to them, the treatise states:
[80] There are fourteen kinds of qualities, such as the impairment of the power of the Māras.
These qualities are the benefits of the application; they consist of the fourteen [qualities] beginning with the obstruction of the power of Māra.
Among these, the first begins with "Then indeed" (*atha khalu*) and extends prior to the words "For indeed, Śāriputra" (*na hi śāriputra*).
"By the power of the Buddhas" means that the power of Māra has been obstructed; he asks because he does not perceive [the cause of] this occurrence.
"For what reason?
[It is because] "they will pay attention" means they will remember;
"they will embrace it" means they will abide in accordance with it. This is the quality of obstructing the power of Māra.
"Indeed, Śāriputra," and so forth,
up until the words "when this had been said.
This is the quality of the Buddha’s knowledge through his mindful attention.
Regarding the passage beginning with "evamukta" and ending with "buddhacakṣuṣā":
*anubhāva* means power (*prabhāva*);
*adhiṣṭhāna* means the conferral of superior capacity.
"Acceptance" (parigraha) means taking [them] as one's own.
Why do they have the empowerment of the Buddha or the acceptance of the Buddha? To this he says: "They are known," and so forth.
"Known" means they have been attended to with mindfulness.
"Empowered" means taken under their care;
"seen" means seen with the fleshly eye; "beheld" means beheld with the Buddha-eye.
Thus ends the quality of being beheld by the Buddhas.
The passage beginning with "those bodhisattvas" and ending before "even those who" [refers to the previous context].
"For the sake of suchness" refers to the quality of drawing near to perfect enlightenment.
"Those who also," and so forth. Indeed, prior to this [point],
they possess great purpose through the bodhisattva stages in the future,
and great benefit through the perfections of a bodhisattva.
It has great fruit because it results in unsurpassed enlightenment;
it has a great ripening through the perfections of family, lineage, physical marks, and so forth, which occur in the final existence;
and "exertion" refers to weariness.
Vibration is activity;
thus are the qualities such as great purposefulness.
The passage beginning with "these indeed" continues until "do not fall into terror.
"Sūtrāntas" refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other such scriptures.
"By means of their passing away" means by means of their parinirvāṇa.
"In Vartanī" means in the eastern region.
Now, one might object: "The Blessed One taught the Dharma in the sixteen great cities of the Middle Country; how then could its propagation occur elsewhere than there? To this, he says:
"Fresh essence," and so forth:
"fresh essence" (*navamaṇḍa*) means fresh, quintessential substance. That has been attained by those to be trained (*vineya*) through this; thus it is called the Dharma-Vinaya.
It is the *dharma* because it is the teaching (*deśanā*), and it is the *vinaya* because it subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, it is the *dharmavinaya*.
After the Blessed One has entered *parinirvāṇa*, the true *dharma* remains in the world for five thousand years, after which is the time of its disappearance.
At that time, when it is present:
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"They were summoned," and so forth.
"In the northern direction" serves to exclude the other directions.
"In the northern direction" means that it moves across the extent of its various sub-divisions; thus it is "extensive.
The expression "the Northern Path" (Uttarāpatha) is used for the purpose of excluding the Southern Path and other regions.
"Many" (*bahavaḥ*) refers to those who possess very few wings; "very many" (*subahavaḥ*) is used to express the excellence of their great number.
"Even though" (*kiñcāpi*) means "even if" (*yadyapi*).
The remainder is easily understood.
In this context, the decline of the teaching is said to occur due to four causes:
because of the passing away of the Blessed One,
and because [the teaching] has reached its ninth stage of decadence.
Although [the teaching] will cease due to the convergence of the time of its disappearance and because of the lapse of time for its propagation,
nevertheless, the teaching will continue by relying upon them; this is the quality of being a support for the teaching.
"From 'after a long time' and so forth, up to 'beginning with perfect enlightenment':
*praśna* means a question;
because they perform that [questioning], they are called *paripṛṣṭāḥ*, meaning those who have thoroughly understood what was asked, or those who inquire thoroughly."
Thus, by acting accordingly, they have been questioned;
their questions have been answered, and they have been made to fulfill their inquiries.
Regarding the word "in the precepts" (*śīleṣu*), the plural number is used in the sense of "and so forth," meaning "in the precepts and the other [virtues]."
The remainder is easily understood. Thus concludes the quality of fulfilling white dharmas.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tatkasya" and ending with "starting from perfect enlightenment":

"even for those who have passed beyond birth" means that even for those who have transcended that particular birth and subsequent births, there are "manifestations," which are applications [of effort].
"Rejoicing" is the longing; the rest is easy to understand.
Thus ends the quality of being a personage of narrative.
Regarding the passage beginning with "in those" and ending with "up to perfect enlightenment":
"by desire or by mantra" means either by intention or by investigation.
The remainder is easily understood. Thus ends the quality of indivisibility.
From the words "And that" up to "in perfect enlightenment," [the text] describes the quality of generating roots of merit for many beings.
Regarding the passage beginning with "For what reason... and ending before "and thus," [the terms] are explained as follows: "we shall set forth" means by the mere act of setting forth;
"we shall fully manifest" means by bringing about the excellence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*);
and "we shall establish" means we shall make it firm.
The remainder is easily understood.
Thus ends the quality of accomplishing the welfare of others as promised.
"Thus," and so forth, up to "they will come to be.
"Thus" means when there is the accomplishment of the welfare of others as previously described;
[it means] they will come to possess sublime resolve.
As it has been stated at length, we shall now state that very same thing in brief:
"Those individuals will indeed possess noble inclinations;
having given noble gifts regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, they will cultivate noble roots of merit."

"Having taken hold of a sublime maturation for the sake of sentient beings, they will take hold of maturation after maturation from that maturation"—this is the quality of taking hold of a sublime fruit.
The passage beginning with "yad" and ending before "evam uktaḥ" means:
"yad" (since) refers to the fact that [the bodhisattva] possesses sublime resolve (*udārādhimukti*);
"adhyālambitavyāni" means they are to be taken up or transferred.
The remainder is easily understood. Thus concludes the quality of accomplishing the welfare of others in detail.
"Thus spoken," and so forth, until the end of the chapter:
"for the sake of the perfections" means for their purpose;
"for the purification of them."

"For the sake of" means for their benefit. "They will seek" means they will go here and there and search, thinking, "Where can this Perfection of Wisdom be found? "They will investigate" means they will pursue it.
Having heard, "One will obtain it here," they speak correctly, saying,
"It is to be addressed."
They will approach through proximity;
they will be reborn through effort and attainment;
and they will come near through attainment without even effort.
The remainder is easily understood.
Thus concludes the quality of the certain attainment of the six perfections.
Thus has the quality been described.
The stabilization and maintenance of the mind within the aforementioned applications is "dhāraṇā" (retention).
Its qualities and benefits are fourteen;
this chapter is the proclamation of them.
The tenth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
11. The eleventh chapter, titled "The Deeds of Māra.
Faults are those which create obstacles to practice;
they must be explained.
Concerning that, the treatise states: "The faults are to be understood as six, together with four sets of ten. (4.12)
The meaning is that there are forty-six faults;
therefore, he says,
"Now then," and so forth.
"Ke-cit" (some) is the question. "Kāṅkṣā" means "for what purpose?
Or rather, the word "cit" should not be read.
When it is stated in general terms that "there are many," a question arises from the desire to know the specific details:
"Of what forms are they?
The answer begins with "Of those... and so forth.
The meaning is that there are forty-six [qualities] which will be explained hereafter.

Words such as "speaking" (*bhāṣamāṇa*) and so forth are indicative of all [bodhisattva] practices. The statement "eloquence will arise after a long time" means that the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramitā*) occurs after a long time.
Consequently, awakening would occur only after a long time;
thus, there is the fault of providing a delayed manifestation.
"And that too," and so forth. "It will be distracted" means it will become agitated.
Because for one who is unskilled in means, pride arises more quickly when that [knowledge] is produced;
consequently, by disparaging other bodhisattvas and being born into low families, awakening would be attained only after a long time—this is the fault of having overly swift eloquence.
"Yawning" means stretching out their bodies with pride; "laughing" means uttering loud, boisterous laughter;
"roaring loudly" means rising up out of arrogance.
Thus ends the deficiency of bodily action.

"Those with distracted minds" means those who are not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*). "Possessing mutual consciousness" means they must be reminded by others; they themselves will not regain mindfulness.
Even when the paths of conduct have been divided, there may be a defect of mental impairment due to forgetting the instruction.
"Mutually," and so forth;
"laughing at one another" means mocking each other;
"with eyes wandering" means looking here and there.

"Incompleteness" (visāmagrī) means that when the arrival of as many [conditions] as would cause the book to be drawn out is lacking—that is, when they are not complete—there is the fault of recitation and so forth being performed in an improper manner.
The passage beginning with "We do not... and ending before "furthermore" [refers to] what was previously stated:
"by means of such and such productions of the thought of awakening.
[They] are not born forth; they are not accomplished.
Thus, the fault is the grasping at signs that cause aversion.
Furthermore, from "punaraparam" up to "tadyathāpīti":
having abandoned [them] with the mind,
having relinquished [them] through body and speech.
Niryaṇa is the reaching of the limit of training;
such is the fault of the loss of the cause.
The passage beginning with "tadyathāpīti" and preceding the word "tadyathāpi" [is as follows]: "piṇḍa" means food; "chorayitvā" means having discarded or abandoned.
*Kavaḍa* means a morsel.

*Patra* refers to a collection of the excellence of leaves. One who has "entered upon what is comparable to a leaf" (*palāśopama-pratipanna*) is one who is devoted to the sūtras that are comparable to leaves.
We shall subdue them by taming the five sense-faculties; we shall pacify them by taming the mind;
we shall bring about their final nirvana through the exhaustion of rebirth.
The "formative activity" (*abhisaṃskāra*) of the roots of virtue refers to the operations of application directed toward their accomplishment; however,
one should not conceive of them as such,
because neither they nor the self are perceived— this is the fault of falling away from the taste of the sublime.
The passage beginning with "tadyathāpīti" and ending before "tadyathāpi": "prakāśam" means "with light"; "upanidhyāyet" means "one should look."
"Color and configuration" refers to color and shape;
this is the fault of not falling away from the supreme vehicle.
The passage beginning with "tadyathāpīti" and preceding the word "prāk" [means]:
"only for the sake of self-restraint and tranquility.
The term "saṃvarṇata" (is praised) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
"‘It is also thus,’ and so forth.
‘Seclusion’ (pratisaṃlayana) is meditative concentration (samādhi).
‘That too’ means in this manner."
It is praised solely for the sake of self-restraint and tranquility.
From "Beyond this" onwards, the text is easy to understand.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In this very life," and so forth:
"In the present life" means in this very birth.
"Without grasping" means without taking hold of anything.
"For all time" means until enlightenment.

This is "constant" (*satata*) because it exists throughout every birth, and "continuous" (*samita*) because it occurs every day; thus, it is "constantly and continuously. The remainder is easily understood.
Thus is the fault of the loss of the summary.
Thus ends the first decade.
The passage beginning with "tadyathāpīti" and ending before "tadyathāpi": *palagaṇḍa* means a carpenter; on the summit of Mount Meru is the golden city of Śakra named Sudarśana.
In its center is the palace of Śakra named Vaijayanta; each side is two hundred and fifty yojanas,
making it one thousand yojanas in total.
The celestial palaces (*vimāna*) of the sun and moon, made of crystal and circular in shape, travel through the sky outside the midpoint of Mount Meru;
they measure five hundred and fifty *yojanas* respectively according to their central axis.
That multi-storied mansion situated in the center of these two is what should be called their "celestial palace" (*vimāna*) here.
And that [palace] is of a much smaller dimension than Vaijayanta. "Nirmāṇa" (creation) refers to a specific activity;
"upanayanti" means they bring about or cause one to reach [the goal], which constitutes the fault of delusion regarding the means (*upāya-saṃmoha-doṣa*).
"Namely, for example," and so forth;
the Blessed One spoke [this] prior to the words "namely, for example."

He is called a *cakravartin* because he sets the wheel (*cakra*) in motion in the world. Furthermore, that wheel is not produced by human effort; it moves through the sky and possesses a thousand spokes, a hub, and a rim. It is made of iron, copper, silver, or gold, as appropriate.
Its color resembles that of gold from the Jambū river.
Physical form is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man;
splendor is that which overcomes all, as is power and the halo of light;
and supernatural power is excellence.

Specifically, the seven jewels are: the wheel-jewel (*cakraratna*), the elephant-jewel (*hastiratna*), the horse-jewel (*aśvaratna*), the counselor-jewel (*pariṇāyakaratna*), the householder-jewel (*gṛhapatiratna*), and the gem-jewel (*maṇiratna*).
It is called "slow" (*dhandhaka*) because it is sluggish and delusive due to its lack of clarity and its smallness.
The cause from which a bodhisattva arises is the "attainment of a bodhisattva" (bodhisattvasamudāgama); this occurs not merely by obtaining [the teachings],
but by having encountered them through hearing and so forth.

"Having abandoned" means having relinquished; "having turned away" means having become averse. Thus, due to its similarity with a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), there is the fault of the disintegration of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The Blessed One said:
"It is just as follows," and so forth, up until the words "it is just as follows" [at the beginning of the next section].
There are six tastes.

Due to the difference in substances and their mutual combination, there are one hundred varieties; hence it is called "food of a hundred flavors. *Ṣaṣṭika* rice ripens in sixty nights; the boiled rice made from that is *ṣaṣṭikaudana*.
Because the substitution of the subsequent form is observed in the group beginning with *śakandhu*,
one should abandon it mentally and relinquish it physically.
Thus, due to the similarity with the consumption of food possessing a hundred flavors, there is the fault of the degeneration of the saṃbhogakāya.
The passage beginning with "tadyathāpīti" and ending before the word "punarapara" [is as follows]:
it is profound because it is the pinnacle of ultimate reality;
it is luminous because it is the supreme, stainless light.
Thus, there is the fault of falling away from the Dharma-body due to [neglecting] the Dharma, which is like a priceless jewel.
From here onwards, by means of two prose passages, the five misconceptions regarding the Bhagavatī are to be refuted—from the words "Furthermore...
up until "...when this had been said.
"Many flashes of inspired eloquence" refers to the flashes of inspired eloquence concerning everything from form (*rūpa*) up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because they do not exist in the Blessed Lady, they cause distraction of the mind; thus, there is the fault of the appearance of those respective entities.
"Thus spoken," and so forth, up until "furthermore," refers to those who think that the *prajñāpāramitā* has been written down,
or that it is non-existent.
To think that it consists of syllables,
or to think that it is without syllables— all such notions are the work of Māra.
For indeed, it is not written down, because it is free from foul odors and the like.
It is not non-existent, because it exists in the ultimate sense;
it is not syllables, because all phenomena are beyond syllables;
yet it is not without syllables, because these syllables are its natural outflow.
And because it is indicated by these very [points], and because that [realization] is attained by taking these very things as objects in that sense;
thus, there are four faults: attachment to writing, attachment to non-existence, attachment to syllables, and attachment to the non-syllabic.
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"Region" refers to Mālava and the like. A "village" is a settlement of non-wealthy people consisting of a hundred or a thousand counted houses.
A city (*nagara*) is the residence of wealthy people consisting of a thousand or a hundred thousand counted houses;
a market town (*nigama*) is essentially a city that abounds in merchandise;
and a district (*maṇḍala*) is a province such as Kāśī.
A collection of those is a kingdom (*rāṣṭra*).
A city inhabited by a king is a capital (*rājadhānī*).
Narrative prose is a prose poem (*ākhyāna*).
A *gulma* is a thicket;
a *viśikhā* is a carriage road;
a *śivikā* is a palanquin.
Requisites for life are those things intended for the purpose of sustaining life;
"itihāsa" refers to ancient history.
The remainder is easily understood.
Thus ends the fault of distraction consisting in mental attention to various objects such as the destination and so forth. This is the second decade.
Furthermore, by the words "Moreover... and so forth, the fault of distraction consisting in mental attention toward objects to be seen, such as kings, is shown.
Furthermore, by the words "Moreover," and so forth, [the text] indicates the fault of distraction consisting in mental attention toward the fire and other things to be attained.
Furthermore, from the words "again moreover" up to before "again moreover," *antarāyāḥ* means obstacles or hindrances;
*lābhaḥ* means the acquisition of robes and so forth.
"Honor" means respect; "fame" means renown. The "relishing" of these is exhilaration.
Mental affliction consists in the deprivation of robes and other necessities; such are the defects of the enjoyment of affliction.
Furthermore, from "punaraparam" up to before the next "punaraparam":
"kiñcāpi" means "even though";
"upāyakauśalyam" refers to that by which one does not fall into an inferior awakening.
For one who lacks skill in means, there is the fault of not seeking the path within the profound sūtras.
Thus, the subsequent deficiencies should be explained extensively;
they constitute a lack of harmony between the Dharma-preacher and the listeners of the Dharma, regarding the preaching of the Dharma.
Who is the speaker? The teacher (guru). Who is the listener of the Dharma? The disciple (śiṣya), for whom the purpose is the hearing of the Dharma. What is completeness? It is the assembly (sāmagrī).
From perversion comes the lack of harmony;
in that regard, there are first two further statements:
*kilāsa* is laziness (*kausīdya*).
Householders have many duties;
this is what constitutes laziness (*kausīdya*), namely, being deprived of aspiration and energy.
Following that, there are two further statements.
The word "even" (*antaśaḥ*) is written as an addition;
one who possesses movement [of wisdom] does so through knowledge of words,
while one who possesses intelligence does so through knowledge of meaning.
"Possessing mindfulness" (*smṛtimān*) is due to maintaining both [mindfulness and clear comprehension].
"Will be cast off" (*kṣepsyate*) is a passive construction used with an active sense;
it means "will go."
One who understands through a brief indication is one who, when something is stated in general terms, knows the specific detail.
One who understands through elaboration is one who, upon even a slight mention, fully comprehends the specific detail. One who lacks understanding is one for whom the words themselves are the limit.
For he knows only that which is spoken, and nothing more.
These are the four deprivations:
the deprivation of going to another region out of desire,
and the deprivation of being one who understands through a condensed explanation versus the opposite.
The absence of both supernormal knowledge and its opposite.
The third decade.
Furthermore, "and so forth": *āmiṣa* refers to material things.

One who has great respect for and attachment to these is "one who values material things" (*āmiṣaguruka*). Likewise, one who values greed and so forth is "one who values greed, etc. (*lobhādiguruka*).
He is one of few desires because he desires only as much as he himself requires; he is content because he does not seek more than that;
and he is secluded because he does not associate with householders.

By this much, the inability of one who has gone forth to give has been described. Or, being unwilling to give, he does not give even though wealth exists, due to grasping and stinginess; thus is the deficiency of seeking material things rather than the gift itself.
Furthermore, from the words "Moreover" up until "furthermore," [it is said]:
"He will become faithful;
therefore, he will desire to hear [the teaching] by way of its words."
"One who desires to understand in terms of the meaning" means one who desires to give the meaning;
"one who desires to relinquish" refers to giving without reservation.
But the Dharma-preacher will not speak because of his lack of faith, due to [the absence of] wealth.
Because of being uninterested, or because of stinginess regarding the Dharma—
these are the three deficiencies.
The absence of lack of faith and its opposite; the absence of lack of desire for giving and lack of acceptance of requests; and the absence of lack of desire to hear and envy regarding the Dharma.
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"Those sūtras" refers to those which one desires to hear.
"Obstruction to the Dharma" (dharmāntarāya) means the ruin of the Dharma.

Because he has rejected the true Dharma in a previous life, this constitutes an obstacle to the Dharma. By that [rejection], through that very state, they will not come into being, they will not exist;
they will not descend, nor will they come from elsewhere.
"Of one who has not attained the status of a Dharma-preacher" means of a Dharma-preacher who has not attained [that status].
"Refusal" means rejection.
Thus, there arises the obstacle of the sūtras due to the lack of that aspiration.
Furthermore,
"and so forth" means that he will not desire to listen because of distraction by other teachings;
therefore, this is a deficiency of another desire due to the deficiency of zeal and laziness.
Then, furthermore, by another pair of statements, there is the deficiency of being weighed down by torpor and of lack of interest.
Furthermore, by another statement, there is the fault of turning away from the fear of suffering in the miserable realms and from the state of non-arising.
Furthermore, by another statement, there is the fault of turning away from the realization that even the pleasures of the happy realms are suffering.
Then, furthermore, by another statement, there is the deficiency of being alone while the assembly is held in high regard;
the deficiency of desiring company while not providing an opportunity [for it];
and the deficiency of traveling to and fro toward regions of famine and the like.
In that regard, the fourth decade consists of [the topics] beginning with solitude, the assembly, the honoring of the guru, and ending with the absence of deficiency.
Furthermore, by another statement, there is the absence of going to and coming from directions where there is fear.
Furthermore, beginning with the words "Moreover," there is the fault of rejecting those who wish to hear the Dharma due to being occupied with many tasks and looking after one's family.
With the words "Thus indeed," and so forth, he explains the abundance of the works of Māra, the necessity of avoiding them by the Buddha, and the reason for Māra’s persistent application toward them.
With the words "Furthermore," and so forth,
[he describes] the fault of casting doubt by means of Māra appearing in the guise of a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, beginning with "Moreover," and so forth:

there is the fault of predicting an inferior enlightenment for those who practice the profound Dharma by means of Māra himself, appearing in the guise of a Buddha along with a created assembly of monks.

With the words "Thus, Subhūti" and so forth, up until the end of the chapter, he explains four points: the abundance of Māra’s vital points (marmas), the cause thereof, the lack of those [points] resulting in small-mindedness and so on, and how Māra exerts effort against them just as all Buddhas exert effort in the protection of Bodhisattvas; thus there are forty-six obstacles.
The deeds of Māra are precisely these obstacles; the chapter that elucidates them is the "Parivarta" (Chapter) on that subject.

That by which something is characterized is the object of knowledge; therefore, the characteristic is threefold: cognition, the specific quality, the activity, and the intrinsic nature that is characterized. (4-13)
That by which something is characterized is to be known as its "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*);
the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). And that [characteristic] is threefold: knowledge (*jñāna*), distinction (*viśeṣa*), and activity (*kāritra*).
And that which is characterized is also a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*);
[the suffix] *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*).
And since that [characterized] is indeed the "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), there are thus four kinds of characteristics.
In that regard, knowledge must first be explained.
Therein, first of all, by way of the aspect of omniscience:

They are called "worlds" (*loka*) because *luj* means destruction;

The sense is: "What excellence does she possess?
[The phrase] *viśvādarśitam* (?

Regarding the phrase "they are not destroyed" (*na lujyante*) and so forth: [an objection is raised]—"Even so, is this not contradictory, since it is said that they are not destroyed (*na lujyante*), they are not utterly destroyed (*na pralujyante*), and therefore it is called the world (*loka*)?"
There is no contradiction;
for its connection here is as follows:

By the phrase "in the mental activities of sentient beings," the knowledge of the mental conduct of immeasurable sentient beings is indicated;
and that [knowledge] cannot exist without the knowledge of their immeasurability.

Then, after stating the knowledge of the immeasurability of sentient beings with the words "Furthermore, moreover," and so forth, he speaks of that knowledge of their mental conduct with the words "And whoever," and so forth.
In that regard, how is there knowledge of the immeasurability of sentient beings? Because, due to their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), they possess neither measure nor number.
How, then, is there knowledge of the conduct of their minds?
Because they are non-existent due to the non-existence of sentient beings,
and because she reveals the world since sentient beings are also the world;
such is the third [insight], the knowledge of the mental conduct of immeasurable sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "its contraction and outward movement": outward movement is distraction (*vikṣepa*).
The outward movement of that mind accompanied by its contraction is "contraction-and-outward-movement."
Therefore, he explains the knowledge of the mind’s contraction and distraction with two further prose passages:
"He understands contraction as destruction and destruction as non-destruction, in accordance with reality.
For contraction of the mind is its abiding in its own nature.
And that [destruction] of his is indeed destruction;
yet it is non-destruction because the nature of the mind is indestructible.
Therefore, that Tathāgata understands, in accordance with reality, destruction as destruction in brief, and non-destruction as non-destruction.
"From the perspective of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)," and so forth.
The ablative case is used here with the elision of a verbal suffix (*lyap*);
that is, one discerns those [states] as distracted because they depend upon the nature of the mind and are directed outwardly.
Regarding what they are like in terms of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), he says:
"unexhausted," and so forth.
They are not exhausted, nor are they partially exhausted; therefore, they are not contracted.
"Undistracted" means they are not distracted either. Why? He says:
"Because they are without characteristics."
Because they are empty of their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa);
this is the fourth knowledge, the knowledge of the contraction and distraction of the mind.
Regarding the phrase "and in the state of being inexhaustible," the reading "kṣaya" (exhaustion) is found in the two great [commentaries].
However, with respect to this [text], the reading is "and in the state of being immeasurable and inexhaustible" (*ameyākṣayatāyāṃ ca*).
For in this [text] it is recited: "the minds are immeasurable and inexhaustible."
He says this with the words "Furthermore," and so forth.
The question "How? introduces the inquiry.
The phrase "its answer," and so forth, means that it is "established" (*adhiṣṭhita*), which signifies that it has never not been present, being without beginning or end;
this is the sense of "by way of its true nature" (*dharmatayā*).
Precisely because it lacks the characteristics of the conditioned, it is without cessation, without arising, and without abiding;
it is without support, because none of the six sense faculties operate upon it;
and it is immeasurable, because there is no means of valid cognition [to measure it].
It is "indestructible" because of the absence of decay.
"By which" means by that [power] such as empowerment (*adhiṣṭhita*) and so forth.
"Like space," and so on.
Just as space is immeasurable and inexhaustible, so too is the mind.
The conclusion is stated with the words "In this way," and so forth.
Thus ends the fifth [topic]: the knowledge of immeasurability and inexhaustibility.
And in the phrase "and in the immeasurable inexhaustibility," the word "and" (ca) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By this, the knowledge of the afflicted and the unafflicted, the knowledge of the sunken and the uplifted, and the knowledge of the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing are included.
Among these, the first [category] is further explained by the following two prose passages.

"Unafflicted yet afflicted" means that "affliction" (*saṃkleśa*) is the act of being defiled by the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). "Non-affliction" (*asaṃkleśa*) is the absence of such affliction;
they are "afflicted" by that [non-affliction].
Since they are beyond convention;

it is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the mind.
That which is not their proper locus, because they are adventitious;
"by nature," and so forth.
For the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the mind is by its very nature luminous, stainless, and eternally undefiled; thus, the knowledge of the defiled and undefiled mind is the sixth [knowledge].
Furthermore, he speaks of the second [point] with another two prose passages:
"not dissolved in the non-abode" (*anālayalīnāni*). "Non-abode" (*anālaya*) means the absence of a place of abiding (*ālayana*).
They are indeed obscured by the ālaya;
for it is the mind that is obscured, not the nature of the mind.
Indeed, the nature of the mind is neither "not mine" nor "not I."
Those minds are ungraspable and should not be grasped; non-grasping is the grasping,
because the prefix *pra-* has the sense of negation (*pratiṣedha*).
The sense is that it is like setting out on a journey and like being away from home.
Thus ends the seventh [knowledge], the knowledge of the sunken and the uplifted mind.
He states the third [point] with another two prose passages,
beginning with "asvabhāvāni" (without intrinsic nature).
*Svabhāva* is existence within itself.
Because those [defilements] are absent, they are without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*).
They are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) because the mind flows out through them; they are non-conceptualizations (*asaṃkalpa*).
Because of their association with these, they are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Why is that? Because they consist of unreal conceptualizations (*asatsaṃkalpa*);
that is, because of the imagining (*kalpanā*) of the non-existent states of existence (*bhava*) belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
They lead to the state of non-existence (*abhāvagatika*), and so forth.
Non-existence is emptiness;

Therefore, they are effortless, because they do not disperse into the realms of desire, form, or formlessness.
Therefore, the meaning is that they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Thus ends the eighth [knowledge], the knowledge of tainted and untainted minds.
Regarding the phrase "in those with passion and so forth":

this refers to the knowledge of those with passion and those free from passion, the knowledge of those with hatred and those free from hatred, and the knowledge of those with delusion and those free from delusion.
Regarding that, he speaks further in two subsequent prose passages.
"Whatever is the state of passion in the mind," and so forth.
The state of passion in the mind does not belong to the nature of the mind;
therefore, the meaning is that they are "with passion" even without passion itself.
"That which is the departure of the mind," and so forth.
Departure is emptiness;
it is not "with passion"—the meaning is that it is precisely "free from passion."
Thus ends the ninth [topic]: the knowledge of the minds of those with attachment and those free from attachment.
The second [knowledge] is indicated by the following two prose passages;
it is easily understood.
Thus ends the tenth [knowledge]: the knowledge of the minds of those with faults and those free from faults.
Then, by means of two further prose passages, the third [is established];

"‘Extensive, vast, and immeasurable’—this is the treatise.

However, regarding this Blessed Lady, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and immeasurable" (*apramāṇe ca*) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; it is connected with the first two [terms], meaning "in the vast and in the non-vast."
In the great, the not-great,
and the immeasurable;

"Those who have set out for the benefit of the world" refers to having fully awakened to enlightenment and, having liberated sentient beings from the five destinies, establishing them in the fearlessness of nirvāṇa; this is the activity of benefiting. "‘We shall become the protection of the world,’ and so forth, is the enumeration of the activities such as protection; the connection is that they initiate vigor of this kind. Following the enumeration, there is the detailed explanation by means of eight statements."
"From that" means from those sufferings;

Thus, and so forth... (RSt 100).
It is called the "egg of ignorance" (*avidyāṇḍaja*) because [the self] is born within this;
and that very thing is a "film" (*paṭala*), because it obstructs vision.
Ignorance itself is the membrane of the eggshell; by it they are enveloped and shrouded.
Darkness is delusion;
overcome by that, they are rendered blind.
Illuminating means producing light;
shaking off means removing. Thus, because they produce light, they are "lights"; this is their function of producing light.
"Non-arising and non-ceasing" is a collective dvandva compound.

The "nature" (*prakṛti*) is the *dharmatā* of all phenomena. Because they teach the Dharma for the sake of their non-arising and non-ceasing through that [nature], they are "guides"—leaders who lead [beings] everywhere and awaken them to the ultimate truth; such is the activity of being a guide.
The final activity of proceeding consists of the direct realization of the fruit through the three vehicles by means of effortless spontaneity; this is the characteristic of activity.
Thus, the meaning is that the activity of going consists in the direct realization of the fruit through the three vehicles without effort (*anābhoga*).
For the "going" of a village is indeed its attainment;
likewise, when there is a going by means of effort, it is also the attainment of the fruit of the three vehicles, yet that [attainment] is effortless.
For a person does not reach that by going there with body or mind, but rather simply through mental application (*ābhoga*);
for all phenomena have the nature of space,
and space has neither going nor coming.
Their very nature is their movement;
therefore, they are said to have space as their movement, meaning they are equal to space. Why is this so? He says:
"Indeed, as it is," and so forth:
it is "uncreated" because it has not been produced;
it is "unchanged" because no other state is produced.
It is "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) because it is not produced by the coming together of causes and conditions;
it is "established" (*sthitam*) because it exists after having arisen;
it is "well-established" (*saṃsthita*) because it is firmly situated on all sides.
They are established only in some [state] because they abide;
by contrast, those that are the opposite of these are non-abiding, unsettled, and unestablished.
Because they are like space, they are non-conceptual and effortless.
The intended meaning is that all phenomena (dharmas) are merely their true nature (dharmatā).
Just as they have space as their destination, so too do they have emptiness and the like as their destination.
Thus, all phenomena are without going or coming; this is the activity of "going."
The tenfold activity has been explained. ... [The] Treatise [states]:
[88] Of the characteristics of the afflictions, their causes, the discordant factors, and the remedies;
Seclusion is the region where difficult tasks are performed; it is characterized by non-apprehension. (4-29)

That which is characterized by the cessation of attachment and that which is designated as the objective support (ālambana), as well as the absence of error and the absence of obstruction—that is without coming, going, or birth. (4-30)
The non-apprehension of suchness and its sixteenfold nature,
as well as its being perceived like a mark— this is considered the fourth characteristic. (4.31)

That which is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is accepted as the fourth characteristic; it is of sixteen kinds. It is the characteristic that accomplishes all activities, because it is that by which [all things] are characterized.
