"Of what, then? is the question.
The answer begins with "For it is form itself," and so forth.
In this context, by the terms "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, the true nature of form and so forth (*dharmatā*) is intended.

Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, even though there is a distinction between form and the rest, there is no distinction in their true nature, because form and the rest are unreal and thus do not differentiate it; at that time, [the former] has subsided. Such is the intrinsic nature of the object of focus (*ālambana-svabhāva*).
Then indeed, from the words "Śakra" up until the end of the chapter:
it is profound because it is difficult to resolve with faith;

it is difficult to fathom by means of the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*); and it is difficult to see by means of the wisdom consisting of mundane cultivation (*laukikabhāvanāmayī*).
The supramundane [wisdom] is difficult to realize;
the failure to perform what one intends to do is a lack of enthusiasm; "bowed" means inclined.
By the passage beginning with "where there is nothing whatsoever," the negation of activity throughout the three times is established;
by the passage beginning with "space," the negation of the object of action is established;
and by the passage beginning with "self," the negation of the agent is established.
It is profound because all dharmas that are to be attained do not come, and those to be abandoned do not go;
it is contrary and opposite [to worldly expectations].
For the sake of favoring beings and for the sake of non-conceptualization, this Dharma exists, yet the world moves about in grasping.
Misconception (*vipratyaya*) is a cognition contrary to the world; such is the intrinsic nature of misconception.
The chapter characterized by the gods, beginning with Śakra and others, is the "Chapter on the Gods."
The fifteenth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
16. The sixteenth chapter, titled "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Now, regarding the passage beginning with "Then indeed," etc.:
"This is not obstructed anywhere" means that because there is no contradiction to it everywhere.
And for this reason, it has the characteristic of being unimpeded and an unimpeded intrinsic nature.
Regarding the phrase "by way of equality with space":
because it is equal to space, it is likewise non-obstructive.
From where does this equality arise? To this he says: because all words and all things are unapprehendable;
it is peerless and incomparable because, being without a second, there is no similar thing.
That which has a defining characteristic as its indicator is "characterized" (*pratilakṣaṇa*);
because that is absent, it is "uncharacterized" (*apratilakṣaṇa*).
It is "without an adversary" (*niṣpratyarthika*) because it is free from contradiction.
Thus, his nature is unimpeded.
"Place" (pada) refers to a foundation, namely the happy realms, the miserable realms, and nirvāṇa;
because these do not exist for him, he is "placeless" (apada).
"Because it is unproduced.
Indeed, that which is unproduced has no station anywhere.
Why is it unproduced?
Since non-arising is devoid of arising,
from what does non-arising come?
It comes from the fact that all productions are non-productions.
For there is no arising of things that already exist, because that would be incompatible with the characteristic of arising; nor is there arising of things that do not exist,
precisely because they are non-existent, like the horn of a donkey.
The paths are the path to the miserable destinies, the path to the happy destinies, and the path to nirvāṇa;
because it lacks these, it is a non-path.
For this very reason, he said:
Because all paths are non-apprehensible;
thus, its intrinsic nature is trackless.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha khalu" and so forth:
the term *anujāta* [is explained as follows]. The root *jan*, preceded by the prefix *anu*, is transitive (*sakarmaka*).
Karma is its producer;
the agent is that which is produced.
The prefix *anu* signifies similarity.
Therefore, in this context, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent and the genitive case is used in the sense of the object; thus,
through the intention to express a relationship, Subhūti is "born after" (anujāta) the Blessed One.
Regarding the phrase "Of whom is that? and so forth, [the question is]: why is he his legitimate son? The answer is given by the words "For thus" (*tathā hi*) and so on.
The intended meaning is that this is the Blessed One’s son and his equal, because he is a proponent of emptiness (*śūnyatāvādin*).
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha khalu" and so forth:
the phrase "because of being unborn" states the reason for the state of being subsequently born;
the intended meaning is that there is a resemblance between the father and the son by virtue of their both being unborn.
If they are unborn, how can they be father and son?
The intended meaning is "conventionally.
By the words "unborn" and so forth, he states another reason.
He is born after [the Tathāgata], having followed the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Tathāgata;
for that reason, he is "born after" the Tathāgata.
The sense is that he is "born after" (anujāta) because he has been born following [that suchness].
If it is argued that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says:
"Just as," and so forth.
"Anāgata" means unarisen (*anutpanna*).
"Has come" means it has not perished.
But does it arise when arhatship is attained, or had it already arisen previously? To this he says:
"From the beginning," and so forth. "Not suchness" means that it is not denotable by the word "suchness."
The conclusion is stated with the words "For thus," and so forth.
"Going" refers to movement;
because that is negated, it has the nature of non-going.
He states another reason for being "born after" [the Tathāgata] with the words beginning "of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
For suchness (*tathatā*) is the abiding state of all phenomena;
it is established as such because it is not to be transcended.
He states another reason with the words "Just as," and so forth;
[the cognition] is unchanging because it follows its prior nature.
It is immutable because no other intrinsic nature arises;
it is non-conceptual because of the absence of a conceptual intrinsic nature;
and it is free from conceptualization because it is not an object of conceptualization.
He states another reason with the words "And as... and so forth:
"It is not obstructed anywhere" because it is all-pervading.
For what reason?
From where does that lack of obstruction arise?
For indeed, whatever suchness belongs to something exists only therein; elsewhere, it is precisely obstructed.
Because of the non-existence of the object.
The response begins with "And that which... and so forth, up to "For thus...
This is the thesis: "This is indeed one."
In that case, is it "one" because it belongs to a single genus? No;
he says, "non-dual" (*advaya*).
"Dual" (*dvaya*) means differentiation; because of the absence of that, it is "non-dual," meaning one.
The referent of a word is one, yet it appears divided due to the difference in its correlates,
just as, for example, "prior space" and "subsequent space."

If it is argued that there is a distinction such as "the suchness of form, the suchness of feeling, and the suchness of perception" in the same way [as the distinction between the eye and its object], he says:
"it is non-dual.
And for this reason, it is non-dual suchness (*advaya-tathatā*).
"Suchness (*tathatā*) is that which is eternally just so.
It is non-dual because it is itself without division, and it is suchness because it is also without division from anything else; thus, it is 'non-dual suchness.
He states the reason [for this]."
By the words "not anywhere," etc., it is meant that for something to exist,
it must either have a substratum or a cause;
for example, well-water or a barley sprout.

Suchness, however, is neither anywhere nor from anywhere. Therefore, because it is unattached to anything, it belongs to nothing. Since it belongs to nothing, it is non-dual, undifferentiated, and the suchness of non-duality.
Therefore, it is not obstructed anywhere;
thus, it is established that Subhūti is "born after" the Tathāgata.
He states another reason:
By the words "For thus," and so forth;
"for thus" means even in this way.
He states that very point:
Regarding the term "uncreated suchness" (*akṛtatathatā*): it is uncreated because it is eternal,
and it is suchness because it is never not suchness, since it exists eternally as just that.
Therefore, it is "non-dual" because there is no difference between this [world] and that [Tathāgata] due to the non-distinction of time.
The word "tathāgatam" is in the accusative case, denoting the object of the action.
He states another reason with the words beginning with "yathā."
"In all places" means in all world-systems;
"in all phenomena" means in all things;
they are non-conceptual because they do not conceptualize those [objects].

It is non-conceptual because it is likewise the abandonment of all conceptual constructions; "and so forth" means that in every respect it is non-conceptual through the absence of conceptualization. "Unimpaired" means uninterrupted.
The conclusion is stated with the words "For thus," and so forth.
He states another reason with the words "as for example" (*yathā*) and so forth. "Not otherwise" (*nānyatra*) means that it is not other, because no differentiator is perceived.
Because there is no second [entity], it is non-other; and since it is suchness (*tathatā*), it is "non-other suchness" (*ananyatathatā*).
Its "pursuit" (*anugama*) is the following after that.
Having approached suchness by way of conventional reality, he speaks of the ultimate truth with the words beginning "And not... and so forth.
"In this"— that is, in this approach—
there is no one, whether Subhūti or another; "nowhere"— that is, he has not entered into a following of either the Tathāgata or anyone else.
The intended meaning is: "because of the vision of the selflessness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya) preceded by [the vision of] the person.
The conclusion is stated with the words "for thus," and so forth.
He states another reason with the words "just as," and so forth.
The conclusion is stated with the words "For thus," and so forth;
thus [it is shown that] its intrinsic nature is unarisen.
The passage beginning with "by the suchness of the Tathāgata" and ending with "this is it" precedes this point.

Here, demonstrating the non-differentiation of all the various distinctions of the Tathāgatas, he negates differentiation; thus, because all suchnesses of form and so forth are non-apprehensible, the non-apprehension of suchness is the sixteenth nature.
He speaks of the majesty of this suchness:
[The text] beginning with "This is the... [explains this].
The root *gam* has the meaning of "knowing"; thus, the sense is that he is a Tathāgata because he has come (*āgata*) to suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding what was miraculous when this was being taught, [the author] says:
By the words "in this" and so forth:
it trembled, up to the point that it roared aloud, in such a way as to possess the sixfold modification and the eighteen great signs.
Here, three verbal roots have the meaning of "to move."
There are three meanings of the word.
Due to the distinctions in weak, medium, and intense activity, there are eighteen great signs (*mahānimitta*). Among these, "movement" refers to the limbs.
Trembling is in its entirety;
shaking is trembling in its entirety and to the utmost degree;
piercing is sound.
The rattling was like that of bronze struck by a staff;
the thundering was like that of a great new cloud.
There were six kinds of transformations, namely: "the eastern quarter of the earth rises while the western sinks."
The western direction rises while the eastern direction sinks;
the northern direction sinks while the southern direction rises.
"It rises in the middle and sinks at the edges; it rises at the edges and sinks in the middle."
He asks, "What [is it] like? and says, "And of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
"For thus" means:

He states another formulation as well, beginning with "Furthermore" and ending with "they would be born," [referring to] the equality of the manifestation of great signs in the Tathāgata’s perfect awakening and in Subhūti’s exposition of suchness.
"They do not exist" is the proposition;
"they are not perceived" is the reason;
"by which" refers to their own characteristics (*svadharma*).
"May they be born after" (*anujāyeyuḥ*) is the optative (*liṅ*) in the active voice (*kartari*).
And "those which" (*ye ca*) refers to the dharmas of the Tathāgata.
"May they be born after" (*anujāyeran*) is the optative in the passive/objective voice (*karmaṇi*).
"Thus indeed" is the conclusion.
How is suchness (tathatā) the practice? Because one abides in that alone.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "In this [place]" and so forth is easy to understand.

As for the phrase "even though" (*kiñcāpi*): although the suffix *-tasi* in *trayastriṃśataḥ* denotes the ablative case (meaning "from among the thirty-three [gods]"), [the bird] is a bird by birth and is called a *śakuni* because of its large body.

"Of the mind in between" refers to those who perceive the space between heaven and earth. "It occurs thus" means that such a discursive thought (*vitarka*) arises. The remainder is easy to understand, up to the point where it says "he becomes devoid [of it]."

Since the characteristics of the nature of specific gnosis and its activity have been explained here, it is now necessary to discuss the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) for bodhisattvas.
To clarify this— which was indicated by the description of the cause for attaining arhatship for those bodhisattvas who lack such [factors]— Śāriputra said:
As it says, "O Blessed One, [I shall practice] thus," and so forth.
The perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is to be cultivated for the sake of knowing the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena,
and for the sake of rendering signless (*animitta*) the practice of the perfection of generosity and the others while one is engaged in that conduct.

"By skill in means" means being skilled in means. In this context, "means" consists of never abandoning the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-citta*) and the correct dedication of all merits toward awakening (*bodhi*).
Since correct dedication and rejoicing have been explained in that chapter, the definition stated in the treatise is thereby established:
"Skill in the full realization of signless giving and so forth, within this awakening to all aspects, is held to be the factor conducive to liberation. (4.32)
These have five divisions within the two great Bhagavatis;
and thus says the treatise:
[92] Faith has the Buddha and others as its object; vigor has the sphere of giving and so forth as its domain.
Mindfulness is the perfection of intention; meditative concentration is non-conceptuality. // 4-33 //
[93] Knowledge regarding phenomena in all their aspects is wisdom (*prajñā*); thus it is fivefold. The Blessed One himself said this, beginning with the words "When this was said," and so forth.
Now, regarding the treatise:
enlightenment is considered easy to understand for those with sharp faculties, but difficult to understand for those with dull faculties. (4.34)
They introduce this very point with the words "atha khalu" and so forth.
Because its attainment is difficult, it is called "durabhisambhavā" (difficult to realize).
This has been stated by the gods without distinction.
Then, with the words "atha khalu" and so forth, the Blessed One spoke by way of a specific type of person.
Regarding the phrase "by those of poor wisdom" and so forth: the distinction indicated by the terms "poor wisdom" and the rest is that their factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are weak.
However, through the sharp factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is fully realized.
Therefore, wishing to demonstrate those [factors], Subhūti said, "O Blessed One," and so forth.
With the words "Thus spoken," etc., the Blessed One provides the reply.

Subhūti has stated that awakening is self-attained because all phenomena are non-existent; however, that is incorrect. For if awakening were self-attained in such a manner, then it would have been so for all sentient beings from the very beginning.
Therefore, attainment results from practice;
and that [attainment] does not exist for those whose factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are weak.
Thus, because such attainment is impossible, we say it is "difficult to realize."

Now, one might ask: since they possess the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) through the power of hearing, reflection, and so forth, how is it that they have not attained perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*)? To this he says:
"Because it is unreal, it is difficult to realize.
For they consider enlightenment to be merely an object grasped by the foolish.
The meaning is that because it is non-existent and unreal, it is not attained.
For instance, they might conceive of conceptual construction as awakening.
Or [the claim that] the object is constructed by conceptualization—
both these positions are untenable,
because awakening is non-conceptual and is not fabricated by conceptualization.
To demonstrate this, he says:
"Because of its non-conceptuality," and so forth.
Then, with the words "At that time," and so on, follows the reply of the Elder Śāriputra.
For he thinks that because of emptiness, this [reason] "is self-established" is a contradictory reason;
and likewise,
by way of its equality with space.
"Because they are equal to space" is the reason (*hetu*).
The intended meaning is that because those [Buddhas] have attained perfect awakening (*abhisambodha*) through that very reality (*tattva*) which belongs to them.

Having thus stated the contradiction (*viruddhatva*), he sets up a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) with the words "And if... and so forth, wishing to demonstrate the sublation (*bādhā*) of the inference.
"But not at all" means "not even.
By the words beginning with "because," he states the opposite [of the opponent's position].
Alternatively, once the opponent's reason has been refuted, this is simply the proof of his own position.

With the words "When this had been said," and so forth, Subhūti refutes the objection in detail. Having stated, "In the conceptualization of the one who turns back, the one who awakens, and that which is to be awakened—what is that dharma which turns back? he says, "He who, in that very [state]," and so forth, in order to establish non-turning itself.
"By means of the yoga of non-abiding in all phenomena":
non-abiding in all phenomena is itself the yoga, the correct method;
by that, one abides in the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is pure awakening;
and its meaning is that it is pure by its very nature.
"Thus it was said," and so forth, refers to the speech of Śāriputra.
The "nature of the method of phenomena" (dharmanayajāti) refers to the various modes of the reality of phenomena.
With the words "and those," etc., he states a distinction; the word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "tu" (but).
Now, with the words "Then indeed," and so forth, Pūrṇa causes Subhūti to remember [the teaching].
The remainder is easy to understand up until the point where the author establishes his own system: "This bodhisattva mahāsattva will go forth by means of unsurpassed awakening.
Therefore, by this much detail...
Endowed with the sharp factors conducive to liberation, there is the realization of perfect enlightenment. Thus,
the factors conducive to liberation have been explained.
The "portion of liberation" (*mokṣabhāga*) refers to its division, enjoyment, or attainment; those things conducive to it are called "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Those conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) must now be explained.
Penetration (*nirvedha*) is thorough understanding, which is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Its "part" (bhāga) is acquisition (prāpti).
Those things conducive to that [acquisition] are the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya);
they are fourfold.
[The stages are] heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas.
Regarding the first of these, the treatise states:
"In this context, it is taught that all sentient beings are the objective support for the stage of heat."
The aspect consists of an even mind and so forth; it is taught as being tenfold with respect to those very [objects]. (4-35)
Therefore, he says: "Then indeed," and so forth, up to "I am the protector. One should "stand" by way of longing;
one should "train" by way of practice.
By the passage beginning with "one should abide equanimously," ten mental states are taught:

an even mind, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind free from deceit, a mind that has subdued pride, a mind [directed toward] one's mother and father, and a mind [directed toward] one's sons and daughters. The Protector acts to provide protection. This is the stage of Heat (*ūṣmagata*).

[95] For one who has personally desisted from evil and is established in giving and the like, there is the enjoining of others to those same practices, as well as speaking in praise of them and acting in accordance with them. (4.36)
[96] This refers to the "summit" (mūrdhan) stage, as stated by the words "himself," and so forth.
"Sins" refers to the ten unwholesome actions.
"From evil" means having desisted and ceased from them.
"Mastery" means repeated practice.
"Formations have ignorance as their condition; consciousness has formations as its condition," and so forth, is the forward order of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
"From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations," and so forth, is the reverse order (*pratiloma*).

"Of others" means of other people; one who encourages them, one who causes them to correctly grasp [the teaching], one who speaks in praise, one who speaks of their virtues, one who is sympathetic, and one who is compliant—this is the stage of the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*).
Patience is considered to be the knowledge of reality that does not waver toward one's own or others' faults;
likewise, the supreme mundane dharmas are to be understood through the ripening of sentient beings and so forth. (4-37)
One’s own knowledge of the truths and the instigation of others toward them constitute "conformity with praise" within the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).

Furthermore, one’s own maturation of sentient beings, purification of the buddha-field, and so forth, as well as the instigation of others toward these, and conformity with praise, constitute [the stage of] the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
He has stated both of these.
Thus, by the words "regarding the truths" and so forth:

regarding the truths—that is, with respect to the objects of the truths such as suffering—one abides in the thorough knowledge, abandonment, realization, and cultivation respectively; in the realization of the knowledge of the five fruits beginning with stream-entry; up to the entry into the bodhisattva’s determination (*nyāmāvakrānti*); and likewise in the maturation of sentient beings and so forth. (RSt 108)

Furthermore, one who speaks in praise of it and gives approval to it should also encourage others to undertake those [virtues] when they have reached the stages of patience and the supreme mundane dharmas.
With the words "of him thus," and so forth, he states the fruit of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*):
"Form, feeling, perception, and so on, up to the endurance of the true Dharma, will become unobstructed."
The chapter in which suchness is the primary subject is the "Chapter on Suchness."
The sixteenth chapter in the *Sāratarā* commentary on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
Chapter Seventeen: The Chapter on the Aspects, Signs, and Characteristics of the Irreversible State.
It was previously stated: "The group of irreversible learners [consists of those] who possess the aids to liberation and the aids to penetration."
In that regard, two have been stated;
the third remains to be stated.
Therefore, the treatise says:
[97] Those bodhisattvas who, having relied upon the factors of penetration, abide on the paths of seeing and cultivation constitute here the group of those who are irreversible. // 4-38 //
"Here" means in the Mahāyāna;
"the group of those who are non-retrogressive"—
this is its characteristic.
One who is capable of turning back is "subject to regression" (*vaivartika*);
one who is not so is "non-regressive" (*avaivartika*), meaning irreversible.
Now, regarding how many signs there are for one established in the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), he says:
[98] By turning away from form and so forth, by the twenty signs such as non-retrogression, and by abiding in the factors of penetration— this is the characteristic of the irreversible state.
The meaning is the thorough knowledge of non-retrogression.
Now, what are these things beginning with the cessation of form and so forth?
[99] They are: the cessation of form and so forth, as well as the destruction of doubt and the momentary destruction [of defilements].
For one who is established in virtue, the application of others to that same state is [the fourth]. (4-40)
[100] Generosity and the other perfections have another as their support; lack of longing even for profound meanings;
friendliness; non-dwelling with body and so forth; and [the absence of obstacles] in five ways through the hindrances. // 4-41 //
[101] There is the abandonment of all latent tendencies, mindfulness and clear comprehension, and purity;
and there is the non-arising of worms within the body, such as in the robes and other belongings. // 4-42 //

[102] Rectitude of mind, undertaking the ascetic practices (dhuta), freedom from stinginess and so forth, proceeding in accordance with the nature of reality (dharmatā), and seeking even the hells for the sake of the world. // 4-43 //

[103] Not being led astray by others, [the teaching] of Māra who instructs in another path; the realization that "this is Māra," and conduct that is approved by the Buddhas—these are the practices. (4-44)
[104] Established in the stages of heat, summits, patiences, and the supreme mundane dharmas, he does not turn back from perfect enlightenment by virtue of these twenty signs.
Therefore, he says: "Then indeed," and so forth.

They are called *ākāras* because by means of them things are manifested (*ākriyante*) or revealed (*vyajyante*). They are called *liṅgas* because by means of them things are characterized (*liṅgyante*) or understood (*gamyante*).
They are called "causes" (*nimitta*) because by means of them things are delimited and determined.
Although the three [terms] have the same meaning, their inclusion is for the purpose of excluding the suspicion that they might be different entities.
This is a synonym for "aggregate" (*skandha*),
or another way of putting it;
as to how this is so, and so forth.
For this very reason, there is the word "vā" (or).
The connection is: "How indeed (*kathaṃ vai*)"—in what manner might we know?
There are extremely numerous indicative marks (*liṅga*); first, among them, he states the initial one with the words beginning "yā ca" (and that which...).
The ground is fourfold,
due to its connection with ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas;
this fourfold [ground] is called the ground of suchness.
To the question "Why?", he says:
"And all," and so forth.
The word "and" (ca) indicates the reason.
Because all these are non-dual through suchness (*tathatā*);
since form and all other phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are non-existent according to their respective characteristics, they are nothing but suchness.
And suchness is one alone—it is neither two nor many.
Therefore, they are non-dual by virtue of suchness; they are undivided because they are not subject to bifurcation; they are non-conceptual because they are devoid of the nature of conceptualization;
and they are free from conceptual construction because they are not within the sphere of conceptualization.
Thus [it is said].
One enters into that suchness, which is characterized in this way, as the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
To explain how one enters it, he says "in suchness," and so forth:
one is established therein by seeing only that [suchness].
One does not conceptualize correctly, nor does one falsely discriminate;
thus one enters, and thus one enters into the truth.
Thus he said.
"Having thus entered," and so forth:
having entered by the sequence already described; "as" means to whatever extent; "even after hearing" means even immediately following the hearing.
"Even beyond that" means even at a later time than that;
"he does not desire" means he does not obstruct [the teaching] by thinking, "It is not thus. This is the connection.
Diverse thought is indecision,
such as whether one should act in this way or not;
for this very reason, it says "one does not doubt."
"It does not delay" is a negation of non-comprehension;
what, then, does it do? He says: "But rather," and so forth.
One resolves with faith that suchness alone is everything and that form and so forth do not exist;
one penetrates this with wisdom.
This very knowledge is the primary sign.
He states the delimitation of this [definition] with the words beginning "And not... (na ca). The plural number is used in reference to the delimitations, namely, "by these marks" (ebhir liṅgaiḥ).
The first irreversible sign among the factors of penetration is the "withdrawal from form and so forth" resulting from the knowledge that suchness alone is everything.
"Furthermore," and so forth. "Of others" means those who are outside of this Dharma.
"Of the śramaṇas" means of those who have gone forth. "He looks up at their faces" means he gazes upon them while bowing low.
To the question "Why?", he says:
"Ime," and so forth:
they know by means of worldly knowledge; they see by means of supramundane knowledge.
"It should be given" means it should be given with devotion.
"By relying upon" means one serves or goes for refuge.
Regarding the truths and the jewels, "doubt" is hesitation or uncertainty.
When that [doubt] is destroyed, one does not perform any of this; thus, "the destruction of doubt" is the second sign among them.
Regarding the phrase "He indeed," and so forth:
the states of woe (*apāya*) are the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals;
the state of being female (*strībhāva*) is womanhood (*strītva*).
And since that [absence] is an indicator for the remaining non-favorable conditions (akṣaṇas), "the destruction of non-favorable conditions" is the third sign among them.
Furthermore, beginning with "punaraparam" and so forth:
having oneself established in the ten wholesome paths of action, to cause others to undertake them and to strengthen them therein—this is the fourth sign among those [signs].
Furthermore,
"whatever dharma" refers to the discourses (*sūtra*), verses (*geya*), and so forth.
He gives it to others for their benefit and happiness, thinking, "May this be for their very benefit and happiness."

In this manner, he makes [the practice] common; and just as with the gift of Dharma, so it is with other practices such as generosity and ethical discipline. Thus, "generosity and the rest being dependent on others" is the fifth sign among them.
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "Moreover" and ending with "does not hesitate," the sixth sign among those very [qualities] is "having no doubt even regarding a profound meaning."
"Kindness of body and so forth" refers to the actions of body and so on.
This is what is expressed by the phrase "speaking beneficial words" and so forth.
Because it is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), "kindness of body and so forth" is the seventh among those signs.
"Non-cohabitation is fivefold due to obstruction," refers to the five hindrances (*nivaraṇa*):
sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt.
Non-dwelling with these is non-possession;
this is what he means.
And because [the phrase] "having little sloth and torpor" is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), it includes other such qualities as well.
Thus, dwelling with the five hindrances is the eighth sign among them.

The abandonment of all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the persistence of hatred (*dveṣa*), exactly as they occur, is "the abandonment of all latent tendencies" (*sarvānuśayahāna*). Thus it is said: "And he becomes free from latent tendencies.
This is the ninth sign among them.
"Mindfulness and clear comprehension" (*smṛti-saṃprajñatā*) means clear comprehension accompanied by mindfulness.
This is what he expresses with the words "while advancing" (*abhikrāman*) and so forth;
here, "advancing" (*abhikrama*) means going forward.
"Without retreating" means not returning;
"not wandering" means not distracted;
"not lingering" is because distraction occurs when one lingers.
"Suddenly" means without having examined the ground;

and this is also an illustration of distraction regarding walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Thus, mindfulness and clear comprehension (*smṛti-saṃprajanya*) are the tenth sign among those [states].
Regarding the passage beginning with "tasya khalu" and ending before "yāni":
[the word] *yūkila* is derived from *yūka* (louse) with the suffix *ilac*, according to the rule for words such as *piccha*. *Ilac* is added because it belongs to the *picchādi* group.
"Clean" means pure.
"Affliction" means suffering; "misfortune" means calamity. Thus, "the state of having clean robes and so forth" is the eleventh sign among them.
"Those which," and so forth, up until "Subhūti said. They "come into being" means they are born for the purpose of devouring the body.
"Exalted" means particularly distinguished.
Thus, "the non-origination of worms within the body" is the twelfth sign among them.
"Subhūti said," and so forth, until "furthermore.
The state of having few tasks for the mind is due to its being limited and because it is undistracted.
Crookedness of the mind is its deviousness.
That which is a means for concealing one's own faults is *śāṭhya* (deceit); that which is for the purpose of deceiving others is *vaṅka* (crookedness);
and the display of non-existent virtues for the sake of deceiving others is *māyā* (guile).

Through the absence of these, there arise respectively: lack of crookedness of mind (*cittākauṭilya*), lack of deceitfulness of mind (*cittāśāṭhyatā*), lack of crookedness of mind (*cittāvaṅkatā*), and lack of guilefulness of mind (*cittāmāyāvitā*).
The remainder is easily understood.
Thus, "crookedness of mind" is the thirteenth sign among them.
"Furthermore," and so forth.
Here, by means of the prohibition against regarding gain and other such things as important, the adoption of the *dhuta* [ascetic] qualities is also understood.
Thus, "the undertaking of the *dhuta* qualities" is the fourteenth sign among them.
By the mention of "miserliness" (*mātsarya*) in the phrase "one becomes full of envy and self-miserliness," the adversaries of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are indicated.
Thus, "the state of being free from miserliness and so forth" is the fifteenth sign among them.
And [the passage] beginning with "not in the profound" and ending before "furthermore" [is explained as follows]:
*saṃsyandana* means conjunction.
Understanding that everything is consistent with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is "going in accordance with the nature of phenomena"; this is the sixteenth mark among them.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover" and ending with "should be upheld" [is as follows]:
"Confess" means confess through the recognition of a transgression;
"renounce" means abandon definitively and completely according to the specific rule.
"Thus" means when there is the abandonment of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
"Even so" means even in such a case as described by Māyā.
The rest is easily understood.
Thus, "for the sake of the world" (*lokārtha*) means that because the purpose of the worlds proceeds from this, there is "the seeking of hell" (*narakaiṣaṇā*), which is the acceptance of hell.
Among those [qualities], that is the seventeenth sign.
Furthermore, from the words "another [point]" up to "should be upheld":

confess whatever you have heard, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and so forth; renounce it! Abandon whatever you have grasped, such as the generation of the bodhicitta and the practice of the perfections!
A poet is one who speaks various things that are unreal;
his work is poetry (kāvya).
The element (dhātu) of the irreversible one is the primordial nature (prakṛti).
The phrase "of a nature not subject to regression" is to be connected with what follows.
The remainder is easily understood.
Thus, "independence from others" is the eighteenth mark among them.
From "Furthermore, another... up to "...should be upheld," [the text] disparages the path of the bodhisattva by means of such passages as "wandering in saṃsāra.
From "But right here, you... onwards, it causes one to adopt the path of the śrāvakas and others.
"Abhinirvṛtta" means one whose life-span is exhausted.
The word "vā" (or) indicates an alternative;
it will later state "in this very [life]," and so forth.
Or [the phrase] beginning with "Aho vatā" and so forth;
because the mind does not become agitated nor waver, one recognizes that which is spoken by Māra as being the inferior path spoken by Māra.
Therefore, this is the realization that Māra—who teaches another path—is not [the true] Māra. This is the nineteenth sign among them.
The passage beginning with "If she... and ending with "...should be maintained" [is as follows]:
seclusion (*viveka*) is the relinquishing of the Mahāyāna; the words for that purpose are the "words of seclusion" (*vivekapada*).
The connection is that, having heard those things from others or from Māra, the mind does not fall away;
the meaning is that it does not waver.
To the question "Why?", he says:

"Of the *dharmatā*" means that the *dharma* itself is the *dharmatā*, namely the practice of the Mahāyāna; "does not turn back" means it does not become averse; "does not become otherwise" means there is no reversal.
The meaning is that there is no great respect for the Hīnayāna.
"Those" refers to the words of discernment.
The word "ca" (and) indicates a reason.
Because he knows the deeds of Māra;
"it is impossible" is to be connected with what follows.
"In that way" means as described by the Buddhas.
The remainder is easily understood. Thus ends the twentieth [chapter], "The Conduct Approved by the Buddhas," among those [chapters], concerning its characteristic mark.
Established in the levels of heat, summits, patiences, and the supreme mundane dharmas,
he does not turn back from perfect enlightenment due to these twenty signs.
This is the summary:
one who, abiding in the aids to penetration such as "heat" (ūṣmagata) and the others, is characterized by these twenty signs, does not turn back from perfect enlightenment;
that is the meaning of being "irreversible" (avinivartanīya).
With reference to one established on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the treatise states:

[105] Six moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) in the path of seeing—these five and five [moments] should be known as the characteristics of the non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) Bodhisattva. (4-46)

The irreversible signs of a bodhisattva established on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) should be known. What are they? They are the moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) and the moments of knowledge (*jñāna*), characterized by receptivity and knowledge. "Six, five, and five" means sixteen.

Which sixteen? [106] The turning away from perceptions of form and so forth; firmness of mind regarding the two inferior vehicles; the cessation of those two vehicles; and the complete exhaustion of the factors of dhyāna and so forth. // 4-47 //
Lightness of body and mind, the skillful means for engaging in sensual desires, constant practice of celibacy, and the purity of one’s livelihood. (4-48)

[108] It is not [the case] regarding the aggregates and so forth, the obstacles, the provisions, the sense faculties and so forth, the battle, and stinginess and so forth; nor is it [the case] regarding application and devoted practice. (4-49)
[109] There is the prohibition regarding the monastery, the non-apprehension of even the subtlest dharma, certainty regarding one’s own stage, and abiding in the three stages. // 4-50 //
[110] The sacrifice of life for the sake of the Dharma—these sixteen moments are the signs of non-retrogression for the wise one established on the path of seeing. 4-51.
Regarding that, he states the first [point] with the passage beginning with "Furthermore" and ending with "should be maintained.
"He brings about" (abhisaṃskaroti) means "he produces" (utpādayati).
"He does not perceive even that dharma," meaning he does not perceive form and so forth;
here, perception itself is the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*),
and that itself is production (*utpādana*).

The term *anutpādajñāne kṣāntir asya* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "one who possesses receptivity toward the knowledge of non-arising. Thus, "the cessation of the perception of form and so forth" is the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
This is the first sign of that [receptivity] on the path of seeing (*dṛṅmārga*).
Furthermore, from "punaraparam" up to "dhārayitavyam":
"vicchandyiṣyati" means he will cause [the mind] to be free from desire;
"ājñāsyati" means he will know by means of supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*).
You are frustrated and afflicted;
"separation" refers to the abandonment of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*);
"therein" means in the context of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
"With a firm mind" means that for the sake of firmness of mind regarding perfect enlightenment, there is the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering;
this is the second sign on the path of seeing.

"Furthermore, from the beginning up to the end"— this is the "turning away from the Hīnayāna," which is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*). This is the third mark on the path of seeing (*dṛṅmārga*).
The passage beginning with "sa ākāṅkṣan" and ending with "veditavya" should be understood as follows:
thus, the "exhaustion of the factors of meditation and so forth" refers to the weakness [of the path] when the arising of desire is obstructed; it is the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering.
That is the fourth sign on the path of seeing.
The section beginning with "Furthermore" and ending before "if he...
[is as follows]: here, the passage starting with "he is not weighed down by names" refers to "lightness of mind";
the passage starting with "as he steps forward" refers to "lightness of body."
The receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding both of those [truths] is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding origination;
it is the fifth sign on the path of seeing.
"Sa cet" and so forth refers to what precedes "anarthikāt. As previously stated, the very designation is the means; by that, it is established as "the means consisting in the practice of non-desire.
That is the dharma-knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering].
That is the sixth [moment] on the path of seeing; that is its mark.
The passage beginning with "and indeed without desire" and ending with "should be maintained" [is explained as follows]:
because they produce extreme mental gladness, they are "of a pleasant form";
because they produce extreme physical pleasure, they are "of a gratifying form."
The suffix *rūpa* is optionally used in the sense of praise;
thus, "only those who are without desire" means they are eternally without desire.
"Not by way of the even and the uneven" means not by what is appropriate and inappropriate.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"By means of dharma alone," and so forth.
*Apamardana* means affliction.

The sixteen terms beginning with "by noble persons" (satpuruṣaiḥ) are due to their association with the five factors conducive to liberation, the four factors conducive to penetration, and the seven moments of vision.
Thus, "always practicing celibacy" refers to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering];
that is the seventh sign on the path of vision.
Furthermore, from "another" (*punarapara*) up to "should be maintained" (*dhārayitavya*):
the class of mantras (*mantrajāti*) is a specific type of mantra belonging to a planetary deity;
the medicinal herb (*auṣadhi*) ends with the ripening of its fruit (*phalapākāntā*).
The mantra of a female deity is a *vidyā*;
"medicine" refers to medicinal herbs; by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of yantras, mantras, and other such means is intended.
"Physical conflict is quarreling with the body, while verbal conflict is disputing with speech"—this is "purity of livelihood. This is the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin [of suffering];
it is the eighth sign on the path of vision.
Regarding five moments from the ninth [moment] onwards, the treatise states: "In the aggregates and so forth, in the obstacles, in the provisions, in the sense-faculties and so forth,
in conflict, and in envy and so forth— there is no [application] in the case of application and further application."
"And there is a prohibition regarding the monastery. "Yoga" is an activity accompanied by attachment;
"anuyoga" is an activity free from attachment.
The dwelling of those two is their "vihāra"; the samādhi possesses that [dwelling].
Its "negation" (apratiṣedha) is due to its connection with the negative particle "na," as indicated by the word "not. This is the meaning.
Furthermore, that dwelling is the first with respect to the aggregates and so forth;
the second with respect to obstacles;
and the third with respect to the provisions.

The fourth [chapter] concerns "battles involving the senses and so forth"; the fifth concerns "envy and so forth. Regarding the former, he speaks starting from "Furthermore... up until "and they do not quarrel... and so on.
"Not those aggregates, sense-bases," and so forth.
"Yogānuyoga" means yoga and subsequent yoga; those who are "anuyukta" are those joined with that [yoga]. The prefix *anu* is used here in the sense of "together with."
The connection is "they do not dwell. Here, the proof has been stated by the two Blessed Ones: "For thus, established in emptiness, he does not perceive any dharma as inferior or superior.
He expresses this very point in two statements.
The side of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*) is "delight in socializing" because it has as its object the delight in socializing due to its lack of essence.
That very [affliction] is "discourse" because, being non-existent, it is a mere talk.
The rest is as before.
Because it is superior, there is the cessation of the defilements of the *rājasa* [nature].
That very thing is called "discourse" (*kathā*) because, being not yet directly realized, it is merely discourse;
these two are indeed the two types of discourse.

As applicable in subsequent instances as well, the absence of dwelling upon the application and investigation of the aggregates and so forth is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation;
that is the ninth sign on the path of seeing.
The five hindrances are thieves because they carry away the wealth of wholesome qualities;
the rest is as before.
This is the dharma-knowledge regarding cessation.
That is the tenth sign on the path of seeing.
The equipment of wholesome dharmas is the army;
the rest is as before.
This is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.
That is the eleventh sign on the path of seeing.
War is the affliction of adversaries by means of that army;
the rest is as before.
When war occurs, cessation is attained.
Cessation is *nirvāṇa*, which is liberation.
And what is this? It is the transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of those representations (*vijñapti*) that manifest as the body, its support, and its enjoyment.
Therefore, because they do not conceptualize the body and so forth, they dwell engaged in the practice of discourse concerning villages, cities, towns, districts, nations, and royal capitals.
In this context, the pentad beginning with the eye is the body (*deha*),
for it is a "village" (*grāma*) because it is a collection of sense-faculties (*indriya-grāma*).
It is the "foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*) or city because it serves as the support for bodies.
Because it is accessible to those with controlled faculties, *nigama* refers to enjoyment, namely the five sense objects;
*janapada* and so forth refer to specific types of dwellings;
and when the conceptualization of "self" and "mine" has ceased, there is liberation (*mokṣa*).
Then, with reference to the conceptualization of a self, he says:
"There is no discourse on a self," and so forth.
With reference to the conceptualization of what belongs to a self, he says:
"O Minister," and so forth.
From this point onward, these discourses should be understood as being, as appropriate, either conceptualizations of self, conceptualizations of enjoyment, or conceptualizations of the foundation.
If they do not dwell in such ways, then how do they dwell? To this he says:
"Is it not so," and so forth.
How is the perfection of wisdom itself discernment?
The remainder is as before.

The meaning is that they dwell exclusively devoted to the application and practice of equality through the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in all respects. "Connected with omniscience" means connected with the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
The absence of dwelling in the application and practice of discourse concerning the faculties for battle and so forth is the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding cessation.
That is the twelfth sign on the path of seeing.
"And regarding envy and so forth," says the scripture.
As it is said in the *Mahatyau*:

"While practicing the perfection of generosity, he does not dwell intent upon the practice of talk concerning envy, up to: while practicing the perfection of wisdom, he does not dwell intent upon the practice of talk concerning depravity."
Regarding this, he says:
"And they do not dwell devoted to the application and pursuit of talk concerning quarrels, strife, conflict, and disputes.
Quarrels and so forth are [listed] because they are adverse factors; [specifically,] stinginess and the like.
Quarrels arise from envy and other such states because they are their opposites;
punishments and the like arise because they are the absence of those opposites.
When both types of factors circulate within the mind with equal strength, there is conflict.
But when the adverse factors are weakened by their counteragents, then there is dispute (*vivāda*).

These two—conflict (*vigraha*) and dispute (*vivāda*)—are forms of discourse because they consist of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*). One does not dwell engaged in the application and practice of such discourse.
Non-differentiation is the knowledge of equality;
differentiation is the conceptualization of manifoldness.
The passage beginning with "those who desire friends" and ending with "should be maintained" is easy to understand.
Thus is the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path;
it is the thirteenth mark on the path of seeing.
From "Furthermore, another... up to "...if that were so," he says this:
"The non-attainment of the subtle dharma."
"And certainty regarding one's own level.
He does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that turns back, nor does he perceive you as turning back by means of such a turning back.
Nevertheless, he becomes free from doubt regarding his own stage of non-retrogression.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is uncertainty;
despondency (*saṃsīdana*) is a lack of enthusiasm.
"By means of an immediate mind" means by means of immediate remorse;
"dispelling" means relinquishing it in every respect.
Obstructing is the act of making [the mind] dull.
The irreversible mind is the certainty regarding one's own irreversibility.
It is unassailable and cannot be turned back.
Thus, on the stage of non-retrogression, "the state of having unshakable certainty" regarding the path is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*);
that is the fourteenth sign on the path of seeing (*dṛṅmārga*).
"The abiding on the three stages" refers to three points:

the deeds of Māra, the alteration of what was spoken by the Tathāgata, and the future attainment of one's own perfect enlightenment; these three points constitute the "three stages. "Abiding" upon them [is the meaning]. (RSt 116)
This is the ultimate certainty;
he states it with the passage beginning "If indeed... and ending with "...should be maintained."
"In this very life" means in this very birth.
The word "before" (pūrva) is to be understood as following the phrase "this Tathāgata is not [so]";
thus, when it is said "it is so and not otherwise," it is understood by implication: "I shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

"Buddha-adhiṣṭhāna" means the emanation of a Buddha. "Addhā" means in reality. Thus, this is the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) on the path of abiding in the three stages.
That is the fifteenth sign on the path of seeing.
Furthermore, from the words "Moreover" (*punaraparam*) up until the end of the chapter:
the abandonment of oneself refers to selling oneself and so forth;
the abandonment of life refers to death.

The Dharma taught by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is that all phenomena are empty; yet foolish people reject that very teaching. For its own preservation and for others to uphold it, one would even sacrifice one's life.
For he applies that same love and reverence toward the Dharma which he has for the Buddhas,
because of his knowledge that the Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body and because of his vision of his own future Buddhahood.
The phrase "of a śrāvaka as well" is an elliptical expression; it includes "of a bodhisattva as well" and "of gods and others as well. The remainder is easy to understand.
"The sacrifice of life for the sake of the Dharma" is the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding the path;
that is the sixteenth mark on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"Thus, these sixteen moments are the signs of non-retrogression for the wise one established on the path of seeing."
Thus is the conclusion.
That chapter which elucidates the aspects, signs, and marks of one who is irreversible is called "that chapter."
The seventeenth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
18. The Eighteenth Chapter, titled "Emptiness.
The signs of non-retrogression regarding the path of vision and the limbs of penetration have been explained both numerically and specifically;
however, the path of cultivation is profound.
Therefore, those [points] cannot be explained in either way;
hence the treatise states:
[111] "The path of cultivation is profound."
This is what he says with the passage beginning with "Then indeed... and ending with "...by the Pratyekabuddhas.
"It is wonderful, Blessed One! is one objection.
To the question "What is wonderful? he replies:
"Of great qualities," and so forth.
(RSt 117) It is a "great accumulation of qualities" because of its supreme profundity and because it is obtained through uninterrupted effort for two incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
For this very reason, they are "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) because they cannot be specifically known, and "unlimited" (*aparimita*) because they cannot be numbered.

"A bodhisattva mahāsattva" refers to one who is irreversible and established on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). "By means of one who is irreversible" refers to one established on the path of cultivation. It is "endless" because it transcends numerical calculation.
Because it is supremely sublime, it is boundless;
it is unassailable, perfectly ungraspable, and impossible even for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to fully comprehend—such is the profundity of the path of cultivation.
Subhūti said, and so forth; [the meaning is that] although he is capable and able to explain it,
the implication is that it would not be for the benefit of sentient beings.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"For this very reason," and so forth.
The particle *eva* is displaced in its position.
It should be understood that "places" (*sthānāni*) follows from what comes after this;
"all are profound" (*sarvāṇi gambhīrāṇi*) has the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
"Places" refers to the objects of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"Connected with the perfection of wisdom" means having that as their support. "They should be pointed out" means let them be indicated. This is Subhūti’s request.
"Thus spoken," and so forth; "having begun" means having first pointed out.
"Desirous of concluding" means desirous of applying [the teaching] to the path of cultivation;
this is the Blessed One’s acceptance. Now, the treatise:
Profundity consists of emptiness and so forth;
that profundity is the state of being free from the extremes of superimposition and denial. (4.52)
It has been stated that "the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is profound.
Its "profundity" is the state of being profound. That by which it becomes profound is emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), and so forth.
The meaning is that the profundity of the path arises from the profundity of its objective support (*ālambana*).
And that objective support is "emptiness and so forth" (*śūnyatādi*).
What, then, is the profundity of emptiness and so forth?
The Blessed One said, "It is profound," and so forth, in order to indicate that which is free from both the extreme of superimposition and the extreme of denial, as he has accepted it.

The emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all phenomena is their mode of existence as they appear and their mode of existence according to reality. That very [emptiness] is the signless (*animitta*), because for one who knows it, signs are ceased.
That very [emptiness] is the wishless (*apraṇihita*), because for those who know it, there is no aspiration toward the triple world.
That itself is their non-conditioning, because they do not perform karma for the sake of renewed existence;
that itself is their non-arising, because there is no arising through that karma;
that itself is their non-birth, because of the knowledge of their innate non-birth.
That itself is non-existence because it is not a substantial entity;
that itself is the purity of dispassion because of the total eradication of the latent tendencies of the afflictions;
that itself is cessation because of the cessation of those [afflictions] from further rebirth.
That itself is their nirvāṇa, because of the total eradication of their latent predispositions; that itself is their departure, because of the cessation of the aggregates associated with outflows.
Thus [is explained] emptiness and so forth.
Subhūti said: this means he asks by way of a rhetorical question.
"Of phenomena" refers to emptiness and so forth;
"of all phenomena" refers to the aggregates, elements, and so forth.
Since forms and so forth are grasped by the ignorant, how can they be profound?
Therefore, he asks himself, "And how," and so on. The answer begins with, "Just as suchness," and so forth.
If it is asked, "Whose suchness is this?", he says "therein," and so forth.
To make it clear, he says "as follows," and so forth.
"Where" means when that suchness of form and so forth is being experienced, the imagined form and so forth do not appear; this is the profundity of form and the other aggregates.
Because they appear in their ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*),
Subhūti, being satisfied by this correct teaching, said,
"It is marvelous," and so forth.
"By the subtle" means by that which is to be known with precision;
and by this, Nirvana is indicated,
because for one established on the path of cultivation who is irreversible, all imagined [phenomena] no longer appear.
And it is excluded from form and so forth,
because their ultimate reality is made manifest therein; thus,
by means of nirvāṇa, the extreme of superimposition regarding form and so forth is eliminated.
Thus is the profundity of emptiness and so forth.
Now, the treatise states:

[112] "Reflection, deliberation, and profound contemplation constitute the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-patha) when occurring repeatedly in the factors of penetration (nirvedha-bhāgīya), on the path of seeing (dṛṅ-mārga), and indeed on the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga). (4.53)

"Constantly" means continuously. Therefore, "reflection, deliberation, and profound contemplation" occurring in a continuous series constitute the nature of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Emptiness and so forth are its objective supports (*ālambana*).
The bases for emptiness and so forth are the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
If it is asked how this alone is the object of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), he says:
[113] "Because it is continuous, this is accepted [as its object]."
For the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is continuous;
therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that first the object (*viṣaya*) is ordinary and subsequently the subject (*viṣayin*) is [supramundane].
Regarding this, the Blessed One spoke in the Sūtra, beginning with the words "The Blessed One said," and so forth.

"These" refers to those previously mentioned [topics] such as emptiness and so forth. "Associated with the perfection of wisdom" means that the very perfection of conceptualization is wisdom; this perfection of wisdom consists of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
However, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) because they have that as their purpose;
the meaning is that they are associated with, connected to, and supported by that threefold [perfection of wisdom].
The connection is: "whoever shall contemplate, weigh, and examine these."
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Thus have I [heard]," and so forth;
one should remain [in that state] by reflecting on it with single-minded certainty.
"One should train" means the arising of calm abiding (*śamatha*) through comparative investigation;
"one should practice" means the arising of insight (*vipaśyanā*) through close contemplation;
and "it has been taught" means through hearing the scriptural texts.
It is "declared" (*ākhyāta*) because it makes the meaning known; it is "instructed" (*upadiṣṭa*) because it proclaims the secret [teachings]. There are four reasonings:
the reasoning of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*), because the arising of an effect depends upon all causes.

The principle of causal efficacy (*kāryakāraṇayukti*) is because specific effects arise from each of those [causes] individually. The principle of logical proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*) is that by which a given object is established through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*) is the fixed nature of things, such as "fire alone burns" and "water alone moistens," and so forth. Based on these,
reflection (*cintā*) consists of investigating the object of meditative concentration in seclusion, having ascended the cross-legged posture, with reverence and continuity.
In that very state, the equalizing and weighing of the mind by means of ninefold calm abiding (śamatha) constitutes close contemplation;
this refers to insight (vipaśyanā) with its four aspects, which consists of discerning, thoroughly discerning, reflecting upon, and entering into thorough investigation of phenomena (dharma).

In this context, the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtatā-jñāna*) is investigation (*vicaya*). The thorough discernment (*pravicaya*) is the knowledge of things as they truly are, such as [the realization] that "there are only the five aggregates" and so forth.
Thorough reflection (*parivitarka*) is the mental formation of signs by means of non-conceptual mentation accompanied by wisdom, such as [the realization] that "all these are empty" and so forth.
Investigation and thorough examination:
such is the intrinsic nature of the path of cultivation.
And it is ninefold by way of its types;
that path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) becomes ninefold according to the distinction of its types. By the word "and" (ca), the counter-factors (vipakṣa) are also ninefold.
He asks, "How so? and replies:
"Furthermore, by way of the distinctions of weak, medium, and intense [levels of the faculties]. (4-54)
The weakest of the weak; the middling of the weak; the strongest of the weak;
the weakest of the middling.
The medium-medium;
the medium-intense;
the intense-weak.
These are the medium-strong,
and the strong-strong;
these same nine types also apply to the opposing factors.
In this regard, these types of the path arise in direct order;
by means of them, the types of the opposing factors are exhausted in reverse order,
from the highest-of-the-high (adhimātrādhimātra) through the middle-of-the-high (adhimātramadhya), down to the lowest-of-the-low (mṛdumṛdu).
And that adverse side consists of the conceptualizations of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, according to their respective order;
for just as coarse dirt is squeezed out from a cloth first and subtle dirt afterwards,
so it is with the mind as well.
Therein, the first [section] is by means of "tathā" and so forth;
the second is by means of "evam" and so forth. Then, from "yathā punaraparam" up to the end of "prasavati," there are two [sections]; then, from "punaraparam" onwards until before "Subhūtir āha."
"Thus," and so forth.
"Thus" means accomplishing by means of *śamatha* according to the sequence already described;
"contemplating" (*upanidhyāyana*) means by means of *vipaśyanā*.
Examining by means of both,
he applies himself through the vigor of calm abiding and exerts himself through the vigor of insight.
Exerting himself with both types of vigor,
the Blessed One himself asks, "How much karma does he perform? and he himself provides the answer, beginning with the words "Just as," and so forth.
The qualities that produce serenity are "inspiring" (*prāsādika*);
the suffix *-ac* here has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
"Appropriated by another" means belonging to another; one should not bring her under one's control, nor would one be able to do so.
"From cyclic existence" means from the continuity of births that does not turn back; "he casts off" means he abandons or turns his back upon it.
Because there is no coming of what is yet to come;
"he brings to an end" means he leads [the past] back to the prior limit from the subsequent limit.
"Just as it was commanded," and so forth, is as explained previously.
"According to what was indicated and according to what was explained" refers to the initial presentation; "he abides" by means of reflection through the cutting off of doubt;
"he trains" by means of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
One practices by means of insight (*vipaśyanā*);
one reflects by means of both.
In this way, one enters into the cultivation of yoga.
By this much, one action has been explained.
He states the second [action] with the words beginning with "tāṃśca" and ending with "samyaksambodheḥ. Thus ends the weak-weak stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
"Thus," and so forth: "thus" means as just stated.
"That much karma" refers to the bringing to completion of many kalpas and the avoidance of faults that cause one to turn back from perfect enlightenment.
He speaks further with the words beginning "yathā" and so forth, prior to the subsequent [verse].
"Tataḥ" means from the donor.
This very [person] is distinguished and excels by virtue of possessing much greater merit;
therefore, he says: "Whosoever this... and so forth.
Thus concludes the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) at the stage of weak-middling.
"Furthermore," and so forth:
one should give with a mirror-like clarity;
one should establish [the gift] with freedom from regret.
Thus concludes the path of cultivation at the stage of weak-intensity-high.
"Again," and so forth.
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) is the dwelling (*vihāra*).
Thus, this is the middle-mild stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
By the words "again," and so forth, the middle-middle path of cultivation is indicated.
"Again," and so forth.
Having emerged from meditative absorption, one should teach the Dharma and dedicate that [merit] toward enlightenment; this is the middle-intense stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

"Furthermore, others... and so forth. And that gift of Dharma should be dedicated by means of the dedication taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*; this is the "superior-mild" stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

having dedicated that gift of Dharma through the dedication described in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he again applies himself to yoga in solitary retreat. This is the "intense-middle" stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, for one who practices that withdrawal from society without being separated from the perfection of wisdom, that is their path of cultivation of the highest-of-the-high degree.
"Subhūti said," and so forth.

Volitional formation (*abhisaṃskāra*) is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Meritorious volitional formation is likewise so.
Therefore, when it is said that "merit is more abundant," it must be understood that conceptual construction is what is meant by "more abundant."
The Blessed One replied with the words beginning with "He too" and ending with "produces," starting from "uttaram bhagavānāha.
"Now" refers to the time of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It is empty because it lacks existence according to its [apparent] characteristics.

It is empty because it lacks an owner;

"Thus" means by means of emptiness and so forth.
The remainder is easily understood.

"Subhūti said," and so forth.
"Excellence" (*utkarṣa*) is also a distinction (*viśeṣa*);

The expressions and sounds for the inexhaustible, immeasurable, emptiness, signlessness, and so forth—surely these sounds are also diverse; how then can they [refer] to a single object?
