For this very reason, it says: "This is the accomplishment of teaching. Teaching (*deśanā*) is that by which something is taught; it is compassion (*karuṇā*). Its accomplishment (*abhinirhāra*) is its outflow (*niṣyanda*), and that is also the exposition (*nirdeśa*).
On this point, the treatise states:
[114] Designations such as "incalculable" and so forth are not tenable from the perspective of ultimate reality;
O Sage, they are accepted conventionally as being the natural outflow of compassion.
"It is not appropriate [to say] 'it is not patient'";
thus are the objections and their resolutions regarding the teaching of the incalculable and so forth.
Subhūti said: "It is wonderful," and so forth, up until the words "but indeed. Because they are beyond the range of speech, they are inexpressible.
"Of the meaning of the perfections" refers to that which has the characteristic of emptiness.
Regarding this, the treatise states:
[115] "Decrease and increase are not applicable to a reality that is beyond verbal expression."
What is lacking in the path called cultivation (bhāvanā), and what has been attained by it? (4.56)
Thus, there is an absence of decrease or increase in that which is ineffable.
How, then, is there awakening? To this he says: "But indeed," and so on, until the end of the chapter.
"He, while giving a gift, [should attend] to those mental orientations and those productions of thought by which he gives the gift."
And those roots of merit are those which are associated with those productions of the thought of awakening; for it is in this way that one transforms them toward awakening—
otherwise, that transformation would not be for the sake of awakening.
The same should be understood for the subsequent [directions] as well.
As it was said, "unexcelled perfect enlightenment," he therefore asks with the words beginning "Then indeed... and so forth.
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, this suchness is unexcelled, perfect enlightenment," and so forth. "Repeatedly" means again and again; "frequently" means in a continuous stream.
The conclusion is indeed expressed by the words "Thus, indeed," and so forth.
On this point, the treatise states:
[116] Just as awakening is, so too is this [path] the accomplisher of the desired goal.
Enlightenment has the characteristic of suchness; he too is considered to have that same characteristic. (4-57)
The term "this one" (asau) and "that one too" (so 'pi) refer to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
The chapter in which emptiness is the primary subject is the "Chapter on Emptiness."
The eighteenth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
Chapter Nineteen: The Chapter on the Sister Gaṅgadevā.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha khalu" and so forth, there is an objection: awakening is attained neither by the preceding thought nor by the subsequent one, because those two do not coexist.
"Thus spoken," and so forth, refers to what was previously stated.
By this much, the refutation has been made by means of the analogy of the lamp.
On this point, the treatise says:
[117] "Awakening is not joined with the preceding mind, nor with the succeeding mind"— this is the objection;
it is resolved by means of the analogy of the lamp.
"Bodhi" is understood [from the previous context];
by this, the refutation is provided.
Now, the treatise states:
"The profound nature of phenomena is eightfold. (4-58)
The term "enlightenment" (bodhi) continues [from the previous context].
In the eighteenth [chapter], the characteristic of enlightenment alone was stated to be suchness itself;
however, for enlightenment together with its equipment, the characteristic is the eightfold profundity.
How is that eightfold?
[118] Depth regarding arising and cessation, regarding suchness, regarding the object of knowledge and knowledge, regarding conduct, and regarding non-duality and skill in means. (4-59)
"Non-duality and skill in means"—
this is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
Therefore, with the words "Thus it was said," and so forth, Subhūti introduces the profundity that was previously mentioned.
"Except for those" means "without those.
When it was thus spoken, from the words "the Blessed One," etc., up to the end of "he practices mastery," he explains the eightfold profundity.
"That which is mind" refers to that which is deluded, consisting of the imagination of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
"Ceased" means exhausted through the destruction of the continuum;
"no indeed" means "not at all.
The sense is that this is due to the exhaustion of the cause of delusion, namely, the adherence to duality.
Thus is the profundity of arising.
The phrase "the mind that has arisen" means it is non-delusory;
the sense is that because delusion is destroyed and because the arising of the mind is dependent upon the mind itself.
"O Blessed One, it is subject to cessation" means it ceases at every moment.
"It will cease" means by the cessation of the continuum;
the sense is that this is not so, because [the mind] arises by its own natural force and has been rendered specifically inexhaustible through aspirations and other means.

Regarding what was said concerning the profundity of arising—that "the mind which has not arisen"—and what was said immediately thereafter that "it is not subject to cessation," there is a redundancy in saying "that which is subject to cessation" in this context.
It may be so.
"That which is mind" refers to the continuum of mind.
"Having the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing" refers to that phenomenon called *nirvāṇa*, which is without beginning or end.
Cessation is that which has ceased.
That which has this as its intrinsic nature is "ceased by intrinsic nature.
Dharmatā is emptiness.
Thus is the profundity of cessation.
It will remain just so as long as space exists;
yet it is not immutable, being like suchness.
The meaning is: "Not indeed so," because of the permanence of the continuum.
The profundity of suchness (*tathatā*) is due to its subtlety even compared to correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
The thought that "the mind is within suchness" implies that it is something to be contained therein because it is experienced as such;
however, this is not so, because where there is no distinction in knowledge, it is impossible for there to be an object of experience.
The intended meaning is that the mind and suchness possess a single characteristic.

It is not so, because even though there is a difference in characteristics, they are identical in essence. Thus, although it is ungraspable, suchness is what is to be known; this is the profundity of the object of knowledge.
"Do you perceive the form of the mind?
"No, indeed," because it is ungraspable.
That very mind knows itself as the object of perception; this is the profundity of gnosis.
"He courses in the profound" means in the sense of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The manifestations are the signs of the objective referents;
they proceed, yet they do not exist.
They do not manifest and they do not appear; this is the profundity of practice.
"He courses in a sign" means he courses in either the sign of duality or the sign of non-duality.
"No, indeed" means neither in the sign of duality nor in the sign of non-duality.
"Sign" refers to the signs of both duality and non-duality.
"Unmanifested" means not abandoned.
"No, indeed" means it is not un-abandoned;
the meaning is that it is precisely abandoned.
Such is the profundity of non-duality.
"Api nu" means "how could it be? The sense is: "Is the sign manifested when all the Buddha-qualities are not yet fulfilled? Subhūti spoke this reply:
"Not so, Blessed One," and so forth; "in this very life" means in this very birth.
To the question "Why?", he says:
"If he were," and so forth.
"He would be a śrāvaka" means he would not be a *samyaksambuddha*.
The conclusion is given by the words "this is that," and so forth:

he knows all that which has a characteristic and that which has a cause—that is, both the characteristic of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*) and the characteristic of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-nimitta*).
He performs mere mastery, which is simply repeated practice.
Such is the profundity of skill in means.
Among these, the eighth profundity is remote;
the remaining [profundities] regarding awakening are proximate—such is the profundity as previously described.
And it has been stated: "The group of those in training who are irreversible."
"The equality of existence and peace" must be explained.
Therefore, the treatise states:
[119] Because all phenomena are like a dream, there is no conceptualization of existence and peace.

The conceptual construction that "this is saṃsāra" and "this is nirvāṇa" is abandoned on the path of cultivation through the knowledge of the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; for one who perceives all phenomena as like a dream, no distinction between the two is apprehended.
Is it not the case that unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is saṃsāra, and that is mere delusion, while the destruction of delusion is nirvāṇa?
When, then, is there the knowledge of their equality?
If you say: "When the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) has become manifest, because of the direct realization of the selflessness of all phenomena," [we reply:]...
If this [equality] exists even on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), what is the excellence of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
Therefore, it must be understood that the knowledge of equality belongs to one who has emerged from that [path of seeing];
and that is untenable.

For the knowledge of one who has emerged [from meditative absorption] is deluded because it is like a dream; the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), however, is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) because it is like the day. In that regard, when would it be appropriate [to say that the former is like a dream]?
If, due to the excellence of daily practice, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) should increase even during sleep,
then the question [is raised] in the Sūtra by the passage beginning with "Then indeed" (*atha khalu*) and ending with "increases" (*vivardhate*).
The reply, beginning with "Subhūti said" and ending with "should be cultivated," states:
"non-conceptual. Here, "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) means differentiation (*viśeṣa*).
Non-conceptual and without distinction;
"through the practice of the perfection of wisdom" means through the practice of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Thus is the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
"Śāriputra said," and so forth.
Here, by the word "dream," the dream itself is meant.
"The perception of destruction" means that destruction is nirvāṇa; it is the perception, that is, the grasping, of that.
Conceptualization (*kalpa*) is the construction of an object as it truly is;
discursive thought (*vikalpa*) is the construction of an object falsely.
It is exactly so.
Like space or like the Tathāgata,
mind, volition, intellect, and conceptualization have one and the same meaning;
"secluded" means they are devoid of intrinsic nature.
For a deranged intellect takes even that which does not exist as its cause and makes it its objective support (*ālambana*).
The passage beginning with "volition (*cetanā*) also" is easy to understand.
Regarding the term "body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*"), the "body" (*kāya*) refers to the basis (*āśraya*).
Through the transformation of that [basis], one who realizes [the truth] with the body is a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*); he will resolve this objection, meaning he will provide the answer.
*Ajita* and *Maitreya* are synonyms.
That dharma which would resolve [the objection] is Maitreya.
"Should be dismissed" is the question;
"by which dharma" refers to speech;
"of which dharma" refers to Śāriputra.
The desire to tremble is *uttrāsa*;
the trembling that has arisen is *santrāsa*;
and the continuous flow of that is *santrāsāpatti*.
The reinforcement [of the path] is cultivation; it is the powerful latent impression (*balavāsanā*).
Regarding this, the treatise states:
"The refutations of objections such as the non-existence of karma have been explained as previously stated. (4.60)
Thus end the objections and their refutations regarding the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
"The supreme purity of action" must be explained.
Therefore, the treatise states:
[120] "By means of bringing about the purification of that impurity which belongs to the world of sentient beings."
Likewise, there is the purity of the vessel-world as a Buddha-field. // 4-61 //
At one time, that in which only a single Buddha is born is a buddha-field.
Its purity is its complete purification. From what does that arise?
"The impurity" of the world of sentient beings— such as that caused by wild beasts and wildernesses— is seen;
[this is for the sake of] its removal through the purification of one's own buddha-field,
so that "in my buddha-field, may such things never exist in any way whatsoever."
This has been explained at length in the *Mahatyoh*;
here, however, it is presented in brief.
Furthermore, from the words "Moreover" (*punaraparam*) up until "Then indeed there" (*atha khalu tatra*), [the intermediate section is provided].
The prohibition against fear and so forth has been stated, and with reference to that, the words "furthermore" (*punar apara*) are to be explained.
A miserable state is a wilderness (*kāntāra*).
A wilderness infested by beasts of prey is a "beast-infested wilderness" (*vyāḍakāntāra*); a wilderness devoid of water is a "waterless wilderness" (*pānīyakāntāra*).
If the word "if" (yadi) is used in the sense of "provided that," then [the phrase] "divine enjoyment" and so forth refers to the sentient beings of all buddha-fields.
This was said in order to exclude the consumption of blood and such things.
Merely the relinquishment of all one's possessions is wholesome;
that these [beings] in this world—the receptacle world—are endowed with happiness.
They are "endowed with happiness" (sukhasamarpitāḥ) because happiness has been bestowed and placed within them. "Everywhere" (sarvataḥ) means in all places.
The "wilderness of disease" (vyādhikāntara) refers to the affliction of illness.

Now, from the words "Then indeed" up to the end of the chapter, he states what occurred during that teaching: "unattached" means unclinging.
"In the intermediate space, in the sky" means in the mere void.

The nineteenth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
Chapter Twenty: The Examination of Skill in Means (Upāyakauśalya).
The purification of the buddha-field has been explained;

Therefore, the treatise states:
[121] "Its object and its application are the transgression of the scriptural prohibitions."

"Transgressions such as those involving the flow [of the mind], etc.

Here, from the beginning up to the words "the limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi), the object is stated;

"Thus spoken," and so forth, up to "tadyathāpi": "not even concentrated" means not yet resolved upon as something to be directly realized; "in the meantime" refers to the period until his buddha-qualities have reached full maturity.

The remainder is easily understood.

pratibhāna means insightful intuition;
pratipatti means practice.
One who knows that which is appropriate for a particular time and so forth through such knowledge is "one who knows the time and so forth.
*Gati* is the serviceability (*karmanyatā*) of body, speech, and mind; one who has gone to—that is, attained—that *gati*.
Weapons and armor refer to things such as coats of mail;
mindfulness is recollection;
and intelligence is deliberation.
Gati is knowledge;
dhṛti is retention;
nīti is the knowledge of policy.
"Confident and wise"—here, "enemies" (*śātravāḥ*) refers to the obstacles themselves;
their transcendence by means of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) constitutes the first skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
The passage beginning with "tadyathāpīti" and ending before "tadyathāpi": "carati" means he moves;
"and he does not fall to the ground" is a negation of falling, which constitutes his staying.
"And not depending on anything" is a negation of a foundation;
"depending" means making it one's basis,
and "dwells" means remains.
"And even there" means that even while dwelling [in those stages], one is not dependent;
"falls because of being incomplete" means here that one does not fall, which is to say, one does not remain [stuck].
Skillful means is non-abiding because it is devoid of fixed abiding.
The phrase "tadyathāpīti" and so forth has already been explained previously.
"Vārayet" means one should place it in space itself.
"One should not allow falling" means one should not allow [the mind] to fall away;
just as an arrow shot upward is kept from falling for a long time by successive arrows, so too is that which brings about the ripening of the Buddha-dharmas.

The impetus given to the mind by successive moments of consciousness for the sake of direct realization— the functioning [of the mind] without deviating from that [impetus] is the means known as "according to the impetus" (yathāvedham).
When this had been said, and so forth, up until the previous section [ending with] "Furthermore":
he practices by means of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and dwells by means of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi-samāpatti*) is by means of both;
"mine" refers to "by me.
"Brings forth" means "accomplishes."
This is both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*), because it is a gateway to release.
It is the arousal of the mind and the actualization of the mind;
by this, he is a performer of what is difficult to do.
And this is an uncommon skillful means, because it is not shared with any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, from the first "again" up to the previous "again":
"sentient being," "self," and "person" [refer to the same];
the "faculties" are the five beginning with faith.
The powers are also five;
the factors of enlightenment are seven;
the path is eightfold.
The view of a sentient being (*sattvadṛṣṭi*) is attachment;
he has attained perfect awakening for the sake of abandoning that [view] among sentient beings.
Having reflected, "I shall teach sentient beings," his meditative attainment on emptiness and so forth is non-attachment (*asakti*).
Through union with that, the means is unattached.
Furthermore, from "another" onwards until "again another":
the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) refers to the notions of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth;
that is an apprehension (*upalambha*).
"For the sake of abandoning that," and so forth, is as explained previously.
Thus, the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) on emptiness and so forth is non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Through union with that, non-apprehension is the skillful means (*upāya*).
From "Furthermore" up to "from another [point]":
"woman," "man," "form," and "sound" are designations based on signs (*nimitta-saṃjñā*).
"For the sake of abandoning that," and so forth, is as explained previously.
In this way, the attainment of the signless is itself the signless;
through its application, the means is signless.

Furthermore, from "punaraparam" up to "yo hi," [it is explained that] the aspiration for the enjoyments of existence— such as the thought, "May I become a god, Śakra, or a universal monarch"— is *praṇihita* (aspiration). Its root is the cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*).
Therefore, for the sake of abandoning the four perversions, and so forth, as previously stated.
Likewise, the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) is itself wishless; through its application, the means (*upāya*) is wishless.
The passage beginning with "whosoever" and ending with "this situation does not exist" [is explained as follows]:
the means such as non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) have been stated to have the three doors of liberation as their object.
Now, he speaks of their further objects, such as the absence of volitional construction (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and their non-futility.
"May he fall into the unconditioned" refers to the inferior enlightenment;
"by means of the triple world" refers to saṃsāra.
"Thus," and so forth, up until "Subhūti said":
A bodhisattva who desires perfect enlightenment should question a wise bodhisattva, asking,
"For the sake of perfect enlightenment, what should I cultivate, and how should I cultivate it?"

If he should say, "Cultivate emptiness and so forth, and through mastery of that, you shall directly realize the Mother," and [should state that] the means therein consists of the mind that does not abandon any sentient being and so on—
this is the mark of the irreversibility of that teacher.
Therefore, that which has its mark in this is the "mark-possessing" (talliṅga) means.
Subhūti said, and so forth, up until the words "If, however... [at the beginning of the next section].
Among those many who practice for the sake of awakening, few are those who answer in this way;
they have been prophesied to be irreversible and are unassailable.
Because they are few compared to the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, they are of small measure; thus, the means (upāya) is immeasurable.
Thus, from the latter half of the ninth chapter through the first half of the twentieth, these eleven chapters constitute the "Complete Awakening to All Aspects" (sarvākārābhisambodhi).
From this point onward, the *mūrdhābhisamaya* (culminating clear realization) must be explained.
Its summary was previously stated in two verses plus one additional line:
Its signs, its increase, its firm establishment, and the stabilization of the mind;
And the antidote to the fourfold conceptual construction is likewise fourfold. // 1-14 //
[124] On each of the two paths called "seeing" and "cultivation," there is the immediate concentration (ānantarya-samādhi), together with the misconceptions.
[125] The Culminating Clear Realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*);
it has eight topics:
"the signs, increase, firmness, and the stabilization of the mind."

On the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are the adversaries and their antidotes; on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are the adversaries and their antidotes, as well as the errors regarding the immediate concentration (*ānantaryasamādhi*).
Regarding this, the treatise states with respect to the signs (*liṅga*):
[126] "Even in dreams, the non-existence of dreams and the vision of all phenomena, and so forth."
The signs of yoga that has reached its culmination are considered to be twelvefold. // 5.1 //
"Of one who has reached the summit" means of one who has attained excellence.
"Of yoga" refers to the practice of the three types of omniscience.
"If, moreover," and so forth, should be understood as follows.
Even when having entered into a dream, one sees all phenomena as being like a dream and does not realize them [as real]; this is the first sign.

Furthermore, from "another [point]" up to "should be known," it should be understood that even when in the midst of a dream, one does not harbor longing for the level of a Śrāvaka, the level of a Pratyekabuddha, or the triple world; this is the second [mark].
Furthermore, from "another" up to "should be known":
he sees himself, having entered into a dream, as the Tathāgata surrounded by a great assembly and encircled by both the Saṅghas; this is the third.
Furthermore, another distinction among the things to be known is as follows:
having ascended into the air while in a dream, he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings and perceives himself to be the span of an outstretched arm;
and he emanates monks who perform the work of a Buddha in other world-systems—this is the fourth.
Furthermore, from "another" up to "should be known":

even when in a dream, having seen the killing, binding, or decapitation of oneself or others, one does not become terrified. Upon awakening, one thinks: "The entire triple world is like a dream; having fully awakened to this, I must teach the Dharma in this way. This is the fifth [mark].
Furthermore, from "another [point]" up to "should be known," it should be understood as follows:
having seen beings such as those in the hells while in a dream, the thought occurs:
"I shall act in such a way that, when I have attained perfect awakening, the three lower realms will not exist at all in my Buddha-field. This is the sixth.
Furthermore, from "another [instance]" up to "another [instance]":
if, while dreaming, one perceives a village fire or similar event occurring, and upon waking, should reflect thus:
"Just as I have seen within my dream the signs of irreversibility in myself, by that truth may this village fire and so forth be extinguished."
If it quakes, that is the seventh sign.
Furthermore, from the beginning until the end of the chapter:
if any sentient being is seized, possessed, or entered by a non-human spirit— whether through external influence or internal penetration—
the Bodhisattva should perform an empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).

"If I have been prophesied by previous Buddhas for unexcelled enlightenment, and if my resolute intention is pure for awakening to it, and as there is nothing whatsoever unknown to the Buddhas—by this truth, let this non-human being depart. If he departs because of that empowerment of truth, that is the eighth sign.
This chapter is for the purpose of investigating and fully understanding skillful means.
The twentieth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
21. The twenty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Deeds of Māra.
Regarding the passage beginning with "There, indeed," this twenty-first chapter concerns the deeds of Māra.
What is their introduction?

It is this: Māras exert themselves in many ways to produce false pride in a bodhisattva who has newly set out in the vehicle, by means such as the fulfillment of the fruits of the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
This is their introduction.
In this context, "therein" refers to the foundation of truth just mentioned.
"Zeal" (*autsukya*) is the enthusiasm for performing an action whose opportunity has arrived.
"Power" (*bala*) is the capacity for such enthusiasm.

*Tejas* means power (*prabhāva-śakti*). As for the phrase "how much more powerful" (*tejovattaram*), since the suffix *tas* has the sense of possession (*matvartha*), there is no occasion for it to be a *bha*-stem; therefore, it should not be treated as a *bha*.
For example, as in the case of the venerable Sarasvat.
Thus, then, from the root *dru* in the sense of "shining," with the suffix *śatṛ* and the comparative *tarap*,
we have *tejovat-taram*, meaning "more shining by means of splendor" or "possessing more splendor."
"Zeal" means self-conceit;
"he will despise [others]," and so forth.
Disrespect is a lack of regard; derision is inward laughter; and deception is the mental act of making something other than what it is.
Censuring is the perception of faults;
reviling is the speaking of faults.
"In awakening" means: [as follows].
The word *iti* indicates the reason [for the following statement],
such as "it will produce a cognition" and so forth.
In this context, the word *sa* (that) means "everywhere."
*Janana* is production;
*vadha* is placing [something] at the forefront;
*stambhana* is making firm.
*Nṛmhaṇa* means nourishment; *utpādana* means raising up or lifting high;
"by means of measurement," and so forth.

The general definition of pride (*māna*) was previously stated as the elevation of the mind by way of superiority over others; here, however, its specific varieties are described. That elevation of the mind toward those who are inferior is *māna*.
That which arises from such [an inferiority] is overweening pride (*atimāna*). Furthermore, that which arises from superiority is pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).
That which thinks "I have attained" when irreversibility has not yet been attained is conceit (*abhimāna*).
Furthermore, to think "I am possessed of qualities" on account of non-existent qualities of irreversibility is false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
Likewise, the phrase "seeing Bodhisattvas as having such forms" is to be connected with the word "great elements" (*mahābhūta*);
the remainder [of the passage] serves as a qualification of those very [elements].
In the form *bhajiṣyate*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* because a rule conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not necessarily permanent.
"That itself is the bond of pride" refers to arrogance.
"Furthermore," and so forth.
"Designation by name" (nāmāpadeśa) means the mention of a name.
"Gentle" (mṛduka) means having dull faculties (mṛdvindriya).
"Dhutaguṇas" refers to qualities such as dwelling in the wilderness (āraṇyaka) and so forth.
Beyond one *krośa* from a village is the great forest;
because he stays in that very place, he is a forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*).
Because he eats only alms-food, he is an alms-food eater (*piṇḍapātika*).

One is a wearer of rag-robes (*pāṃsukūlika*) because of wearing clothing made from discarded rags, like refuse-rags. One is a "one-after-midday-meal" practitioner (*khalupaśśabdakika*) because of eating only at the very end of the midday period. One is a "single-seated" eater (*ekāsanika*) because one eats while remaining on a single seat.

One who always sleeps on what has been spread out once is a *yāthāsaṃstarika*. One who renounces anything in excess of the three robes is a *traicīvarika*. One who dwells only near a cemetery is a *śmāśānika*.
One who stays at the foot of a tree is a *vṛkṣamūlika*. One who spends the night in a sitting posture is a *naiṣadyika*.
An unsheltered open space is an *abhyavakāśa*.
By staying in that very place, one is an "open-air dweller" (*ābhyavakāśika*);
by wearing only woolen blankets and the like, one is a "clothed-in-rough-fiber" practitioner (*nāmantika*);
and by having few desires, one is "one of few wishes" (*alpeccha*).
He is content because he is satisfied with just that much;
he is secluded because of his solitude.
"Pertaining to the present life" (*dṛṣṭadhārmika*) means existing in this very life, in this very birth.
Therefore, he will instruct and designate [it].
To the question "How so?", he says: "Even previously," and so forth.
The word *yat* has the sense of *tasmāt* (therefore).
*Adhiṣṭhāna* means manifestation.

*Saṃlekha* refers to the thinning or emaciation by means of the *dhuta* qualities, like the drawing of a bowstring; the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used because it causes [the mind] to become haughty (*manyāṃ karoti*).
The meaning of "conceit" (*manyana*) is "pride" (*māna*).
The remainder is easily understood, up to the point that the qualities of ascetic purification (*dhutaguṇa*) exist.
As for the passage beginning with "Of him indeed," and so forth: [the text continues].
Regarding the phrase "by means of the empowerment of the name," what is the name here?
It is the word "irreversible" and the words denoting its qualities.
As for "overcome by arrogance," arrogance is a lack of respect toward one's gurus.
To the question "What is that name?", he says: "That which... and so forth.
"By him" means by the bodhisattva.
"Anuvartitam" means "anuvicintitam" (thoroughly reflected upon).
The latter two [verses] provide its explanation: "What indeed might my name be?"—this is "anuvitarkitam."
"This name shall be mine"—this is what has been reflected upon by me.
"He will prophesy" means Māra will declare it. "Anuvartita" means desired.
"It comes together" (*sameti*) means "it corresponds.
To the question "What corresponds with what?", he says: "Name with name.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "It is thus explained," and so forth.
"Having wandered and transmigrated," meaning having been born in various miserable states;
"and if" (*yadi cet*), the word "and" (*ca*) serves to indicate a conjunction; "subtle-subtle" (*sūkṣma-sūkṣmāṇi*) means difficult to perceive;
and "the forest" (*araṇya*) is as previously described.
The term "forest-dwelling" (vanaprastha), "mountain cave" (giriguhā), "charnel ground" (śmaśāna), and "heap of straw" (palālapuñja) form a copulative compound (dvandva).
By the word "etc. (ādi), one includes [other places] such as the foot of a tree. "Belonging to the forest" (āraṇyakāni) means those things that exist in the forest.
For this very reason, "border regions" (*prāntāni*) are places devoid of people (*vijanapadāni*);
they are secluded (*viviktāni*) and empty (*śūnyāni*). "Secluded" (*vivikta*) means free from [crowds]; it refers either to the outskirts of a village or a nearby portion of it.
"Seclusion from mental attention" means seclusion from mental attentions.
One is "dependent" through weak attachment;
one is "clinging" through middling [attachment].
He is intensely attached;
because of that very [attachment], he has fallen into self-exaltation;
he is entangled with householders and renunciants.
He is a "Bodhisattva-cāṇḍāla," being crowded with those who have gone forth [as monks] because they are unfit to dwell together with them;
he is a "defiler of Bodhisattvas" because he defiles them through his own faults;
and he is a "counterfeit Bodhisattva" because of the mere similarity of their physical bodies.
A counterfeit bodhisattva is so called because of the similarity in name;
he is a *kāraṇḍavaka* among bodhisattvas, like a crow among swans, because of his blackness amidst those who are not black;
he is a thief because he adopts the Dharma while wearing the garb of a śramaṇa.
He is a thief because he is not approved by the Bodhisattvas;
he is a thief because he is a false object of offerings for the world including its gods.
By the phrase "of that kind" and so forth, he explains at length how such a person is unfit to be associated with or served.
Stability and strength;
the ignoble and the wicked;
agitated and terrified.
"In that case as well" (*tatrāpi tāvat*) means "even in such a situation.
By the phrase beginning with "acting as if one were a mantra" (*maṃtrāyamāṇena*), he states the distinctions among the objects of the fourfold set beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
By the phrase beginning with "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*), he states the aspirational vow (*praṇidhāna*).
"This one too" refers to the entire passage beginning with "Furthermore, for whomsoever... and so forth.
"Having understood" means:
Exceedingly intense is the prowess and human effort.
With the words "this too," and so forth, there is a conclusion regarding the final work of Māra.
The chapter that explains the deeds of Māra is thus called.
The twenty-first chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
22. The Twenty-second Chapter, titled "The Good Spiritual Friend.

Now, from the words "atha khalu" up to "prāk" [before] "āsu khalu punar," the term "prajñāpāramitaiva" (the perfection of wisdom alone) is used as a definitive restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) due to its preeminence.
And since that one [consciousness] together with those [five] makes six,
he says: "And all of them," and so forth.
To the question "Why?", he says:
"Only six," and so forth.
Those very [six] have reached their culmination; the Teacher is that which is the supreme fruit.
Therefore, the path is indeed the prior limit (*pūrvānta*);
"light" (*āloka*) is supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*), and that too consists of those same [stages] in the *pramuditā* stage.
The "torch" (*ulkā*) is the path that carries effort, and that too consists of those same [stages] in the six stages beginning with the *vimalā*.
"Radiance" (avabhāsa) is the light of day;
it is the path that proceeds without effort on the stages beginning with the Immovable (acalā), and those [stages] are also [the radiance].
For this reason, they alone are the Three Jewels.
Therefore, they alone are the refuge, up to being the lamp. The meaning of the terms is as before. They alone are the mother, because of their sustaining and nourishing.
These very [qualities] are the father because of the sowing of the seed;
for "knowledge" means for the sake of vision;
for "awakening" means for the sake of the path of cultivation.
"For what reason? means: why is it that only the perfection of wisdom possesses the aforementioned qualities and not the others?
The answer is given with the words "For here," and so forth.
Furthermore, he says this in order to explain that the omniscience of the Buddhas of the three times is indeed produced from that [perfection of wisdom].
"Those which also," and so forth:
"produced" means accomplished;
"included" means, as appropriate, subsumed within [the aforementioned categories].
The terms "Buddha-knowledge" and so forth have already been explained.
The connection is that he becomes a benefactor to all living beings.
To the question "When?", he says "When," and so on.
Thus, service to spiritual friends is the ninth sign.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In these indeed... and ending before "Subhūti said":
because this alone is the guide, therefore there is "not being led by others," and so forth.
Thus, not being led by others is the tenth mark.
"Subhūti said," and so forth;
it means that both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) are cognized.
"Characterized by non-attachment" means characterized by non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
Because the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are not perceived therein;
likewise, form and the other [aggregates] are also [non-existent] because they are empty and secluded.
By the words "that which," etc., the objection is shown to be no objection at all—the meaning being "it is not so."

Apprehension is the grasping of a sign as a real entity through dogmatic adherence. Thus, while the Blessed Lady and all phenomena are characterized by non-attachment, there nevertheless exists affliction and there exists purification; this is the eleventh mark.
"Subhūti said," and so forth, up to "if, moreover... [as previously stated].
"Unassailable" (*anavamardanīya*) means unseizable (*asaṃhārya*).
By this as well—that is, by the passage beginning with "since all phenomena are non-distinct"—the attainment of unassailability is the twelfth mark.
Thus have the indicative signs been explained.
The increase must be explained;
therefore, the treatise states:
[127] "The quantity of people in Jambūdvīpa, the worship of Buddhas, merit and so forth..."
Having made various comparisons, [one understands] the sixteenfold increase. // 5-2 //
The sixteenfold increase has been described in the Sūtra.

Having done what? "Having made a comparison. Of what kind? [It is] that merit and virtue which arises from the worship of the Buddha—characterized by the generation of the human mind and the greatness described in the Sūtra—as performed by those people and beings who exist in Jambudvīpa according to their number.
That simile of which that is the beginning;
[the word] "beginning" (ādi) implies [the inclusion of other types].
The acquisition of great jewel-treasures and so forth is the stage of Buddhahood; it has been described in many ways, even without the use of metaphors.
Therein, the first [type] is that which begins with "If again... and precedes "Just as if..."; "for as long as life lasts" means for the duration of one's lifespan;
"that gift" refers to that which is given to the Buddhas and to all sentient beings.
"He dwells with mental attentions" means with those comprised of increase. "Having set aside" means having abandoned. For what reason is there that setting aside of them?
"Like those led to execution" means like those who have been brought to the place of execution.
"Becomes dispassionate" refers to one who has not yet attained [the goal].
Thus, by passing days and nights with mental attentions associated with the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this is the first increase.

The phrase beginning with "tadyathāpīti" and ending with "na ca parihīyate" is connected as follows: "One should seek the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) by means of what kind of mind? By a mind that is not devoid of the thought of omniscience (sarvajñatācitta)."

In some manuscripts, the word "unseparated" (*avirahita*) is read before [the phrase], while in others it is read as "that or another" (*sā vānyā vā*), depending on the variation of the texts. The second increase consists in not being separated for even a single moment from mental attentions (*manasikāra*) associated with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

"Subhūti said," and so forth, up to "this situation does not exist. Because of the attainment of the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding non-arising phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma*), there is the acquisition of the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*); this is the third [stage].
From "Subhūti said" up to the end of the chapter,
the fourth [cause] is due to being free from pride regarding prophecy and perfect awakening.
The chapter beginning with "the spiritual friend" is the Chapter on the Spiritual Friend (Kalyāṇamitra-parivarta).
The twenty-second chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
Chapter Twenty-Three, titled "Śakra":

Furthermore, from the words "Then again... up until "...training in this way," it is stated that a bodhisattva surpasses the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, as well as all those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who lack skill in means.
And he becomes unconquered by them; this is the fifth increase.
"Training in this way," and so forth, up to the end of the chapter;
the sixth [benefit] consists of the praises beginning with, "The four world-protectors, Śakra, and the other gods will approach him."
The chapter spoken by Śakra is the "Śakra Chapter."
The twenty-third chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
Chapter 24, titled "On Conceit," the forty-fourth.
Now, from the words "Then indeed... up until "And how, Ānanda...":
"He becomes cowering" means he becomes attached.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"This," and so forth, up to "will bring to fulfillment"; and then:
"For it is not thus," and so forth.
The meaning is that, as in other sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, there is nothing here that is logical.
*Gādha* means a foundation;
*āsvāda* means a relish.
The mention of name and clan, as well as the proclamation of the qualities of ascetic purification (*dhutaguṇa*), are as before.
"Bodies that are abundant and accumulated" refers to the seventh increase, which consists of masses.
The entire passage beginning with "And how? and ending with "the opposite" is easily understood.
Thus ends the eighth increase.
This chapter, characterized by the fact that this non-regressive conceit of a bodhisattva is the cause of much harm, is therefore called the "Chapter on Conceit."
The twenty-fourth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
Chapter 25, titled "The Chapter on Training.
Now, from the words "Then indeed" up to "he goes to the further shore," there is the question:
"Training in what does one train in omniscience?"
The subsequent [explanation] is: "training in cessation, non-arising, non-cessation, non-birth, non-existence, solitude, dispassion, space, the dharma-realm, and nirvāṇa.
Herein lies the proof.
For that *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata, by which he is a Tathāgata, does not diminish because of the inexhaustibility of the inexhaustible;

nor does it arise, nor does it cease, nor is it born, nor does it come into being, nor does it perish, nor is it differentiated, nor does it become attached, nor does it become like space, nor does it become a phenomenon (*dharmin*), nor does it enter *nirvāṇa*.
Training in this way, one trains in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). By this, he teaches the path.
By the phrase "one trains on the Buddha-stage," he states the fruit.
"The deathless realm" is the realm of liberation. "Desiring a protector" means desiring the state of being a protector.
"Abhyudgatata" means excellence.
"Śākunikas" are bird-killers;
"niṣādas" are hunters (mṛgayavas).
Fishermen are those who catch fish;
sheep are *urabhras*;
those who kill them are called *aurabhrikas*.
Blind means sightless;
deaf means lacking hearing; one-eyed means having only a single eye.
*Kuṇṭha* means one with crooked arms;
*kubja* means one with a bent back;

*Laḍga* means one whose knees are joined together;

one with impaired limbs is one whose limbs are incomplete;
one with deformed limbs is one whose limbs are unlike those of a human being.
"Enters into" means he accomplishes it;
"attains that" refers to the purification of the powers and so forth;
[it is said] "we shall know, we shall see."
From a word ending in a present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is added in the sense of "to cause to do.
There is the elision of the *ṭi* portion.
The remainder is easy to understand up to the point where they go to the further shore (*pāram*).
Thus ends the ninth increase.
The passage beginning with "tadyathāpīti" and ending before "punaraparam" [is as follows]:
gold, native silver, and so forth; by the maxim of "cattle and oxen," [these are distinct from base metals]; and saline soil refers to earth containing alkaline salt.
Ujjaṅgalas are high, waterless [lands].
*Tṛṇa* refers to vīraṇa grass and the like.
*Khāṇḍa* is [a type of] sugarcane.
*Ṣkatarukīlakaḥ* means those in which various thorny trees such as *kaṇṭakī* and *madana* are planted; the rest is easily understood. Thus ends the tenth [chapter].
From "punaraparam" up to "punaraparam": that which is called *saṃvartanīya* is so named because the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravarti-rājya*) dissolves from it;
thus ends the eleventh [section].
From "punaraparam" up to "punaraparam": that from which Śakra is destroyed is called "tatsaṃvartanīya. This is the twelfth [section].
From "punaraparam" up to "punaraparam prāk":
it is called "saṃvartanīya" because Brahmā undergoes dissolution (*saṃvartate*) from this;

Furthermore, from the phrase beginning with "another" up to the statement on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*):
attachment, aversion, and delusion are the fallow wastes that obstruct the growth of the crop of wholesome qualities;
doubt is the lack of conviction regarding the Truths and the Jewels.
Envy is resentment toward the prosperity of others.
The remaining six are the opposites of the perfections.
The rest is easily understood.
Thus ends the fourteenth [chapter].
The passage beginning with "tadyathāpīti" and ending before "sa cet punar" [is as follows]:
"In ignorance" means in that which is the opposite of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
"supreme in merit" means foremost among merits.
To demonstrate that very point, he says "What is that? and so forth.
The "domain of the Buddha" refers to the totality of the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*).
"The sovereign bull" refers to one who exercises mastery.
Its existence is its suchness;
its playful sport is through the miracle of supernormal power;
and its roaring of the lion’s roar is through the miracle of instruction.
The excellence of the Buddhas and the sovereignty of both types of noble Saṅghas are investigated through thorough knowledge;
yet one does not oppose them, because they do not abide therein.
The remainder is easily understood. Thus ends the fifteenth [chapter].
If, however, from the words "sa cet punar" up to the end of the chapter, he does not even perceive that [perception], how so? It says: "This is it," and so forth, ending with the word "vā."
"Even so" means by these same three modes.
"If he courses thus" means in that very way, being without perception and without mental observation.
This is the sixteenth stage of increase.
The chapter that explains the training is the "Chapter on Training" (Śikṣāparivarta).
The thirty-fifth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
26. The twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Simile of Illusion.
Growth has been explained; now, firm establishment must be discussed.
Therefore, the treatise states:
[128] "The supreme fulfillment of the qualities of the three types of omniscience, which does not abandon the welfare of sentient beings, is designated as 'firm establishment' (nirūḍhi). // 5-3 //
The dharmas subsumed under the three types of omniscience are the "dharmas of the three omnisciences.
Deliverance, liberation, consolation, and leading to final nirvana are the "benefits for sentient beings.
Therefore, in the Sūtra, from the words "Then indeed" up to "they dwell," [these points are explained].
"Even while practicing" means while practicing what? While increasing [the perfections].
What is he practicing? Generosity and the other [perfections].
"The mind strides forth" means it goes; that is to say, it becomes serene.
"The thought has been produced: 'Oh, how I might attain this!
'Being carried away' means being swept off.
'Equal' means balanced and faultless."
"On the further shore" refers to *nirvāṇa*.
"May these [aspirations] of theirs be fulfilled" connects with the subsequent mention of the "arising of the thought" (*cittotpāda*). They are "desired" because they produce joy.
They are "thoroughly contemplated" because they are produced again and again;
they are "embraced" by way of not abandoning them.
Regarding the phrase "of the Buddha-dharmas," the Buddha is the Omniscient One.
"Of those phenomena"—this is the brief statement (*uddeśa*).

Its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) consists of the three types of omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), which are the states of an omniscient one; for by means of these he becomes omniscient, and there is both omniscience itself and self-existence (*svayaṃbhūtva*), as well as invincibility (*asaṃhāryatā*).
In this context, "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) refers to the correct knowledge of all phenomena in all their aspects.
He is called "Self-Existent" (*svayaṃbhū*) because these phenomena arise for him from his own mind alone;
the meaning is that he has mastery over all phenomena.
Those qualities of his which are comprised by the state of being self-arisen have no withdrawal;
thus he is "inwithdrawable" (*asaṃhārya*).
This means he is liberated from all obscurations along with their latent predispositions (*savāsana*).
"May all those qualities of his that are comprised by way of being unshakeable become fulfilled"—by this much, fulfillment is described.
He speaks of not abandoning the welfare of sentient beings with the words beginning "O Blessed One, for me... and so forth;
"by these" is the scriptural (sautra) designation.
Therefore, *ais* is substituted for *bhisa*, and the substitution of *idaḥ* does not occur;
thus it is said: *imair*.
To the question "By which [means]? he says: "What is it that... and so forth.
The word "what" (kimiti) has the conventional meaning "how indeed" (kathaṃ nāma). This is the established usage.
The stabilization of the mind must be explained;
it means meditative concentration (samādhi).
Therefore, the treatise states:

[129] "By means of the vastness of merit acquired through creating thousands of world-systems consisting of four continents, two thousand, and three thousand worlds, this samādhi is fully proclaimed. (5-4)
In the Sūtra, concentration is described by way of the abundance of merit rather than directly.

How so? By using as analogies a world-system of four continents, a thousandfold world-system, a second-order intermediate thousandfold world-system, and a third-order great thousandfold world-system. By which passage?
From "O Bhagavat, those of theirs... up to "...are brought forth by the Bhagavat," the word *teṣām* (of them) refers to all [of them],
and *tān* (them) refers to the corresponding forms.
*Dharmatā* refers to the collection of phenomena (*dharmasamūha*) or their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"By a *pala*" means by the measure of a *pala*, in order to grasp the measure [of the earth], thinking, "It consists of this many *palas*.
Now, what here is the comparison for what?

The measure of the merit is expressed through the metaphorical application of the dimensions of Jambūdvīpa and so forth in the treatise. But is this measure of merit not for mere rejoicing (anumodanā) alone, and not for meditative concentration (samādhi)?
There is no fault [in this] because the intention is that the merit becomes vast through the rejoicing in the merit of others.
Furthermore, he says "In this way," and so forth, for the purpose of fulfilling the act of rejoicing and for the purpose of censuring those who do not perform it.
"Empowered by Māra" means they have been rendered dispirited by Māra, the great evildoer;
thus they do not hear it in terms of the words,
nor do they understand it in terms of the meaning.
They do not see [them] with respect; they do not pay attention, meaning they do not bring them to mind. Those who belong to the faction of Māra are "those on Māra’s side" (mārapākṣikāḥ).
In the same way, because they cause the obstruction of the great welfare of sentient beings,
it is said that "they have fallen from the abodes of Māra";
for they are indeed Māras themselves due to their absolute similarity to them.
"Accomplished" means brought to completion.
By what means? He says:
"By which," and so forth.
The passage beginning with "Of those who...
and so forth, and ending with "should be rejoiced in" following the words "Thus spoken," constitutes the praise of Śakra.
The section beginning with "By whom... and extending up to "by those also... [is the next part].
The benefits of rejoicing for those who have set out in the Mahāyāna:

by the words "by whomsoever," etc., it is shown that not only is there rejoicing, but [the roots of merit] are also planted and brought to fruition within one's own continuum, even for those who have merely first generated the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpādika*).
Having rejoiced, one must necessarily perform the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
And how those [deeds] are to be performed should be understood from the chapter on rejoicing (*anumodanā*) and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*),
as it is stated in the two great *Bhagavatīs*: "Having rejoiced in those roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*), they should be dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksambodhi*)."
And they should be dedicated in such a way that the mind does not course in the mind, nor elsewhere than the mind,” and so forth.
Thus, the root of virtue accompanied by rejoicing is the objective support (*ālambana*) for this samādhi; its dedication toward perfect enlightenment is its aspect (*ākāra*);
and the stabilization of the mind is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Where is its establishment?
It is not in the mind by way of the characteristic of a grasper, nor elsewhere—that is, not in any phenomena.
What then? The establishment of the mind is in the non-dual suchness of all phenomena.
The conceptual constructions to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaheya*) must be stated along with their antidotes. With reference to them, the treatise says:
"In both [the process of] proceeding and ceasing, each of those two consists of nine aspects."
The two conceptualizations regarding the apprehended object should be understood as having the nature of being non-correspondent with their objects. // 5-5 //
First, there are two types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) which are "without an object," because they conceptualize that which is not an object. How are they "conceptualizations"?
Because their nature is a false construction (*vitatha-kalpa*), insofar as it is a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that does not correspond to its [supposed] object.
Furthermore, in what domain do these two occur? In the category of active engagement (*pravṛtti*),
and "each" refers to both categories.
"Consisting of nine" means having nine divisions.

The conceptualizations of existence as a substantial entity and as a designation are considered to be the two types of subjects; these are each ninefold, distinguished by the categories of ordinary persons and noble ones. (5–6)
The other two are "conceptualizations of the grasper," because they conceptualize the grasper.
How are there two? Because one conceptualizes a being as substantially existent and as nominally existent, respectively.
Therein, the first pertains to ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) and the second to noble ones (ārya).
Each of these two consists of nine aspects.
How are these two the conceptualizations of the grasper (grāhakavikalpa)?
Because the apprehender is imagined as being non-existent; for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indeed a false imagination (*vitatha*). This very point is stated:
[132] "If the two objects to be apprehended do not exist in that way, of what are those two considered to be the apprehenders?"
Thus, their characteristic is emptiness by way of the nature of the apprehender. // 5-7 //
‘By way of the apprehender’ means by way of the nature of an existing apprehending subject;
‘of those two’ refers to the two conceptual constructions of the apprehender.
These four types of conceptualization are each ninefold according to the distinction of their objects.
Therefore, with reference to the first [type], the treatise states:
[133] "This [conceptualization occurs] regarding intrinsic nature, the lineage, the path, and the full attainment."
In the non-delusion regarding the object of knowledge, and regarding the counteragent and its opposite, // 5-8 //

[134] Regarding one's own realization, the agent, the action performed by that agent, and the fruit of that action—conceptualization based on the side of active engagement is considered to be ninefold. (5.9)
The phrase "the agent, that which is performed by him, and the fruit of the action" means: the agent, as well as that which is performed by him and the fruit of the action.
The ninefold set beginning with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) constitutes the side of active engagement (*pravṛtti*), because it is to be adopted by a bodhisattva.
This conceptual construction has that as its basis;
therefore, it is the first.
Consequently, with reference to this first conceptual construction, there are nine statements in the Sūtra.
Regarding that, the first [point] is addressed by the Sūtra:
Subhūti said, "And how, Blessed One, is it like an illusion? and so forth, up until the words "just as, for example."
An elephant or the like created by a magician is an illusion (*māyā*);
likewise, whatever else appears here that does not exist is "like an illusion" (*māyopama*).
And so too is the mind.
Because it has the characteristic of a grasper, and because the grasper does not exist;
for when there is no object to be grasped, a grasper is not tenable.
If it is asked, "How is there an absence of the object to be grasped? [the answer follows].
If an object were illuminated by cognition, it would possess the status of being an apprehended object; yet it is not illuminated,
because that which is itself unilluminated is contradictory to being illuminated.
Now, if the object is of the very nature of illumination, what need is there for cognition?
Therefore, the question is: how can that unreal mind, which is like an illusion, be fully awakened to?
The answer is given by the words "What is that? and so forth.
The meaning is that this is not so, because it is not the case that "this is not" (no hīdam), since such a thing lacks existence.
"Elsewhere" means in another [place].
"Taṃ dharma" refers to the self.
"No hīdam" (it is not so) means that it is absolutely non-existent; this is the intended sense.
To clarify this very point, he says:
"‘I am not,’ and so forth:
it does not admit of the designation ‘it exists’ or ‘it does not exist.
The meaning is that there is no connection with affirmation or negation regarding that which is non-existent and whose form is unknown."
The passage beginning with "whatever phenomenon" (*yo pi dharma*) and so forth is easy to understand.
As for the passage beginning with "therefore then" (*tasmāt tarhi*),
the word *tarhi* expresses impatience [with the opponent's position].
"Therefore" means because it has the characteristic of being a grasper; for [otherwise] the state of being a grasper would be impossible.
And by the inclusion of the word "absolutely," he says this: [that it is not a grasper even in the slightest degree].

Just as this [consciousness] is empty of its own characteristic, namely the characteristic of being a grasper, so too is it empty of all associated factors, because they also possess the characteristic of being graspers,
and of all phenomena that serve as objects.
Because the object of cognition has the characteristic of being the grasped (*grāhya*),
and because phenomena (*dharma*) possess, as the case may be, the characteristics of both the grasped and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
But how is it that the two graspers do not exist?
Because, if there were non-difference, the relationship of grasped and grasper would be impossible,
like the tip of one's own finger;
and if there were difference, it would be impossible for an insentient thing to be manifested even by another.
Because that which is non-inert is self-luminous,
it does not need to be brought into being; nor can it be repeatedly introduced into the mind, like the horn of a donkey.
"Nor is this," and so forth.
"Of some dharma" refers to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and the like. "Bringing about" (*āvāhaka*) means that which produces (*āhāraka*).
The "accomplisher" (nirvāhaka) is the producer;
for that which is non-existent is incapable of performing any action.
If it is argued that this dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), having reached [the Bodhisattva], causes him to awaken, he says:
"And how so? and so forth.
The meaning is that what is non-existent cannot be attained.
"Even the unsurpassed," and so forth.
The Perfection of Wisdom is absolutely secluded;
how could it come into being? It does not come into being at all.
The meaning is that it is impossible for that which is absolutely non-existent to function as either the probandum or the means of proof.
Regarding the phrase "when it was thus said," and so forth: "precisely because of this" means that the fruit conforms to its cause.
With the words "If he... and so forth, he completes the logical reason:
for if he were to perceive, then there would be conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), not the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
With the words "In this way... and so forth, he provides the conclusion.
The meaning is that "one does not fully awaken" because there is no conceptualization regarding full awakening.
As for the phrase "and yet one fully awakens," and so forth:
the point is that these three do not exist in their imagined form, but they do exist in the form of representation (vijñapti), which is empty of that [imagined nature].
Nevertheless, their conventional reality exists because they are equal in terms of appearance;
emptiness, however, is the ultimate truth.
"He courses in the profound meaning" means that others are unable to course in this meaning.
"One who performs what is difficult to do" means that although the Blessed One is capable of realizing it, he does not realize it out of regard for sentient beings.
"The meaning of what was spoken" refers to the intentional meaning (*ābhiprāyika-artha*).
The sense is that what is difficult for others is easy for a bodhisattva. Why is it easy?
Because of skill in means,
and because that very means is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) itself,
he says "for thus" and so forth to explain that very point.
"Who" refers to the bodhisattva;
"what" refers to the profound meaning;
and "by what" refers to that which is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Now, as to the question of how that practice of one who courses in this perfection of wisdom comes to be, he says:
"If... and so forth.
"Does not sink" means it does not break down.
This is the summary;
its detailed explanation is sixfold.
"It does not sink" means that there is no middling affection for it.
"He does not shrink back" means he has no weak affection for her;
"he does not turn his back" means he has no lack of affection; "he does not tremble" means he has no desire to abandon her.
"He does not tremble" means he does not abandon it;

"he does not fall into terror" means he does not abandon it continuously. Thus, by the negation of these six types of failure, it is understood that whoever is intensely delighted when this [perfection] has become manifest is one who courses in it.
Another [objection] is stated with the words "If it were," and so forth.
Another [objection] is stated with the words "Proximate," and so forth.
Another [author] says, beginning with "distantly removed" (*dūrīkṛta*) and so forth.
Here, there are nine topics, such as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because they are to be adopted by Bodhisattvas on the side of active engagement (*pravṛtti*).
Among these, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is delusion (*sammoha*), which is incorrect knowledge (*asamyagjñāna*).
Of these, the first is the conceptual construction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavikalpa*);
"intrinsic nature" here refers to one's own intention (*svābhiprāya*).
"I shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of that path"—
this is the meaning of *bodhicitta*;
it is a conceptual construction regarding that [attainment].
The aspect [of obscuration] regarding awakening and the perfection of wisdom consists of ignorance and non-concentrated knowledge with respect to emptiness;
and within concentrated knowledge, there are three types of conceit:
"I am practicing," "great awakening is near to me," and "I might be far from inferior awakening."
Regarding its antidote, O Blessed One, [the section] beginning with "How is the mind like an illusion? and preceding "Just as... is the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavikalpa*).
"Namely, 'tadyathāpī'tyādi": the delusion that "great enlightenment is near to me, while inferior enlightenment is far away, because I belong to the Buddha-lineage";
this [verse] is its antidote.
Because the lineage (*gotra*) is equal to space, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is likewise non-conceptual; this is the conceptualization of the lineage.
"Namely, 'tadyathāpī'tyādi":
"I possess the full realization of my practice;
therefore, great enlightenment is near to me and inferior enlightenment is far away"—this is delusion.

Its antidote is the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because the realization [of the path] is like an illusory person; thus, this is the conceptualization regarding the realization of the path.
"Namely, for example," and so forth.
"Appearance" (*pratibhāsa*) means a reflection (*pratibimba*). It is that which is knowledge by virtue of being the appearance of knowledge itself, and not [the appearance] of an object (*ālambana*).
This is an error regarding the objective support of knowledge;
it has arisen in me.
Consequently, there is the delusion that "great enlightenment is near to me, while inferior enlightenment is far away."
Its antidote is the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom, which is like a reflection; this is the conceptualization regarding the absence of error in the objective support.
"Namely, for example," and so forth.
The delusion consists in thinking that "the counteragent is the slayer" and "the adverse element is the slain.

Its counteragent is as follows: just as the Tathāgata has neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant, so too it is for one practicing the non-conceptual *prajñāpāramitā*; thus, there is no conceptualization of counteragent and adverse element.
For just as [in the case of the Tathāgata], "abhūtakalpanāt" means conceptualization (*kalpa*) because it is the construction of what is unreal;
"vikalpa" is so called because it is the conceptualization of the departure of that [unreal construction].
Just as those two have been abandoned in the Tathāgata, so too it is for one who courses in the non-conceptual *prajñāpāramitā*.
In this context, the departure from conceptualization is non-conceptualization; it is the delusion regarding one's own realization.
Its antidote is the perfection of wisdom that has abandoned conceptualization and discrimination; thus, there is the conceptualization regarding one's own realization.
"Namely, 'tadyathāpīti' and so forth:
'I am cultivating the perfection of wisdom;
therefore, great enlightenment is near to me and the inferior enlightenment is far. This is delusion regarding the agent."
Its antidote is as follows:
the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom regarding the agent—viewing the agent exactly like a Tathāgata’s emanation—is the antidote to conceptualization regarding the agent.
It is as follows:
that emanation of the Tathāgata performs the very function for which it was emanated,
yet it does not conceptualize that activity.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom and does not conceptualize it; this is the antidote.
Conceptualizing awakening is the conceptualization of the fruit of action.
"Namely, for example," and so forth, up until the end of the chapter:
Just as a wooden automaton created by an artisan performs its intended function without conceptualizing it,
in the same way, the bodhisattva acts for the sake of awakening, but does not [conceptualize] that [awakening].
"One will attain awakening and yet does not conceptualize it" is the antidote;
the conceptualization of awakening is the conceptualization of action and its fruit.
The chapter characterized by the perception of the mind as being like an illusion is the "Chapter on the Illusion-like."
The twenty-sixth chapter in the *Sāratamā*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
27. The twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Essence.

At the end of the chapter on the "Illusion-like," the first conceptualization regarding the grasped was explained; the remaining three conceptualizations are to be explained here in this chapter on the "Essence."
Regarding that, the treatise addresses the second type of conceptualization concerning the object of apprehension:
"Because of falling into existence or peace, because of the deficiency in realization, because of the absence of spiritual support, and because of incompleteness in the practice," (5.10)

[136] In the case of relying on others for understanding, in the turning back from the general teaching, in partiality, in diversity, and in the delusions regarding the state of abiding and the point of departure; // 5-11 //

[137] And regarding the notion that [the Buddha] moves behind [his retinue], this conceptual construction consists of nine aspects; it is based on the side of cessation and arises from the minds of the Śrāvakas and others. // 5-12 //

Because defects such as deficiency in realization—which must be abandoned by a Bodhisattva—are absent [in the Śrāvakas], the mental states of the Śrāvakas and others consist of nine kinds based on the side of cessation (*nivṛtti-pakṣa*), since they are not to be abandoned by them.
He speaks of these starting with "Then indeed... and ending before "Then indeed, the Blessed One...". In that context, he says "Śāriputra" once.
Then Subhūti [recited] one, then the sons of the gods three,
and again Subhūti four;
here too, the counteragents are recited.
By the opposite of that, conceptual constructions are understood.
"This is indeed solid"—the word *bata* expresses joy.
The excellent fruit is perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
That is the "conformity";
for that purpose the bodhisattva practices.
To the question "What is it?", he says:
"Ya ityādi" and so forth.
Here, "perfection of wisdom" (prajñāpāramitā) refers to the knowledge of the selflessness of both [person and phenomena].
For one who courses in that, there is no extreme revulsion toward saṃsāra, nor is there any extreme longing for nirvāṇa.

Because both are non-apprehendable, he may thereby realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the antidote. Otherwise, however, he might fall back into saṃsāra despite [practicing] the five perfections.
Or [it is due to] the knowledge of the selflessness of the person regarding *nirvāṇa*.
For this very reason, a bodhisattva does not receive the designation "bodhisattva" without the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

This is, for example, like the son of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), who even though he has been duly consecrated, does not receive the title "universal monarch" without the seven jewels; thus, it is a conceptualization regarding deficiency in realization.
*Saraṇa* means essence (*sāra*).
*Dharma* means action (*karman*).
It signifies that which is to be approached because it is difficult to overcome.
By contrast, that which lacks essence is difficult to overcome;
therefore, one who courses in the perfection of wisdom courses in the invincibility of the perfections,
for it is she who is capable of encompassing them all.

For example, on a city street frequented by women, the perception of a man with a weapon in his hand serves as an antidote; otherwise, they would be easily overcome. This is the conceptualization regarding the absence of possession.
The section beginning with "This occurred to him" and ending before "Then indeed... [explains] that they are to be honored.
Why are they to be honored?
Because their practice is complete, because they are not dependent on others, and because they have fulfilled their objective.
Therefore they say, "by those," and so forth.
"All have been brought forth" means by means of the five perfections through practice.
"Here" refers to that which realizes the selflessness of both [person and phenomena].

Therefore, "in the profound" is the antidote; for those who do not practice therein, there would be a deficiency in their spiritual practice (*pratipatti*). Consequently, they would be easily overcome by Māra and others.
"Like warriors whose armor is unbroken by their adversaries"—this is the conceptualization of the deficiency of practical application.
"Thus," and so forth.
The word "and those who" (ye ca) is understood from the context.
"Thus" means while practicing the perfections in which the perfection of wisdom is predominant; here, the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used in the sense of a causal reason.
The meaning is "by practicing in such a manner.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"the limit of reality," and so forth.
For just as a universal monarch is preeminent because of his great power, so too are the minor kings.
Likewise, for those who follow that [path], the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is primary, because through it there is the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

Just as they are not cast down into saṃsāra by the perfections, so too, by the power of the knowledge of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya-jñāna*), they do not directly realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

However, if the perfection of wisdom were not primary, they would indeed directly realize the limit of reality as an inferior awakening; this is the conceptualization regarding "being dependent on others" (*parapratyayagāmitva-vikalpa*).
"By this also," and so forth.
"By this" refers to what is about to be stated.
He states that very point with the words beginning "those who say... up to "...do not directly perceive."
Why? Because their aspiration is for perfect enlightenment.
Why, then, would they turn back from it?
Because the perfection of wisdom does not turn them back, since they practice within it for that very purpose.
Nor do the others [cease],
because even those that have entered into them do not cease;
just as all small streams, having entered a great river, go only toward the ocean and do not turn back— this is the analogy for the cessation of the heading.
These nine conceptualizations are also applied with reference to the fulfillment of their own purposes regarding the two great Blessed Ones.
Therefore, we shall first explain the conceptualizations of partiality and multiplicity as they were stated in relation to those two:
the five perfections are like the left hand.
The sixth [consciousness] is like the right hand;
it is the counter-argument that because the accomplishment of all activities occurs through both [the sixth and the five sensory consciousnesses], [the sixth is not limited].
However, if the sixth were merely like the right hand, then its activity would be localized; thus, there is the conceptualization of localization.

Just as small rivers and great rivers with various flavors become of one flavor upon entering the great ocean, so too the five perfections with their various flavors become of one flavor upon entering the sixth; this is the antidote.
To think that they remain with various flavors even in the case of perfect enlightenment is the conceptualization of diversity.
In this *Bhagavatī*, with reference to the armor for the sake of others (*parārtha-sannāha*), Subhūti speaks these two [types of] conceptualizations, beginning with the words "Then indeed...
and so forth. By the phrase "they arm themselves" (*sannahyante*) in that passage, the difficulty is shown, because it is impossible to accomplish the welfare of infinite sentient beings.

Nevertheless, the armor must be donned in this very way; for without such a great resolve (*mahāśayatā*), it is impossible to accomplish the welfare of both oneself and others—this is the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*).
The conceptualization of partiality is the thought that one should don the armor for the sake of training oneself alone, rather than acting for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Equanimity is the antidote to the conceptualization of diversity.
Desiring to explain that very point, [the author] speaks of its supreme difficulty with the words beginning "And those... and so forth.
"Those to be trained" (*vainayika*) refers to sentient beings who are worthy of being disciplined.
Nevertheless, to the question "For whom is this difficult?", he says:
"And thus," and so forth.
He speaks in order to reinforce [the point] by means of an analogy.
"Space," and so forth.
"For what reason? means "on account of what similarity? To this, the answer begins with "space," and so forth.
"By this" is the conclusion.
Furthermore, in order to make it firm, he says:
"By space," and so forth.
The meaning is: "by beings who are like space.
To the question "From what [does] dispute arise?", he says:
"And this," and so forth, up to the word "to be known."
The word "ca" (and) indicates the reason.
"Vivāda" means quarrel.
Because they desire to discipline beings who are not sentient, yet they avoid them precisely because they are non-sentient, it is called a quarrel.
"Those to be trained," and so forth.
Just as those to be trained do not exist, so too does the trainer.
Therefore, due to the non-existence of both, this is all the more supremely difficult to perform.

In this way, a bodhisattva should perceive this equality of self and all sentient beings so that he may be able to accomplish the welfare of both himself and others. Furthermore, as he practices in this [equality], how is he to be known? To this, he says:
"Sa cet... and so forth.
