For it is said: "A bodhisattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening (prathamacittotpāda) onwards, through mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), resolves upon all phenomena as being of the nature of non-existence and cultivates the six recollections (ṣaḍanusmṛti). He cultivates them himself and establishes others in them; he speaks in praise of them, and for those others who practice them, he becomes a speaker of their praise and one who approves."

Cultivating those [factors] in such a manner through the yoga of the nature of non-existence, he fulfills the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Having fully awakened to all phenomena precisely by way of their nature as non-existence, he turns the wheel of Dharma and liberates all sentient beings.

In that regard, one does not bring to mind the Buddha, the Blessed One, by way of the aggregates such as form, nor by the primary and secondary marks, nor by the aggregates such as ethical discipline, nor by the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges, nor by great compassion, nor by great loving-kindness, nor by the eighteen unique qualities, nor even by way of dependent origination.
Why is that? Because they have non-existence as their intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāvatva*), mindfulness [of them] is non-attention; this is the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
While practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he does not attend to wholesome or unwholesome phenomena (*dharma*);
because they have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, this non-attention is the recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*).
That which is the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples—the four pairs of persons, the eight great individuals—has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The absence of mental attention toward that which has no intrinsic nature, thinking "that is non-existence," is the recollection of the Saṅgha.

By one practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in this way—in a manner that is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, untarnished, independent, and praised by the wise—[the Saṅgha is recollected].

Abiding in ethical discipline conducive to meditative concentration, one should attend to that very discipline as being of the nature of non-existence; this lack of mental engagement is the recollection of ethical discipline.

While practicing the perfection of wisdom, when giving away material goods or even one's own limbs and members, one attends to all of it as being of the nature of non-existence; this lack of mental engagement is the recollection of relinquishment.

Those gods who are stream-enterers (śrotaāpanna), from those born among the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods up to those born among the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods—all these have non-existence as their intrinsic nature (abhāvasvabhāva). This mental attention (*manasikāra*) consisting of the recollection of that is the "recollection of the deities" (*devatānusmṛti*).
Thus, by means of these six recollections, there are six successive practices (*anupūrvakriyā*).
"The perfection of wisdom is to be followed by way of the non-arising of all phenomena.
Phenomena (*dharmas*) are so called because they maintain their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

All phenomena consist of the aggregates (*skandhas*), elements (*dhātus*), sense-bases (*āyatanas*), factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣas*), perfections (*pāramitās*), and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Their non-occurrence—meaning, through the knowledge of their non-occurrence—the sequential practice is to be understood.
Non-occurrence is the nature of non-existence.
For it is said: "They have no intrinsic nature."

That which has no intrinsic nature is "without intrinsic nature. Practicing in the perfection of wisdom, beginning from the first production of the thought of awakening, he resolves upon the fact that all phenomena have the nature of non-existence, and he cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects.

Having fully awakened to all phenomena as being of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva*), he turns the wheel of Dharma and liberates sentient beings from cyclic existence by means of the three vehicles; such are the thirteen successive actions performed on account of the fact that phenomena have the nature of non-existence.
From this point onward, the objections are to be inferred by oneself, but the refutations must be stated.

If the perfections (pāramitās) are cultivated as having non-existence as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then that cultivation is fruitless, like the cultivation of a horse's horn—this is the objection. He states the refutation:
"All phenomena are equal in being changeless," and so forth.
The *dharmadhātu* is changeless; all phenomena are equal to it, not merely by way of non-existence.
Furthermore, when the *dharmadhātu* is taken as an object of focus, it becomes the cause for the noble qualities (*āryadharma*).
For this very reason, it is called the *dharmadhātu*.
How, then, could it be fruitless?
Is it not the case that the self and representation are both to be personally realized within oneself (*pratyātmavedya*)?
Therefore, the objection that "since there is a grasper, there must also be an object grasped, and thus the non-existence of all phenomena is not tenable," is raised. He provides the rebuttal:
"Because all phenomena are understood through wisdom as being without self and as mere representation," and so forth.

"By way of the representation of non-self" means that because it is of a different characteristic from a self, it is by way of the aspect of non-self, and because it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, it is by way of the aspect of non-representation.
"By way of awakening through wisdom" means that it is realized through valid cognition;
for a self would be permanent, unitary, and a knower, whereas the aggregates and so forth are not of such a nature.
Therefore, they are established as being without self-nature;
and because they are devoid of the relationship between apprehended object and apprehending subject,
for this very reason they are also established by way of the aspect of representation-only (*vijñapti*).
Because that [cognition] has the characteristic of a grasper, and because of the absence of a grasper, the grasped also does not exist; thus, the non-existence of all phenomena is established.
Those very things which are expressed by words such as "form" (rūpa) and so forth are themselves form and the rest.
Moreover, there exists in the world their expression, as well as the linguistic usage and mutual communication of those who hear them;
so how can it be argued that all phenomena are non-existent? This is the objection.
He states the rebuttal with the words beginning "by name alone" (*nāmamātreṇa*).
A name devoid of referential meaning is "name alone."
Therefore, all those phenomena are expressed by means of that [mental representation].
For their object is not the form of cognition itself as something external, since [the mind] functions with respect to the external.
Nor is the object external, because the comprehension of an object occurs from a word even when an external object is absent.
If it is argued that cognition itself is the meaning of the word, appearing in the form of an external object;
Nor is form the object of this [cognition], because they are absolutely distinct;
or, if there were no distinction, there would be no discrepancy [between them].
The wise would possess actual objects;
therefore, due to the absence of objects, they are designated by name alone and through mere conventional usage.
If it is argued that conventional usage nonetheless exists, he says:
"Conventional usage," and so forth:
"nowhere" because of the absence of objects; "from nothing" because of the absence of designators.
Nor is there anything whatsoever— neither vocal, nor physical, nor mental—
because of the non-existence of both the signified and the signifier.
The conclusion is made with the words "all phenomena," and so forth.
They are "beyond conventional usage" (*avyavahārā*) and "beyond verbal expression" (*avyāhārā*) because those two do not exist within them;
for this very reason, they are "unexpressed" (*avyāhṛtāḥ*).

Now, one might object: since form and the other aggregates possess valid means of cognition (*pramāṇavat*), their emptiness must also possess valid means of cognition; therefore, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) which has that as its object would itself possess valid means of cognition.
The objection is that it is not so intended;
he states the rebuttal:
"Because all phenomena are immeasurable."
Because they are immeasurable.
For indeed, there is no measure of all phenomena because they are characterized by non-existence,
just like space, which is characterized by the absence of form.

Consequently, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even for those [categories of] emptiness, because there is no delimiter (*avacchedaka*). Therefore, there is also no [means of valid cognition] for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because its objective support (*ālambana*) is non-differentiated.
If, then, form and the other [aggregates] do not exist, why is it that—
Blue and other such things appear;
these are signs of phenomena (dharmanimitta), not the actual entities of phenomena (dharmavastu),
because they lack a nature that is either unitary or manifold.
Furthermore, that which is non-luminous by nature cannot be luminous.
The causes of phenomena (*dharmanimitta*), however, are the forms of the delusions regarding phenomena.
For these [delusions], being of the nature of luminosity, appear as manifest while appearing through those very forms that are dissimilar [to the objects].
Because errors are characterized by the manifestation of the non-existent (asatkhyāti),
if that were so, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) would not be established;
for while it is indeed non-erroneous, cognition possessing mental aspects (sākāra-buddhi) is nothing but erroneous.
And as for the objection that cognition devoid of form is not experienced even in a dream,
he provides the rebuttal with the passage beginning "because all phenomena are signless" (*sarvadharmanimittata*).
The signless (*animitta*) regarding all phenomena is the non-appearance and formlessness of knowledge due to the subsiding of signs;
from that, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is to be understood.
The sense is that this is because of the complete relinquishing of mental aspects (*ākāra*), just as in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

Now, an objection is raised: "Is this not simply the correct mental attention toward the *dharmadhātu* through the avoidance of the signs of conceptual construction, and not the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) itself?
The response is stated as "through the penetration of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmanirvedhataḥ*), and so forth. Here, by the word *nirvedha*, "penetration" (*prativedha*) is intended.
The penetration (*nirvedha*) of all phenomena is the realization through knowledge (*jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*) by means of their perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-rūpa*).
"From that" (*tataḥ*) means [it is so called] because of that characteristic; that is to say, it is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
In the preceding [verse], the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
The suffix -tam follows that [word].

For, through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and cultivation of that very right mental attention (*samyag-manasikāra*), there arises, effortlessly and without volitional construction, the non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*) regarding the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
That is the penetration (*prativedha*) of it.
Now, what is the meaning of the purity of the perfection of wisdom? This is not tenable;
for it is as follows:
By what is it purified?
Not by the self, because that is not accepted;
nor by the mind, because it perishes moment by moment.
Now, as for the mental continuum:
would it be impure or pure by nature?
In the former case, there can be no purification of it, just as there is none for charcoal being rubbed.
In the second case, there is futility. If it is argued that it is purified by the nature of the mind (*cittadharmatā*), that too is incorrect because that nature is immutable; such is the objection.
He states the rebuttal:
"Because of the natural purity of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena," and so forth.
Since the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure, for that purpose—that is, by means of that—one should follow the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The meaning is that it is to be performed.
But was it not said that even this is incorrect because she (the intellect) is changeless?
This has indeed been said, but it is not tenable,
because the reason is inconclusive.
For it is pure by its very nature due to being non-substantial;
it is defiled by adventitious stains of obscuration, just as the sky is [darkened] here by darkness, frost, and so forth.

Subsequently, through the very perfection of wisdom, it becomes purified by the removal of those [stains], just as the sky is [cleansed] by the dispersal of clouds and so forth by means of wind and so forth.
But is it not the case that the Perfection of Wisdom was also taught by the Blessed One himself?
And since teaching produces knowledge that possesses signs (*sanimitta*),
the objection follows that the Perfection of Wisdom itself cannot logically be signless (*nirnimitta*).
He states the rebuttal with the words "because all phenomena are ineffable," and so forth;
that is, because all phenomena are inexpressible.
Because it indicates [reality] without revealing the true nature of speech itself,
the *Prajñāpāramitā* must be followed for the sake of seeing the ultimate truth.
Now, what indeed is this purity?
If it is argued that [the cessation] refers to the destruction of the side of the afflictions (*kleśapakṣa*),
then rebirth would still occur.

Alternatively, if birth itself is destroyed due to the destruction of its cause, then the remaining formative forces (*saṃskāra*) remain for as long as the lifespan lasts and then cease of their own accord.
Thus, it would follow that there is only the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, and not the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Or, if such enlightenment exists, its distinction must be stated—this is the objection.
He provides the rebuttal in three statements.
"Because all phenomena are non-ceasing. The perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the inexhaustibility of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
How is there no cessation?
By way of the equality of abandonment;
because there is no distinction in abandonment as it is taught,
the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to be understood through the attainment of nirvāṇa regarding all phenomena— that is, all phenomena associated with affliction.
The knowledge that "they are exactly as their suchness is" is the equality of suchness (*tathatāsamatā*).
To explain how there is equality of suchness by means of that [knowledge], he says:
"all phenomena," and so forth.
They do not come from the future time-period,
nor do they go to the past time-period, because that from which they would have to come and that to which they would have to go both lack intrinsic existence.
And because they are unaware— due to ignorance of the paths within their own pure consciousness—
and because going and coming are preceded by knowledge,
therefore they are unborn, being absolutely unborn.
By this much, the perfection of the Bodhisattvas' own welfare has been established.

Let it be granted that they possess this perfection of their own welfare, since one's own welfare is by its very nature dear to people in the world, and they therefore resolve upon even difficult tasks for its sake.
However, an objection may be raised: the welfare of others is difficult because it is so vast, because it concerns others, because it involves contrary dispositions, and because it is so abundant.
He states the rebuttal with the words "the self," and so forth.
The meaning is that because the distinction between "self" and "other" is not perceived, there is the perception of the equality of self among all sentient beings.
And so it is said in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*: "Having generated a view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as high as Mount Sumeru, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is generated;
from that, all dharmas grow.
From this point forward, in order to counteract the notion that [the practices] are difficult, he speaks—as far as the word "ocean"—of how one should enter [them].
In this regard, first, for the purpose of dispelling the notion that it is difficult for sentient beings to attain arhatship and so forth, he says:
"All phenomena are the objects of the conventional discourse of sentient beings;
because the noble arhats are by nature completely pure."
Because it is merely the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
By the phrase "not imposing a burden," he indicates that because an entity lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), there is no burden to be imposed.
To dispel the notion of "difficult practice" regarding his journey to the Buddha-fields of the ten directions for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, he says:
Because all phenomena are without location and without spatial extension;
and because they are without location, they are by nature their own intrinsic being (*svabhāva*). This is the intrinsic nature of form and the other [sensory objects].
For it has no location because it possesses the nature of non-falling,
nor does it have a spatial extension because, like space, it is partless.
He says this in order to eliminate the notion that the pleasures of saṃsāra are difficult to renounce.
When all worldly phenomena cease, there is a state of refreshment and the arising of the perception of bliss; therefore, one should follow the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā):
"Alas, conditioned things are impermanent, subject to the nature of arising and passing away.
Having arisen, they indeed cease; their pacification is bliss."
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the training for the śrāvakas. With reference to the training for bodhisattvas, he says:
"by means of non-detachment from detachment."
Delight (*rati*) is an extreme longing for *nirvāṇa*;
the absence of that is the "non-delight" (*arati*) of Bodhisattvas.
Dispassion (*virati*) is an extreme revulsion toward *saṃsāra*.
The absence of those two is the lack of delight for Bodhisattvas; through those two, there is the perfection of wisdom.
Thus, it is the discernment for the sake of not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
By the phrase "neither attached nor detached" and so forth, there is contemplation for the sake of dispassion;
all phenomena are unattached,
meaning they are non-adherent.
Attachment and non-attachment are the counterparts to one another;
they are "devoid of that" because neither of them is perceived—this is the analytical observation for the sake of abandoning conceptual construction.
All phenomena, all paths, and the seven clear realizations [are included herein].
These very [factors] are enlightenment,
because they bring about the attainment of enlightenment;
for this very reason, it is said:
Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is so called because it is the awakening to the Buddha-knowledge; "awakening" means bringing [it] to attainment, thus it is enlightenment.
There is contemplation for the sake of easily attaining awakening,
because all phenomena maintain their own specific characteristics;
they are empty, signless, and wishless, because, being mere consciousness, they are devoid of external objects and because all signs have subsided.
And because there is an absence of aspiration for the three realms within the body of delusion, respectively;
such is the summary of the path.
If the gates of liberation were also their path, then by cultivating them, they would fall into an inferior enlightenment.
To this he says: "All," and so forth. "All dharmas" refers to all the paths of the bodhisattvas.
"Medicine" refers to those things that remove the great disease of longing for the Hīnayāna. Why is this so?
He says: "Because they are preceded by loving-kindness (maitrī)."
Because loving-kindness precedes them;
moreover,
because they dwell together with all four immeasurables, they are "those who dwell in loving-kindness."
"Become Brahman" means equal to Brahman;
this is the brief statement (*uddeśa*) based on the fact that, just like that [Brahman], faults do not arise.
"By the non-arising of all faults" is the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*).
All faults are the opposites of loving-kindness and the others, respectively: malice, harmfulness, discontent, aversion, and attachment.
It is "wishless" because it is devoid of longing for nirvāṇa;
it is "unimpeded" because it is not utterly weary of cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
Thus concludes the thirteenfold unprecedented realization along with its associated factors.
The realization in a single moment must be explained:
realization in a single moment is fourfold by way of its characteristics. (1-16)
How is that which was previously mentioned fourfold? It is:
the realization in a single moment of mind of all dharmas, both with and without outflows;
and the realization in a single moment of mind of all resultant dharmas, both with and without outflows.
The realization in a single moment of mind of all phenomena as being without characteristics;
and the realization in a single moment of mind of all phenomena as being non-dual.
Regarding that, with reference to the first [case], the treatise states:
[169] Because all untainted [phenomena] are subsumed even by a single one, this realization in a single moment by the Sage through giving and so forth is to be known. (7-1)
Just as even a single bucket of a water-wheel, when pulled by men, causes everything to move all at once, so too does knowledge cause [everything] to move in a single moment. (7-2)

For a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because of the "comprehension"— that is, the inclusion or projection— of "all" untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas by even "each single" moment of mind engaged in giving and so forth, there is "realization in a single moment," which is the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) in a single mental instant.
This is the first.

For it is said: "Just as even a single water-wheel, when set in motion by a person, causes all the buckets to move simultaneously," so too a single instance of the mind directed toward giving and so forth, when applied, draws forth the entire mass of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas all at once; this is the meaning.
Therefore, it should be understood that because the ocean has no limit, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) has no limit;
for herein, one is embraced by the perfection of wisdom and is never separated from the mental attention to the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
Each single moment of mind consisting of giving and so forth, being profound and vast,
is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Its boundlessness consists in its capacity to attract the untainted phenomena (*anāśravadharmas*).
Because their mutual relationship has been cultivated for a long time, it should be understood as something to be followed along with its attendants.
How so? He says:
"by virtue of being bounded by the ocean."
The boundlessness of the deep and vast ocean consists in its simultaneous drawing in of the waters of boundless rivers;
this occurs through their mutual confluence.
By means of that analogy of the ocean's boundlessness— [the text continues].
The meaning is "in that same way.
Thus concludes the single-moment realization of all dharmas free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
Concerning the second, the treatise states:
[171] When the state of the nature of maturation consists entirely of the pure, then the Perfection of Wisdom arises as gnosis in a single moment. (7.3)

A dharma born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is a matured dharma; its state is "thatness" (*tattā*), which is the aforementioned perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). "Consisting entirely of white" means all wholesome dharmas, both with outflows (*sāśrava*) and without outflows (*anāśrava*).
Those which were previously cultivated by him through their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) subsequently become born of maturation.
Therefore, by its very nature, it is the perceiver of their lack of intrinsic existence;
consequently, it consists entirely of purity.
When such [wisdom] has arisen—that is, when it is perfected—then at a single moment, "knowledge" (jñāna), which is the mind, [perceives] all of them effortlessly.
Among all those that are untainted (*anāśrava*), the first is accompanied by effort (*sābhoga*);
this second one, however, is both tainted and untainted, and is effortless (*nirābhoga*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"One should understand that because space is limitless, the perfection of wisdom is limitless.
This refers to the state of the perfection of wisdom as its matured dharmatā, which consists entirely of purity;
for this very reason, it is limitless.
In all of these, it has a single flavor regarding both existence and non-existence;
and because it is born of maturation, it is effortless.
Its boundlessness should be understood in this way.
He asks, "How so? and replies, "By the example of the boundlessness of space.
Space refers to the sky (*ākāśa*).
And that [space] is of a single flavor consisting solely in the absence of material substances, it is limitless, and it is effortless due to the absence of movement;
therefore, since both are equally limitless, the second realization is the momentary integration of all pure dharmas born of maturation into a single mind-moment.
Concerning the third [stage], the treatise states:
[172] Abiding in phenomena that are like a dream, while practicing the excellence of giving and so forth, one realizes the signlessness of all phenomena in a single instant. (7-4)
"In things comparable to a dream, comparable to a city of Gandharvas in motion"—thus it is recited in the two great Bhagavati scriptures.
However, in the Śāstra, there is only one term, because all [terms] have the same meaning.

Furthermore, that meaning is the "lack of characteristics" (*alakṣaṇatā*) of these [things], because they lack existence according to their respective characteristics even while appearing through various characteristics.

Then, by not abiding in all phenomena—which, being like an illusion, are without characteristics—and while fulfilling the six perfections, he "finds," that is, knows, the lack of characteristics of all phenomena in a single moment alone;
for the root *vid* functions as knowledge because its meaning is "oneness.
This is what is said:
"The variety of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the variety of Mount Meru.
Here, the perfection of wisdom is that single-flavored gnosis which, by virtue of being without characteristics, [perceives] all phenomena as being like an illusion.

Therefore, although it (the sky) is of a single flavor, the diversity produced by the appearances of all phenomena— which are like an illusion— is to be understood through the analogy of the diversity of Mount Meru.
For just as the diversity of Mount Meru appears despite the sky being formless and thus lacking such diversity,
because the four-colored sides of Meru manifest in all directions with their respective colors.
Likewise, for her, the third [moment] is the clear realization in a single moment of mind that all phenomena are without characteristics.
Concerning the fourth [moment], the treatise states:
[173] "Because of the non-existence of duality, one does not perceive the dream nor the one who sees it;
in a single moment, one perceives the non-dual reality of all phenomena. (7-5)
Regarding the phrase "the bath and the one who sees it," how is the accusative case [used] in this *kud-yoga* (improper connection)?
Effort must be made here;
or else:
The suffix *tṛn* should be read as "not seeing" (*anīkṣita*).
In the third [stage], there is a manifold appearance of all phenomena through forms resembling dreams and illusions.
In the fourth, however, because of their subsiding, it is like the sky at midday when free from clouds—a state devoid of all delusion.
In that context, the dream-object consists of dreams such as hell or mental fluctuations;
the seer of those is the self alone, because of the subsiding of both [the object and the subject] when they are transformed.

"By means of yoga," that is, through non-differentiation, he "sees" in a single moment alone the "reality"— the ultimate truth— of phenomena as "non-dual," being devoid of the grasped and the grasper.
This is stated by the passage beginning with "by the boundlessness of form," and so forth.
Herein is the fourth [type of] realization in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisamaya*).
It is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which is boundless;
for by means of it, one experiences the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena, which is absolute and resembles the utterly stainless sky.
That [perfection] is to be understood. How so? He says:
"By means of the boundlessness of form and so forth."
How is their boundlessness established?
Because of the subsiding of the appearance of duality.
For as long as there is duality, so long is there a limit, because of its being finite.
Is it not the case that there is also a limit [to the world] through the disappearance of both form and its grasper?
Who says "of form alone"?
What then?
[This applies] to form up to consciousness.
If it is argued that even so, the disappearance of the grasper has not been stated, [we reply]:
no, because that too is included within the aggregates themselves.
Because that which is non-luminous by nature cannot function as a grasper, there is the fourth clear realization: the single moment of mind that is the non-dual reality of all phenomena.
The seventh clear realization is the clear realization in a single moment.
The eighth realization is the Dharma-body. It has four constituent elements: the three bodies and its activity.
For thus was the summary previously stated: "The Dharma-body, along with its activity, is proclaimed to be fourfold, being threefold as the essential, the enjoyment, and the emanation. (1.17)
Thus: "Dharma" means the path (*mārga*).
And here, due to its excellence and the context, it is understood as characterized by the seven realizations (*abhisamaya*).
The body obtained through the Dharma is the "Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*).
*Kāya* means body (*śarīra*).
The three bodies of the Buddhas are the *trikāya*.

For it is said in the two great *Bhagavatīs*: "The nature of all phenomena (*dharma*), which are pure in every aspect and untainted (*anāśrava*), should be known as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha."

Furthermore, having realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment through the realization of those very same dharmas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha— whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics— teaches the supreme Mahāyāna dharma to the bodhisattvas for the enjoyment of the highest delight, joy, gladness, and bliss.
Furthermore, by realizing the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment through the realization of all those very dharmas,

the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, at all times and throughout the infinite and boundless world-systems in the ten directions, effects the welfare of all sentient beings through clouds of various emanations.”
And it is said in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*: “The collection of the bodies of the Buddhas is to be understood through three bodies;
this basis for the welfare of oneself and others is demonstrated by means of these three bodies.”
Thus,
for this reason, the *dharmakāya* is said to be fourfold by means of three bodies, as well as by its activity and its delimitation.
In that context, "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the fundamental essence (*prakṛti*).
"Essential" (*svābhāvika*) means "the very nature itself" (*svabhāva*).
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of the base meaning itself according to the rule *vinayādibhyaṣṭhak*.
Alternatively, the essential body is the pure, supreme excellence that exists within that very same nature.
It is called "sāmbhogika" because it is capable of [providing] enjoyment (*sambhoga*).
*Nirmāṇa* means creation;
the body produced by that is the "nairmāṇika."
Regarding that, the treatise states with reference to the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*):
[175] Those untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects—their essential body is considered to be characterized by their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*). (8.1)
Their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is the *dharmatā*, which is the *dharmadhātu*.
But is it not the case that the *dharmadhātu* is not the Tathāgata, for fear of over-extension?
What then? It is the purification of the *dharmadhātu*.
And so it is said in the *Āryabuddhabhūmi-sūtra*: “The inclusion of the perfectly attained stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*) should be understood through five aspects.
Which five?

Through the purity of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), and the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).”

The purity of the *dharmadhātu* is the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*; there is no difference in meaning between "the *dharmatā* of perfectly pure phenomena" and [the purity of the *dharmadhātu*]. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
One should understand that because the solar orb has boundless illumination, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) must be understood as having boundless illumination.
All [the gems] are free from defects such as fear and are pure like crystal.
Among them, those other than the moon and sun serve as analogies for the liberation-body (vimuktikāya) of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Even the sun and moon are like pure crystal; yet they possess this superiority: they produce a web of rays that pervades the ten directions. Therefore, they serve as a metaphor for the liberation-body (*vimuktikāya*) of the Buddhas, which generates infinite knowledge whose object is the infinite range of the knowable.
For this very reason, it is designated as the *dharmakāya*,
because it is the locus of infinite dharmas.
Thus, in this context, the infinite gnosis born from the purification of the *dharmadhātu* is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Its illumination of infinite objects of knowledge should be understood through the analogy of the sun’s disk illuminating without limit.
For the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) of the Buddha-qualities is like the sun;
the wisdom born from it, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), is like the sun’s disk of rays.
That which is its infinite illumination is like the infinite illumination of the solar disc by the rays of the sun.
By this, it is shown that the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu* of the Buddhas is the *svābhāvikakāya*, and that there is mastery of knowledge regarding all objects of cognition (*jñeya*).
With reference to its very mastery over the welfare of sentient beings and its pervasive permanence, the treatise states:
Whenever and for whomever the cause has reached maturity, that [Bodhisattva] manifests himself to perform whatever is beneficial for each of them. [8–9]

[177] For even when the rain-cloud pours down, that which is not a seed does not sprout; likewise, even upon the appearance of Buddhas, one who lacks the potential does not enjoy the auspicious. 9–10.
[178] Thus, because of the vastness of his activity, the Buddha is described as all-pervading; and because that very activity is inexhaustible, he is also said to be eternal. // 8-11 //
"‘He’ refers to the natural body (*svābhāvikakāya*).
‘Expands’ because of the expansion of emanations (*nirmāṇa*).
It is understood as ‘then, then,’ because of the expression ‘whenever, whenever.’"
It is understood from the context that this is for the sake of performing what is beneficial;
therefore, to address the point that it must be done at that very time, he says:
"Even while it rains," and so forth.
The phrase beginning with "iti" refers to the following:
"the vastness of activity" means activity toward all those who are capable [of liberation];
"of that very [activity]" refers to that same activity.
Thus is the intrinsic body (svābhāvikakāya).
Much remains to be said regarding the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*).
With reference to that enjoyment, it is said:
"Because all sounds are infinite, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) should be understood as being infinite."
The supreme realization of the Mahāyāna Dharma by the Bodhisattvas who listen as the Teacher teaches is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
That itself is the "enjoyment" (*sambhoga*), because it is the cause of enjoyment.

Furthermore, the experience of joy, delight, gladness, and bliss—characterized by mild, moderate, and intense mental well-being—among those who possess that [realization] is the primary enjoyment (*mukhya-sambhoga*).
The boundlessness of that perfection of wisdom should be understood. How so? It says: "Because all words are boundless."
The instrumental case is used for the reason (*hetu*).
Since those two types of awakening possess, respectively, infinite teachings that are both produced by sound and productive of it, how can they all be [described]?
Because they manifest in every possible form, in accordance with the various capacities of those to be trained.
How are they infinite?
Because that body is without end, the teaching is likewise without limit;
thus, the perfect awakening of the Tathāgata is also infinite.
Why is this so? He says:
"Because the attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha is limitless, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is limitless.
As it has been stated, the perfect awakening to the Mahāyāna Dharma by the Teacher himself is here what constitutes the perfection of wisdom.
Its boundlessness means that its cause— the complete realization of all the qualities of a Buddha— is itself boundless. Furthermore,
those qualities are recited in the two great Mother Scriptures (the *Prajñāpāramitās*).
The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment,
the eight liberations,
and the nine successive meditative attainments.
The ten spheres of totality,
the eight spheres of mastery, and the concentration of non-affliction.
The knowledge resulting from aspiration; the four analytical knowledges;
and the four purities in all their aspects.
The ten masteries,
the ten powers,
and the four grounds of self-confidence.
The three things that need not be guarded,
the three foundations of mindfulness,
and the quality of non-forgetfulness.
The eradication of latent predispositions,
great compassion,
and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
and omniscience in all its aspects.
Therefore, the treatise states:
[179] The factors conducive to enlightenment, the immeasurables, the liberations in their successive order, the ninefold attainment, and the tenfold totality. (8-2)

[180] The bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are of eight kinds according to their classification; [as well as] absence of conflict (araṇā), knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna), the superknowledges (abhijñā), and the analytical knowledges (pratisamvid). // 8-3 //
[181] Furthermore, there are the four purities in all their aspects, the ten masteries, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the state of having nothing to guard. // 8-4 //
The threefold application of mindfulness, the threefold quality of non-forgetfulness, the total eradication of latent predispositions, and great compassion for living beings. (8-5)
The eighteen qualities said to belong exclusively to the Sage, as well as omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), are designated as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). (8-6)
"Bodhipakṣyas and apramāṇas" is a dvandva compound. Regarding the term "anupūrvaśaḥ," it is connected with what follows.
"Non-protection" (*arakṣaṇa*) means the non-protection of that which should not be protected; this is the meaning. It is of three kinds.
Regarding the term "dharmakāya": it is the untainted collection of dharmas belonging to the Buddhas.
We have explained this extensively on many occasions as appropriate.
We shall now explain the remaining [topics] here:
"The eight liberations. One who possesses form sees forms—whether beautiful or ugly, blue, yellow, red, or white; this is the first liberation.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally as before; this is the second.
Having personally realized the beautiful liberation with the body and attained it, one dwells therein; this is the third.
There are four liberations beginning with the sphere of infinite space.
The cessation of perception and feeling is the eighth.
They are called "liberations" (vimokṣa) because one is liberated from obscurations by means of them.
Among these, the first three are liberations consisting in liberation from the obscuration regarding emanation.
The remaining ones are the liberations consisting in the attainment of peaceful dwellings.
Three are material;
five are immaterial.
The eighth is supremely tranquil.
"Possessing form" means perceiving the notion of form within oneself.
"Sees" means one sees with the mind those things produced through resolute intention (*adhimokṣa*).
Being internally percipient of the formless,
one perceives the name within oneself;
this is the beautiful liberation.
Having manifested beautiful and ugly forms, because of attaining a single perception toward one or the other,
[the practitioner] sequentially abandons engagement and aversion.

The cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāveditanirodha*) is the cessation of unstable minds and mental factors, as well as those comprised within the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), prior to emerging from that state.

The eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāvabhibhvāyatanāni*): because they master their objects, these mastered bases—which are states of mental stability—are the eight bases of mastery. Among them, two are brought forth from the first liberation (*vimokṣa*).
From the second [meditative attainment] there are two;
from the third, four:
one who perceives forms internally sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly, inferior or superior.
Having indeed mastered those forms, one knows them;
having mastered them, one sees them, and one becomes percipient in that way— this is the first [base of mastery].
Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are extensive, beautiful or ugly, and so on, until one becomes percipient in that way—this is the second [liberation].
Being percipient of the formless internally, one sees external forms that are limited, and so on—this is the third.
Being percipient of the formless internally, one sees external forms that are extensive, and so on—this is the fourth.
From the third liberation, four [perceptions] are accomplished:
being internally percipient of the formless, one sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, appearing blue, and radiating blue light.
Just as, for example, an *umakā* flower or a fine cloth from Vārāṇasī is blue, blue in color, appearing blue, and radiating blue light.
And having mastered those forms, one knows them, one sees them, and one possesses the corresponding perception; this is the fifth [base of mastery].
In the same way, "yellow" and so forth;
for example, "like the *karṇikāra* flower" and so on is the sixth [type]. Likewise, "red" and so forth.
The seventh [simile] begins with "just as the bandhujīva flower," and so forth;
likewise, "the white [objects]," and so forth;
and the eighth begins with "just as the form of a star at dawn," and so forth.
In that regard, they are "limited" because the number of sentient beings is small due to their very limited size;
they are "of good or bad color" because of being beautiful or ugly;
and they are "inferior or superior" because of being terrestrial or celestial.
Having become resolved through the liberations (*vimokṣa*), one masters them through the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) by repeatedly causing them to disappear from view.
Having mastered them, one knows through calm abiding (*śamatha*) and sees through insight (*vipaśyanā*); thus one becomes free of such perceptions because of being devoid of conceit (*nirabhimāna*).
"Excessive" refers to houses,
celestial palaces, mountains, and so forth, which are reckoned as non-sentient because of their immense size.
"Blue" is the general designation.
The remaining [terms] provide the explanation:
"blue-colored" refers to their natural color;
"blue-appearing" refers to their derivative color.
"Having a blue radiance" means that they are luminous in both ways;
[this refers to] the *umakā* flower.
*Karṇikāra* is well known;
*bandhujīva* is *bandhūka*;
*uṣas* is the end of the night.
"Entirety" (*kṛtsna*) consists of ten types.

Because one overcomes earth and the other elements through the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and then pervades them entirely on all sides, they are called "entireties" (*kṛtsna*). Sometimes these very spheres are called the "spheres of entirety" (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
However, they are sometimes specified by way of the earth and so forth:

the earth-totality, the water-totality, the fire-totality, the air-totality, the blue-totality, the yellow-totality, the red-totality, the white-totality, the space-infinity-sphere-totality, and the consciousness-infinity-sphere-totality.
"The four purifications are of all aspects" means:

purification of the basis (*āśraya-pariśuddhi*), purification of the object (*ālambana-pariśuddhi*), purification of the mind (*citta-pariśuddhi*), and purification of knowledge (*jñāna-pariśuddhi*). Among these, the complete cessation of all factors belonging to the side of the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*) from the basis, as well as mastery over the taking up, remaining, and discarding of one's own personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) according to one's will, constitute the [purification] of all aspects.
Purity of the basis;
mastery over the manifestation, transformation, and appearance of all objects of focus constitutes purity of objects in all their aspects.
As previously described, the departure of all mental dysfunctions and the accumulation of all forms of roots of virtue within the mind constitute purity of mind in all its aspects.
As before, there is the removal of all dysfunctions belonging to the side of ignorance, mastery over the knowledge of all that is knowable, and the purification of knowledge in all its aspects.
"Ten masteries" means the ten masteries. Mastery over life (*āyur-vaśitā*) consists in the ability to maintain or relinquish one's lifespan according to one's wish.

Mastery over the mind (*cittavaśitā*) is due to the attainment of meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth according to one's wish; mastery over requisites (*pariṣkāravaśitā*) is due to the presence of necessary implements according to one's wish;
and mastery over action (*karmavaśitā*) is due to the accomplishment of physical and vocal actions according to one's wish.
Mastery over rebirth is due to taking birth according to one's wish in all places of rebirth; mastery over supernatural power is the supernormal knowledges according to one's wish;
and mastery over aspiration is due to the fulfillment of all aspirations.
Mastery over resolve is such that whatever one resolves upon becomes exactly so.
Mastery over knowledge is such that whatever one wishes to know, one knows.
Mastery over phenomena is skillfulness in the systematic arrangement of the teachings, such as the sūtras and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "three things that need no protection": the Tathāgata’s conduct of body is completely pure; there is no impurity in his bodily conduct that the Tathāgata would consider needing to conceal lest others should find out—this is the first thing that needs no protection. Likewise, his verbal action is the second.
In this way, mental action is the third.
"The three applications of mindfulness" are as recited in the text: "When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, some listen with a desire to hear; they lend an ear;
they apply their minds to understanding; and they practice in accordance with the Dharma."
Because of that, the Tathāgata feels no delight, no mental satisfaction, and no elation of mind;
nor does he feel displeasure because others do not wish to listen, do not lend an ear, and so forth.
Because of that, the Tathāgata feels no resentment, no impatience, no ill-will, nor any dissatisfaction of mind;
some listen with respect, while others do not listen with respect.
"Therein, the Tathāgata has no duality—neither delight nor resentment;
he dwells everywhere with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending."
The quality of non-forgetfulness belongs to the Buddhas because they do not let the time for acting for the benefit of sentient beings pass by;
for this very reason, it is established as a formal characteristic.
Regarding the term "eradication of latent tendencies" (*vāsanāsamuddhāta*):
even for one who has abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*), that which appears as the behavior of one whose afflictions have not been abandoned is the latent tendency of affliction (*kleśavāsanā*).
Since that too has subsided in the Tathāgata, the Blessed One is said to be one who has eradicated the latent tendencies of the afflictions.
"Great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) is the intention for the welfare [of others];
by means of this, the Blessed One surveys the world six times every day and night, [thinking], "Who is declining? Who is prospering? and so forth.
"Omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*) means the knowledge of the ultimate limit of the distinctions between the intrinsic natures and specific characteristics of all phenomena.
"Battle" (*raṇa*) refers to disputes, quarrels, and the like;
however, in this context, the affliction that is the cause of battle is itself called "battle.
It is by taking that [affliction] as an object that one gives rise to battle.

The concentration which one enters, and having emerged from which, no conflict arises among those in a village or similar place by taking that [state] as an object upon entering— this is "non-conflict" (*araṇā*).
It belongs to both the disciple (*śrāvaka*) and the Buddha.
There is a distinction in the functional activity (*kāritra*) of these two.
With reference to this, the treatise states:
[184] "Because a disciple has not seen the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), he has not abandoned the afflictions."
In villages and other places, the Jinas possess the araṇā [meditation] for the purpose of cutting off the stream of those afflictions. (8-7)

The *araṇā* of the Śrāvakas consists in the avoidance of the cause of affliction, namely [wrong] view; it does not consist in the direct removal of the affliction itself. However, that of the Sugata is for the purpose of cutting off the stream of another's afflictions, and not merely for the sake of [removing] wrong view—this is the meaning.

The "knowledge resulting from resolve" (*praṇidhijñāna*) of the Śrāvakas is that knowledge which arises regarding worldly events and so forth for one who has entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) after making the vow, "May I know this.
Regarding the Tathāgata, the treatise states:
[185] "Effortless, without conceit, unimpeded, and always present."
The knowledge resulting from aspiration is held to be that which dispels all doubts. // 8-8 //
It is "effortless" because it is free from conceptual construction;
it is "unattached" because it is without expectation;
it is "unobstructed" because it is unimpeded everywhere.
"Always abiding" means that it abides even when the mind is not in a state of meditative equipoise. It is called "the dispeller of all questions" because it cuts through all inquiries.
And that *sambhogakāya* arises in its own perfectly pure Buddha-field and remains as long as space endures.

Whence, then, does the "Buddha-field" derive its name? Primarily because it is there that he himself is reborn. It is called "loka" (the world) because it is broken (*lujyate*) and utterly destroyed (*pralujyate*).
And there is the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Therefore, the world-system (*lokadhātu*) is twofold: the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and the receptacle world.
With reference to the purification of the world of sentient beings therein, he says:
One should understand that the perfection of wisdom is followed by the boundlessness of the accumulations of merit and knowledge of the entire realm of sentient beings;
for by means of the Blessed One’s wisdom, those sentient beings who have been brought to maturity arise therein as far as space extends,
and once arisen, they are brought to full maturity for enlightenment by that same wisdom.
This is the perfection of wisdom;
its boundlessness is to be understood.
How so? He says:
"Everyone," and so forth: whatever beings are born there,
they are all bodhisattvas who have attained the noble stages.
All of them—
that is, the entire realm of sentient beings, the mass of sentient beings—
their accumulation of merit and wisdom.
Because those two are limitless— due to the limitlessness of the earth element— the limitlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood.

Likewise, due to the limitlessness of the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element, the limitlessness of the perfection of wisdom should be understood.
For instance, the receptacle world therein has a ground level like the palm of a hand;

its inhabitants consist of palaces, gardens, ponds, wish-fulfilling trees, and other such surroundings made of the seven most brilliant precious gems, emitting great rays of light that illuminate many other world-systems above, while the sky appears as a corresponding radiance, and the sentient beings possess the six elements.

Because of the statement, "O monk, this person consists of six elements," their bodies also possess a radiant luster, with physical refinements and colors corresponding to the ground of the surrounding halo of light.
Furthermore, the enjoyments and resources of the sentient beings there are superior to those of all the celestial worlds.
The enjoyment of those [beings] is exclusively blissful, exclusively irreproachable, and exclusively under their own control.
Such purification of the six elements is limitless because it is boundless and exceedingly vast.
Therefore, from that limitless purification which serves as its cause, one should understand the limitlessness of the Blessed One’s wisdom.
And there, the bodhisattvas who have arisen go to infinite world-systems and destroy the accumulations of unwholesome [deeds] of the sentient beings dwelling therein.
They also discern the accumulations of the wholesome, which are the antidotes to those [unwholesome states].
Because those accumulations are immeasurable, it should be understood that the wisdom which delimits them is also immeasurable; this is what is meant by the statement:
"Because the accumulations of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should be understood as immeasurable."
Furthermore, whatever Dharma those bodhisattvas teach for the sake of generating wholesome qualities in others—all that is the accumulation of all dharmas.
Because that [accumulation] is immeasurable, it should be understood that the wisdom which establishes it is also immeasurable; this is what is meant by the statement:
"By the immeasurability of the accumulation of all dharmas, the immeasurability of the perfection of wisdom should be understood."
"One should understand that because all phenomena (*dharma*) and meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are limitless, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is to be understood as limitless.
'Phenomena' refers to the dhāraṇīs and meditative concentrations, which are the stabilizations of the mind.
Both phenomena and meditative concentrations—these are all 'phenomena-and-meditative-concentrations.'"
The meaning is that their boundlessness—
their attainment and their acquisition thereof— should be understood as the boundlessness of the Blessed One’s wisdom that produces those [qualities] for the bodhisattvas therein.
Because all buddha-dharmas are boundless, the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is to be realized.
In that context, the Buddha is the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
All its qualities are the "all-Buddha-qualities," namely the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics.
And the secondary marks;
their boundlessness and indefinability—by what are they indefinable? By the scale.
Because there is no one other than the Tathāgata who possesses such [qualities],
the boundlessness of the Blessed One’s wisdom should be understood as being exactly like that. Of what wisdom?
Because all their causes were correctly understood and properly implemented by her, the treatise states:
[186] "This [body] of the Sage consists of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics."
The enjoyment body (sambhogika-kāya) is considered such because of its enjoyment of the Mahāyāna. // 8-12 //
With the fourth line, he states the reason for his being a *sambhogika* (enjoyment-body).
Therein, first, he describes the marks with five *indravajrā* verses: "His hands and feet are marked with wheels; his feet are like those of a tortoise; his fingers and toes are joined by a web."
His hands and feet are youthful and soft; with these seven elevations, he is the refuge.

[188] He has long fingers, broad heels and limbs, expansive and straight feet with prominent ankles, and body hair that grows upward; he has calves like those of the eneya antelope, and his arms are long and well-proportioned; his private organs are sheathed within a supreme, well-concealed loins. // 8.14 //

[189] He is golden-hued with delicate skin; his body hairs grow individually, curling to the right; his face is marked by a *ūrṇā*; his torso is like that of a lion; his shoulders are rounded and the space between them is well-filled. // 8.15 //
[190] His inferior taste is known as the most excellent of tastes; his body is like a *nyagrodha* tree, equal in its circular proportions;
he has a crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*) on his head, broad and beautiful tongues, a voice like that of Brahmā, a jaw like a lion’s, and teeth that are perfectly white. 8-16.
The teeth are equal in size, closely set, and four in number with no fewer than ten in each row;
his eyes are blue, and his eyelashes are like those of a bull—these indeed are the thirty-two marks. (8.17)
"He whose feet and hands are marked with wheels" is *cakrāṅkahastakramaḥ*.
"He whose feet are like those of a tortoise because they are well-established" is *kūrmāpādaḥ*. [The compound] *sa cāsau sa ca* is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
"His fingers, hands, and feet are webbed," thus it is "one whose fingers, hands, and feet are webbed.
"His hands and feet are youthful and soft"—this is to be connected with what follows.
"His physical frame is supported by seven protuberances."
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The "basis" (*āśraya*) is the body; the meaning is that his body is characterized by seven elevations.
By this, the five characteristics have been stated.
The hands and feet are marked with wheels; the feet are well-placed; the hands and feet have webbed fingers and toes; the hands and feet are soft and youthful; and there is a height of seven [parts].

Long fingers, long heels and body, broad and straight [feet] like those of a conch, hair growing upward, shanks like those of an antelope, and thighs and arms that are firm and well-proportioned, [with private parts] sheathed...
He whose secret organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a stallion.
*Dirghāngulitvam* (long fingers) and *āyatapārṣṇiḥ* (broad heels) form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
"A body that is expansive and straight" means a large and straight body.
He is both *ucchaṅkhapādaḥ* (having high-arched feet) and *ūrdhvaromā* (having upward-pointing body hair).
The Sūtra states that he is "ucchankhapāda" because his knees and ankles are very well-concealed;
thus, the word *ut* has the sense of excellence and concealment,
while the word *śaṅkha* refers to the bones of the knees and ankles.

It is understood that "all" refers to the feet from the base of the thighs downwards. "Vastiguhyam" means the private parts at the base; he is so described because his excellent sheath-like covering is located over those private parts.
By this, eight marks [are established]:
long fingers and broad heels.
The quality of having broad and long limbs; the quality of having high-arched feet; and the quality of having body hairs that grow upward.
Thighs like those of the eneya antelope, arms that are powerful and straight,
and the private organ being concealed within a sheath.

"He is golden-hued and of slender skin; his body hairs grow singly, each curling to the right; his face is marked by a *ūrṇā*; his forebody is like that of a lion (*hari*); his shoulders are rounded and the space between them is well-filled. Regarding the phrase "his forebody is like that of a lion," it means his forebody is like that of a lion (*haripūrvakāya*).
"In the two shoulders" means well-covered; because the neck is well-knit and perfectly rounded,
there is no space between the two shoulders and the upper chest.
Because his [shoulders] are developed by that, he is "one whose shoulders are well-filled" (*citāntarāṃsa*).
By this, seven characteristics are indicated:
the golden color of the skin (*suvarṇavarṇatā*), and so forth.
Smooth skin; body hairs that grow one by one and curl to the right;
and a face marked with a *ūrṇā* (tuft of hair between the eyebrows).
The torso is like that of a lion;
the shoulders are well-rounded;
and the space between the shoulders is filled out.
His inferior taste is renowned as the most excellent of tastes; his body is like a *nyagrodha* tree, equal in its circular proportions;
he has a crown-protrusion on his head, broad and beautiful tongues, the voice of Brahmā, a jaw like that of a lion, and perfectly white [teeth].
"The teeth are equal in size, sparse, and four sets of ten without deficiency;
his eyes are blue, and his eyelashes are like those of a bull—these indeed are the thirty-two marks.
By these two verses, twelve marks have been described.
The knowledge of the tastes of flavors;
a body as well-proportioned as a nyagrodha tree;
and a head crowned with a protuberance (uṣṇīṣa).
Broad tongue;
the voice of Brahmā;
and a jaw like that of a lion.
The quality of having very white teeth; the quality of having even teeth;
the quality of having teeth without gaps.
Having forty even teeth, having deep blue eyes,
and having eyelashes like those of a cow—
because this collection consists of ten such features, it is called a "decad" (*daśikā*).
Those four; that is to say, forty. *Govṛṣau* means a cow and a bull (*gobalīvardau*).

Alternatively, "bull" (*govṛṣa*) means a preeminent bull (*puṅgava*). As for the statement that "these thirty-two marks are indeed [the characteristics] of the totality of all," their explanation, their cause, and their nature as prior signs are found in the *Dharmadāna-sūtra*.
[192] Whatever cause there may be here for the accomplishment of each respective characteristic, this [path], characterized by full attainment, fulfills each of those. Regarding this,
"whatever cause there may be for the accomplishment of each respective characteristic..."
Having fulfilled each of these, this is characterized by complete attainment.
This is the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*).
To the question of what, then, is the cause for which, he says:
following after one's gurus and so forth, and firmness regarding the vow (*saṃvara*).
Giving consists of attending to those who are to be gathered and providing excellent material things. // 8-19 //

The release of those condemned to death, the formal undertaking [of virtue], and the increase of the wholesome—such causes, as set forth in the sūtras, establish the [Buddha’s] defining characteristics. (8-20)

In that regard, through following and welcoming one's gurus, and by offering service in such acts as listening to the Dharma, presenting garlands and offerings, and attending at shrines (*caitya*), one attains hands and feet marked with wheels.
Through firmness in undertaking commitments, one attains well-placed feet. Through the cultivation of the articles of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one attains webbed hands and feet.
From the giving of excellent food, drink, and so forth, there arise the marks of having soft and youthful hands and feet,
and having seven protuberances on the body.
The plural form in the phrase "releasing those to be executed" (*avadhyamokṣāḥ*) is used for the sake of including other such acts.
From the act of releasing those condemned to death and thereby bestowing the favor of life,

and from the practice of abstaining from taking life, [he attains] long fingers, long heels, and a large, straight body. From the increase of the undertaking of wholesome dharmas, he attains high-arched feet.
"And having body hair directed upward," and so forth— this refers to such qualities as these.
"According to the sūtra" means as it will be recited in the *Dharmadāna*.
Because they possess the deeds of a great person (*mahāpuruṣakāra*), the Tathāgatas and the great Bodhisattvas are "great persons" (*mahāpuruṣa*).
The thirty-two marks of a great person are the indicators of them; the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) serve to beautify those very marks.
With reference to these, there are twelve verses:
[195] The nails of the Sage are copper-colored, glossy, and prominent; his fingers are rounded, well-defined, and tapering; and his veins are hidden and without knots. (8.21)
By this, the eight secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are stated:
copper-colored nails, glossy nails, and prominent nails;
rounded fingers, well-filled fingers, and tapering fingers; and hidden veins and veins without knots.

[196] His ankles are hidden, his feet are even, and he has the stride of a lion, an elephant, a twice-born bird, or a lord of cattle; his gait is courageous, graceful to the right, and straight in its movement.
[197] Regarding "the sequence of the fists," there are twelve [marks] described by a verse exceeding six syllables:
the hidden ankles (*gūḍhagulphatā*).
The state of having even feet;
the gait with the stride of a lion;
the gait with the stride of a swan.
The gait of one who strides like a bull;
the gait that turns to the right;
the graceful gait.
Straightness of the limbs, roundness of the limbs, smoothness of the limbs, and gradual tapering of the limbs.
Purity of body consists in its being clean and soft; it consists in the fullness of the secondary marks and in the limbs having beautiful, broad, and well-rounded contours. // 8-23 //
Thus, with twenty-six syllables, there are five secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*):
purity of the body, softness of the body, purity of the body, the perfection of the secondary marks, and the beauty of the broad, circular body.
[198] There is evenness of gait, purity of the eyes, and delicacy.
The state of having limbs that are not sunken and the state of having well-knit limbs.
By this [verse], six [marks] are [indicated]: evenness of stride, purity of eyes, delicacy of limbs, protuberance of the limbs, and well-knit limbs.
[199] Well-proportioned limbs, purity of light unobscured by darkness, eyes that are rounded, polished, and unblemished, a slender abdomen, and depth. // 8-25 //
[200] The navel is spiraling to the right and beautiful from every side.
With this half-verse, nine [marks] are [described]:

well-proportioned major and minor limbs; pure radiance free from darkness; a polished belly; an unbroken belly; a non-emaciated belly; a deep navel; a navel spiraling to the right; and being pleasing from all sides.
and so forth.
One's conduct is pure, and the body is free from dark spots and blemishes. // 8-26 //
The hands have lines that are soft as cotton, glossy, deep, and long;
the mouth is not too wide, and its face reflects like a bimba fruit.

Because reflections arise within this, it is so described; that which has such a face or mouth is called "one whose face is the arising of reflections. By means of this half-verse, eight [marks] are indicated: purity of conduct; a body free from moles or spots; hands as soft and delicate as cotton; glossy lines on the palms; deep lines on the palms; long lines on the palms; a face that is not overly long; and a face that displays reflections like a mirror.
And: the tongue is soft, slender, and red; his voice has the resonance of a thundercloud;
his voice is charming and melodious; and his fangs are rounded, sharp, white, and even.
The nose is gradually elevated, prominent, and supremely pure. // 8-28 //
"Supreme" means absolute.
With this verse and a half, there are twelve [qualities]:
having a soft tongue, having a slender tongue, and having a red tongue.
The voice is like the roar of an elephant and the thunder of a cloud;
it possesses a sweet, lovely, and charming tone. His fangs are rounded, sharp, white, even, regular, prominent, and clean.
The eyes are wide, the eyelashes are dense, and the gaze is like that of a lotus petal.
His eyebrows and arms are long, smooth, very glossy, and have even hair;
his ears are plump and long, symmetrical, and free from any defects.
[205] An unfaded forehead, a broad head, and the state of having a full crown;
"samaromā" (having even hair) takes the feminine suffix *ḍāp*.
By these two verses, thirteen [marks] are [enumerated].

Broad eyes, eyelashes like those of a cow, eyes with white and black parts like the petals of a white lotus, long eyebrows, smooth eyebrows, glossy eyebrows, eyebrows with even hair, thick and long arms, symmetrical ears, unimpaired ears, a well-developed forehead, a broad forehead, and a perfectly formed head.
They were adorned with bees and clouds, smooth, and possessed of unagitated forms.
The hair of men is not coarse and captivates the senses with its fragrance;
the *śrīvatsa* and the *svastika*—these are considered the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) of a Buddha. (8.32)
By this half-verse and the following verse, seven [marks] are described:
hair resembling bees, well-parted hair, smooth hair, unentangled hair, non-coarse hair, and having hands and feet beautiful with the *śrīvatsa*, *svastika*, and *nandyāvarta* symbols.
In all Buddhas, there are eighty secondary marks by virtue of their universal oneness.
Thus is the enjoyment body (sāmbhogika-kāya).
Concerning the emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*), the treatise states:
"That by which the Sage performs various benefits for the world equally, remaining uninterrupted until the end of existence—that is the emanation body. (8.33)
[208] Likewise, it is maintained that his karma remains uninterrupted throughout cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"By virtue of the boundlessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), the boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is to be understood."

To whatever extent there are phenomena comprised of body and speech belonging to all beings— whether moving or stationary, whether dwelling on land, in water, or in the air— that have been manifested by the Blessed One throughout infinite world-systems for the sake of training those beings, one should understand that because all those phenomena are limitless, the wisdom of the Blessed One is likewise limitless.
"Of what are these emanations made?
One should understand that because emptiness is limitless, the perfection of wisdom is likewise limitless.
Just as the bodies emanated by the Tathāgata are infinite, so too their emptiness is infinite."
By what is it empty?
It is empty of the mind and mental factors that are under its own control, like a magical illusion-man.
Therefore, because that [emptiness] is also limitless, it is "limitless by way of being limitless," as explained previously.
Just as their bodies and speech are emanated, why are their minds and mental factors not also emanated?
Because there is no appropriation for them, and because no previously non-existent sentient being is brought into existence.
But is it not accepted that Buddhas also possess emanations of mind and mental factors?
For it is said: "Its function consists of the application of means for the emanation of body, speech, and mind."
This is indeed accepted; however, when there is a basis [of reality], it occurs through the empowerment of a deity, like seeing a dream,
or by means of speech, for the sake of [conveying] the meaning of words.
And because it possesses feeling,
he therefore says:
"The boundlessness of the perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the boundlessness of the conduct of the mind."
And by taking as their object the Dharma taught to those beings, the wholesome factors that serve as antidotes arise;
and by means of these, their unwholesome factors that cause distraction are abandoned.
Therefore, it is said:
"One should understand that the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable because wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are immeasurable.
Now, as for those who are emanations, how are they the bodies of the Blessed One?
If it is argued that they are so because they were emanated by the Blessed One;
In that case, the elephants and other beings created by a magician would be the bodies of the magician himself, because he creates them by presiding over them as his own body;
and because they are employed in difficult tasks such as walking and speaking just like his own body, they too are bodies— this is the Blessed One’s emanation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*).
The three bodies have been explained; their activity must now be discussed. He states it briefly as follows:
"The perfection of wisdom is to be understood through the roaring of the lion's roar.
The lion is the supreme among beasts;
by virtue of this common characteristic, the supreme among men are called lions among men.
In this context, however, because he has reached the highest excellence, the Tathāgata— the supreme among all persons, including gods and humans— is called the "Lion.
His Dharma is called the "Lion’s Roar" because it fulfills all aspirations and terrifies all the deer-like proponents of opposing views,
just like the banner of a lion.
Its "flowing" (nadana) is its teaching;
its state of being that is "tathatā" (suchness).
By means of that, the Blessed One’s wisdom is to be understood as a *pāramitā* because of its reaching the further shore (*pāragamana*); this is the meaning.
Furthermore, that roaring of the lion’s roar is the teaching on twenty-seven kinds of activity;
it should be seen in detail in the two great *Bhagavatīs*. With reference to that, the treatise states:
The activity of pacifying the realms of existence and the fourfold means of attraction. // 8.34 //
[209] It is the settling upon affliction, upon the realization of purification, upon the true nature of the welfare of sentient beings, and upon the six perfections. // 8-35 //

[210] In the Buddha-path, in the emptiness that is intrinsic nature, in the cessation of duality, in conventional designation, in non-apprehension, and in the maturation of embodied beings; // 8-36 //
[211] Regarding the Bodhisattva’s path, the prevention of attachment, the attainment of enlightenment, and the certainty regarding the purification of the Buddha-field. 8-37.

[212] And regarding the immeasurable welfare of sentient beings, the qualities such as serving the Buddhas, the factors of enlightenment, the non-perishing of karmic actions, and the vision of the truths; // 8-38 //
[213] And regarding the abandonment of error, the principle of its lack of substantiality, purification, the accumulations, and with respect to the conditioned and the unconditioned; 8-39.
The non-perception of distinctions and the establishment in nirvāṇa—this is considered the twenty-sevenfold activity of the dharmakāya. (8-40)

The Blessed One creates those emanations which, by extinguishing the fires of hell for the denizens of hell and by teaching the Dharma, as well as by giving his own flesh, blood, and so forth to animals, and by giving food, drink, and so forth to hungry ghosts and by teaching the Dharma, cause their minds to become serene; and through that serenity, once they have passed away from their respective states of existence, he causes them to be reborn among gods and humans.

The activity of pacifying rebirth destinies consists in inspiring even those gods who are inclined toward the Lesser Vehicle through the teaching of the Dharma, and then establishing them— once they have been reborn among humans— in the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka or the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha.

The activity of introducing the means of integration (*saṅgrahavastu*) consists in training humans in the giving of material goods, both external and internal, as well as in the giving of the Dharma, mundane and supramundane, and in purposeful conduct and common purpose.
Defilement consists of the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration of the knowable;
purification is the cessation of these two.
And that [cessation] occurs through the knowledge of the selflessness of persons and phenomena—this is the conventional truth.
But since the ultimate truth is nothing other than the dharmadhātu, it is the activity of establishing the knowledge of affliction and purification.

For just as a magician, having conjured various objects—even things to be chewed and eaten—delights the world, and that world does not realize that all this is without substance; so too, one who courses in the perfection of wisdom perceives nothing whatsoever apart from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), neither a sentient being nor even the designation of a sentient being, because of the selflessness of all phenomena. This is the activity of establishing beings in the reality of their true nature.

He himself gives gifts and encourages others to give, speaks in praise of giving, and commends and approves of those others who give. In the same way, it should be stated that he himself maintains ethical discipline (*śīla*), and so forth; this is the activity of establishing [beings] in the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
One should say that he himself undertakes and abides by the ten paths of wholesome action;

he himself undertakes the five precepts, and so on, up to himself accomplishing the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics—this is called the activity of establishing others in the path of the Buddha.
In this regard, a bodhisattva teaches sentient beings all dharmas, such as the perfections;
he teaches them the natural emptiness of those [dharmas], their three limits, and their fruit.
Cultivating them in that manner, they attain distinction.
